card.back: Smoked oysters are blended into the Caesar emulsion in place of anchovy, briny and smoky. Flag it as shellfish on the ticket and check with the kitchen.

components.name: Grana Padano
components.explain:
Grana Padano is a hard cheese from the Po Valley of northern Italy, made from partly skimmed cow's milk and aged for at least nine months, usually longer. It has protected status, and its origin story credits Cistercian monks in the Middle Ages. Grana means grainy, for its crumbly, crystalline texture.

It is milder, younger and sweeter than Parmigiano Reggiano, and it melts smoothly.

We use it twice: shaved over the Creole Caesar and finishing the Shells & Cheese. A guest who asks whether it is Parmesan can be told it is its milder Po Valley cousin.

card.front: Is Grana Padano the same as Parmesan?
card.back: No: it is a milder, younger hard cheese from the Po Valley, grainy and nutty. It is on our Creole Caesar and finishes the Shells & Cheese.

components.name: The Eggs Hussarde name
components.explain:
Hussarde is French for hussar style, after the hussars, the light cavalry of Hungary. Eggs Hussarde is poached eggs on Canadian bacon over a toasted base, with marchand de vin beneath and hollandaise on top.

The dish is older than the restaurant: a recipe for poached eggs à la Hussarde was printed in 1895, credited to the chef Adolphe Gallier of the Hotel Brunswick in New York, and Escoffier gave a version in 1903. Brennan's made it famous from about 1950, and it became the house's signature egg dish.

So call it our signature and New Orleans' answer to Eggs Benedict, and never say it was invented here.

card.front: Was Eggs Hussarde invented at Brennan’s?
card.back: No: a poached eggs à la Hussarde recipe was printed in 1895, and Escoffier gave one. Brennan’s made it famous from about 1950; it is our signature.

components.name: Housemade English muffins
components.explain:
An English muffin is a flat, round yeasted bread cooked on a griddle rather than baked, dusted with cornmeal, and split with a fork so its holes and craggy surface catch butter and sauce.

The classic Brennan's Hussarde was built on Holland rusks, dry, crisp toasts; the restaurant now bakes its own English muffins, a change a returning guest may notice.

The muffin is the base that soaks up both sauces without falling apart. On the Eggs Hussarde the stack goes muffin, coffee-cured Canadian bacon, marchand de vin, poached egg and hollandaise. Saying the muffins are made in house is a small detail guests remember.

card.front: What base does the Eggs Hussarde sit on now?
card.back: Housemade English muffins, griddled and split so they catch both sauces; the old house build used Holland rusks, which returning guests may remember.

components.name: Coffee-cured Canadian bacon
components.explain:
Canadian bacon is cured, lightly smoked pork loin, lean and ham-like, sliced into rounds; it is the meat of Eggs Benedict. A coffee cure rubs the loin with salt, sugar and ground coffee before it is smoked or roasted, adding a roasty, slightly bitter depth to the sweet, salty pork.

The coffee echoes the city's chicory coffee and gives the lean meat more savour.

It is the meat layer of the Eggs Hussarde, between the English muffin and the marchand de vin. The guide confirms the coffee cure; how long it cures, and whether the kitchen makes it in house, are questions for the chef.

card.front: What is the meat on the Eggs Hussarde?
card.back: Coffee-cured Canadian bacon: lean cured pork loin rubbed with salt, sugar and ground coffee before smoking or roasting, roasty and sweet.

components.name: The Eggs Sardou name
components.explain:
Eggs Sardou was created at Antoine's and named in honour of the French playwright Victorien Sardou on a visit to New Orleans; sources disagree on the year. Antoine's original was poached eggs on artichoke bottoms with hollandaise, finished with ham, anchovy and truffle, with no spinach.

Most later versions dropped the ham, anchovy and truffle for creamed spinach, and the creamed spinach version is the one Brennan's made its own.

Our Sardou varies the house classic again: crispy artichokes, Parmesan creamed spinach, poached eggs and Choron sauce in place of hollandaise. Never present it as a Brennan's invention; it is Antoine's dish in the Brennan's style.

card.front: Where was Eggs Sardou created, and who is it named for?
card.back: At Antoine’s, named for the French playwright Victorien Sardou. Ours is the Brennan’s style: crispy artichokes, Parmesan creamed spinach and Choron.

components.name: Crispy artichokes
components.explain:
The artichoke is the flower bud of a thistle. Its heart and the fleshy base of its leaves are tender and nutty once trimmed and cooked; the classic Sardou sits the eggs on artichoke bottoms, the cup-shaped base of the heart.

Ours are crispy: trimmed hearts, cooked until tender and then coated and fried, so they bring crunch against the soft eggs and creamy spinach.

The guide notes that crispy artichokes are likely breaded or floured before frying and asks servers to check with the kitchen on any question about the coating. It is the texture guests notice first on our Eggs Sardou.

card.front: How are the artichokes on our Eggs Sardou cooked?
card.back: Trimmed hearts cooked tender, then coated and fried crisp for crunch against the eggs and spinach. Check the coating with the kitchen.

components.name: Creamed spinach
components.explain:
Creamed spinach is spinach blanched, plunged into iced water, squeezed hard and chopped, then bound with reduced cream or a light béchamel and finished with Parmesan and a little nutmeg. Squeezing out the water is the step that keeps it rich rather than watery.

It is a New Orleans and steakhouse classic, and the base of the Brennan's Eggs Sardou.

We serve Parmesan creamed spinach under the eggs on the Sardou and offer creamed spinach as a breakfast and lunch side. Whether the side and the Sardou's spinach are the same preparation is worth confirming with the kitchen before you say so.

card.front: How is creamed spinach made?
card.back: Spinach blanched, squeezed dry and chopped, bound with cream or light béchamel and finished with Parmesan and nutmeg; under our Sardou and as a side.

components.name: The Eggs Owen name
components.explain:
Eggs Owen shares its name with Owen Brennan, who founded the restaurant in 1946, and guests often guess it was named for him. The menu does not say so, and the restaurant has not published that story, so the guide's instruction stands: confirm at lineup before you tell it.

What can be said is how the plate relates to its neighbours. It takes the Hussarde's two sauces, hollandaise and marchand de vin, and replaces the Canadian bacon and muffin with red wine-braised short rib débris and a Creole-spiced potato, topped with a soft-boiled egg.

It is the heartier choice at $32 against the Hussarde at $27: steak and eggs, New Orleans style.

card.front: Is Eggs Owen named for Owen Brennan?
card.back: The menu does not say, and the house has not published it: confirm at lineup before telling that story. It is the Hussarde’s sauces over short rib débris.

components.name: Short rib débris
components.explain:
Débris is Louisiana French for scraps, and in New Orleans it means the shreds of meat that fall into the gravy as a roast cooks and is carved. Mother's Restaurant on Poydras Street, opened in 1938, made the word famous with its debris roast beef po-boy.

Ours is short rib braised slowly in red wine until it falls apart, then pulled into its own reduced braising liquid: the same idea, richer.

On the Eggs Owen it replaces the Hussarde's Canadian bacon, under hollandaise and marchand de vin. Say DAY-bree, the local way, and describe it as slow-cooked beef that falls apart into its own gravy.

card.front: What does débris mean on the Eggs Owen?
card.back: Louisiana French for scraps: meat that falls into its gravy, made famous by Mother’s. Ours is red wine-braised short rib, pulled into its own sauce.

components.name: Braising in red wine
components.explain:
Braising cooks a tough, well-worked cut slowly in a little liquid in a covered pot, so its connective tissue melts into gelatin. Short rib is ideal: marbled, sinewy and full of flavour.

The ribs are seared hard for colour, the vegetables sweated, the pan deglazed with red wine and reduced, then stock added; the pot goes into a low oven for about three hours, until a fork turns the meat. The liquid is skimmed and reduced into a glossy sauce, and the meat is pulled back into it.

That is the short rib débris on the Eggs Owen: meltingly tender beef in a deep, winey gravy, which echoes the marchand de vin on the same plate.

card.front: Why is short rib braised rather than grilled?
card.back: It is tough and sinewy; slow, covered cooking in red wine and stock melts its connective tissue into gelatin, giving tender meat and a glossy sauce.

components.name: Confit
components.explain:
Confit comes from the French confire, to preserve, and it is the larder technique of Gascony in south-western France. Duck legs are rubbed with salt, garlic and herbs and left for up to a day and a half, rinsed, then cooked slowly submerged in duck fat at a bare tremble for hours, and stored under the fat.

To serve, the leg is crisped skin-side down, so the skin shatters and the meat pulls from the bone.

On the Duck Confit Waffle the Rohan duck leg is confit. The menu idiom says cooked in its own fat; kitchens use pooled duck fat, so describe the method in general and promise no house times.

card.front: What does confit mean?
card.back: From confire, to preserve: salted duck legs cooked slowly submerged in duck fat until tender, then crisped. Our Rohan duck leg on the waffle is confit.

components.name: Cornbread and chive waffle
components.explain:
A cornbread waffle uses a cornmeal batter, the Southern skillet cornbread, cooked in a waffle iron so it gets a crisp, deep-pocketed crust and a tender centre. Chives make it savoury rather than sweet.

The pockets catch sauce and syrup, which is the point.

On the Duck Confit Waffle it is the base under the Rohan duck leg, with foie gras butter, mustard maple syrup and a sunny-side-up egg: chicken and waffles made luxurious. The guide notes the waffle likely contains wheat flour as well as cornmeal, so check with the kitchen for any guest who asks.

card.front: What kind of waffle is on the Duck Confit Waffle?
card.back: A savoury cornbread and chive waffle, cornmeal batter crisp in the iron with pockets for the foie gras butter and mustard maple syrup.

components.name: Foie gras butter
components.explain:
Foie gras is the fattened liver of a duck or goose, a French delicacy of the south-west with a rich, silky, buttery texture. Foie gras butter is foie gras puréed into soft butter, so a spoonful melts over hot food and spreads its richness through it.

It is a luxurious touch in small amounts rather than a main ingredient.

On the Duck Confit Waffle it melts into the cornbread waffle's pockets with the mustard maple syrup. Some guests avoid foie gras by choice; the guide asks you to check with the kitchen whether it can be left off before you promise it.

card.front: Can the foie gras butter come off the Duck Confit Waffle?
card.back: Ask the kitchen first. Foie gras butter is fattened duck or goose liver puréed into soft butter, melting into the waffle’s pockets.

components.name: Mustard maple syrup
components.explain:
Maple syrup is the sap of the sugar maple boiled down, with a woody caramel sweetness. Sharpened with mustard, Dijon or whole-grain, it becomes sweet, tangy and gently hot, the same balance a honey mustard strikes.

The mustard keeps the syrup from tasting like dessert, so it works with savoury, fatty meat.

On the Duck Confit Waffle it ties the plate together: sweet against the salty, crisp duck, sharp against the foie gras butter and the egg yolk. It is the savoury-sweet note the guide's description promises, so name it when you describe the dish.

card.front: What is the syrup on the Duck Confit Waffle?
card.back: Mustard maple syrup: maple sharpened with mustard, sweet and tangy, cutting the rich duck, foie gras butter and egg yolk.

components.name: Shrimp and grits
components.explain:
Shrimp and grits began as a breakfast for shrimpers in the South Carolina Lowcountry: fresh shrimp cooked in bacon fat over hominy grits. Charleston recipes for it were printed by 1930, and it went national in 1985, when Craig Claiborne published Bill Neal's version from Crook's Corner in Chapel Hill, with cheese and bacon, in The New York Times.

Charleston's dish uses a bacon and lemon pan gravy. Ours is Creole instead.

Our New Orleans Shrimp & Grits is Louisiana shrimp with a fried pimento cheese grit cake, a tomato Creole sauce seasoned with tasso, and fried okra chips. That tomato and tasso is the difference to name.

card.front: How does our Shrimp & Grits differ from the Charleston dish?
card.back: Charleston’s is shrimp in a bacon and lemon gravy over grits. Ours is Creole: a tomato Creole sauce with tasso over a fried pimento cheese grit cake.

components.name: The omelette
components.explain:
An omelette is beaten eggs cooked quickly in a hot buttered pan. The French omelette is stirred as it sets, then rolled into a smooth, pale cylinder with a soft, creamy centre and barely any colour. The American omelette is set flat, filled, and folded in half, firmer and lightly golden.

Either way the filling goes in warm, so the eggs are not overcooked waiting for it.

Our Crab & Corn Omelette is filled with Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn, with miso butter, lemon, basil and a Marcona almond gremolata. Which style the kitchen makes is a fair question to ask at lineup, so you can describe it before it lands.

card.front: What is the difference between a French and an American omelette?
card.back: A French omelette is stirred and rolled, pale and creamy inside; an American one is set flat, filled and folded, firmer and golden. Ask which ours is.

components.name: Roasted sweet corn
components.explain:
Sweet corn is corn picked young, while its kernels are still full of sugar and milky juice. Roasting it, on the cob or in the pan, caramelises some of that sugar and adds a toasty, slightly smoky note.

Corn and crab are a summer pairing all along the Gulf and the Atlantic coast, both naturally sweet.

In the Crab & Corn Omelette the roasted kernels add pops of sweetness and a little chew against the soft eggs and lump crab. Whether the corn is roasted on the cob, and whether it changes with the season, are good questions for the chef.

card.front: Why do crab and corn go together in our omelette?
card.back: Both are naturally sweet summer foods of the coast; roasting the corn adds a toasty note and chew against the soft eggs and lump crab.

components.name: House-made miso butter
components.explain:
Miso is a Japanese paste of soybeans fermented with salt and koji, a mould grown on rice or barley. White miso is mild and sweet; darker misos are saltier and stronger. Beaten into soft butter, it makes a compound butter that is salty, nutty and deeply savoury.

It brings umami, the savoury depth of aged cheese and cured ham, without tasting obviously Japanese.

On the Crab & Corn Omelette the house-made miso butter rounds out the sweet crab and corn. The guide names soy from the miso on this dish, so send dietary questions to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: What is miso butter?
card.back: Miso, a fermented soybean paste, beaten into soft butter: salty, nutty and savoury. It rounds out the sweet crab and corn on our omelette.

components.name: Marcona almonds
components.explain:
Marcona is a Spanish almond variety, shorter, rounder, softer and sweeter than the Californian almonds most guests know. In Spain they are blanched to remove the skin, fried in oil and salted, which makes them rich and tender with a gentle crunch.

They are one of the luxury snacks of Spain, eaten with sherry and cheese.

We use them twice: in the gremolata on the Crab & Corn Omelette, and with the sorghum, crab and olives in the Gulf Fish en Papillote, where they add a nutty crunch. Nut questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: What is a Marcona almond?
card.back: A round, sweet, tender Spanish almond, usually blanched, fried in oil and salted. In the omelette’s gremolata and the en papillote.

components.name: Gremolata
components.explain:
Gremolata is the Milanese finish for osso buco: finely chopped parsley, garlic and lemon zest, scattered over a rich braise at the last moment so its sharp, fresh perfume wakes the dish up.

Modern kitchens vary it with other herbs, citrus and nuts, keeping the idea of a bright, raw topping.

On the Crab & Corn Omelette it is a Marcona almond gremolata, with basil and lemon on the plate as well, so it adds crunch as well as freshness against the buttery eggs. Describe it as a crunchy herb, citrus and almond topping.

card.front: What is a gremolata?
card.back: The Milanese parsley, garlic and lemon zest finish for osso buco. Ours adds Marcona almonds for crunch on the Crab & Corn Omelette.

components.name: Cauliflower, puréed and smoked
components.explain:
Cauliflower is a brassica whose tight white head is mild and nutty, and it changes completely with the cooking. Simmered in milk and cream and blended, it becomes a velvety purée, lighter than potato. Roasted or smoked, it browns, sweetens and takes on a meaty depth.

Smoking it after blanching or roasting lets it absorb smoke without turning soft.

We use it both ways: a cauliflower purée under the Pecan Gulf Fish, and the Smoked Cauliflower side at dinner with preserved lemon and harissa. Whether the side is cooked with butter or oil is a question for the kitchen for any guest who asks.

card.front: How do we serve cauliflower?
card.back: Two ways: a velvety purée under the Pecan Gulf Fish, and smoked as a dinner side with preserved lemon and harissa.

components.name: Creekstone Farms beef
components.explain:
Creekstone Farms is a Black Angus beef producer. John and Carol Stewart founded it in 1995 as a purebred Black Angus farm in Kentucky, and since 2003 it has processed its beef at a plant in Arkansas City, Kansas. Its beef is graded USDA Prime and Choice.

A Prime grade marks the most marbled beef, which is richer and more tender when cooked.

The menu names Creekstone on all three of its beef dishes: the Prime hanger at breakfast and lunch, the dinner hanger, and the tenderloin for the Roasted Chateaubriand. Say Black Angus from a Kansas producer, and Prime where the menu says so.

card.front: What is Creekstone Farms?
card.back: A Black Angus beef producer founded in 1995, processing in Arkansas City, Kansas. It supplies our hangers and the Chateaubriand tenderloin.

components.name: Hanger steak
components.explain:
The hanger steak, onglet in France, hangs from the diaphragm near the kidneys. There is only one per animal, which is why butchers used to keep it for themselves and why it was long called the butcher's steak. A tough sinew runs down its centre and is cut out, leaving two loose-grained lobes.

It is intensely beefy and best cooked hot and fast to medium-rare or medium, rested, and sliced across the grain; past medium it tightens and tastes of liver.

We serve two: the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak at breakfast and lunch with béarnaise and an egg, and the Creole Hanger Steak at dinner with chilli crisp. Always take the temperature.

card.front: How should a hanger steak be cooked, and why?
card.back: Hot and fast to medium-rare or medium, sliced across the grain; past medium it tightens and tastes of liver. One per animal, the butcher’s steak.

components.name: Vital Farms egg
components.explain:
Vital Farms began in 2007 near Austin, Texas, with twenty hens, and now works with hundreds of family farms. Its eggs are pasture-raised, which means each hen has at least 108 square feet of outdoor space on rotated pasture.

Hens that forage outdoors often lay eggs with deep orange yolks, and a sunny-side-up egg shows that colour off.

The menu names Vital Farms on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, where a sunny-side-up egg sits beside the steak and the smoked potato pavé, and the Fall 2026 sheet names its egg yolk on the Steak Tartare with Rye. A one-line guest answer is: pasture-raised eggs, every hen with over a hundred square feet of grass.

card.front: What does pasture-raised mean for our Vital Farms egg?
card.back: Each hen has at least 108 square feet of rotated outdoor pasture; Vital Farms began near Austin in 2007. The egg sits on our breakfast hanger, and the yolk on the fall Steak Tartare with Rye.

sources: page:brennans-fall-2026-training-sheets-2026-10-15.txt lines 4-15 (Steak Tartare with Rye: Vital Farms Egg Yolk)

components.name: Smoked potato pavé
components.explain:
Pavé is French for paving stone, after its neat rectangular shape. Potatoes are sliced paper-thin on a mandoline, layered with cream and butter in a lined tin, baked until tender, then pressed under a weight overnight and chilled. The block is cut into bricks and seared until each face is crisp, so you see dozens of fine layers.

It takes a day to make and seconds to finish, which is why kitchens love it.

On the breakfast hanger it is a smoked potato pavé. Whether the smoke is in the cream, the butter or the finished block is the kitchen's detail, so say it has a smoky note and leave the method to the chef.

card.front: What is a potato pavé?
card.back: Thin potato slices layered with cream and butter, baked, pressed overnight, cut into bricks and seared crisp: dozens of fine layers. Ours is smoked.

components.name: Chateaubriand
components.explain:
Chateaubriand is the thick centre cut of the beef tenderloin, roasted or grilled whole and carved for two. The name is said to come from a chef called Montmireil, who around 1822 cooked it for the writer and diplomat François-René, Vicomte de Chateaubriand, traditionally between two lesser steaks that were thrown away. Escoffier later fixed the name to the cut itself.

Tenderloin is the tenderest and mildest muscle on the animal, so a rich sauce does the flavour's work.

Our Roasted Chateaubriand is Creekstone Farms tenderloin with glazed summer squash and sauce Foyot, served for two at $120. A whole roast takes time: tell the table when you take the order.

card.front: What is a Chateaubriand?
card.back: The thick centre cut of the tenderloin, roasted whole for two; said to be named for the Vicomte de Chateaubriand, whose chef cooked it around 1822.

components.name: Roasted and glazed summer squash
components.explain:
Summer squash are the tender, thin-skinned squashes picked young, zucchini, yellow squash and pattypan among them, eaten skin and seeds and all. They are mild and sweet, and roasting browns their edges and concentrates them.

A glaze, usually butter with a little stock, honey or reduced juice, gives them a gloss and a touch of sweetness.

On the Roasted Chateaubriand they are the light, seasonal vegetable beside a rich roast and sauce Foyot. They change with the market, so expect a different vegetable when the season turns; the guide suggests Maggie's Mushrooms or Shells & Cheese as add-on sides for the table.

card.front: What vegetable comes with the Roasted Chateaubriand?
card.back: Roasted and glazed summer squash, tender young squash browned and glossed; a light seasonal partner to the rich roast and sauce Foyot.

components.name: Véronique
components.explain:
À la Véronique means served with grapes. The classic is Sole Véronique, traditionally credited to Auguste Escoffier at the Carlton in London and named for André Messager's comic opera Véronique: poached sole in a creamy sauce with peeled green muscat grapes, glazed under the grill.

Dates and the chef's name vary between tellings, so frame it as a story.

Our Redfish Véronique makes three changes: Gulf redfish for sole, a preserved lemon beurre blanc for the creamy sauce, and grapes pickled in hibiscus instead of fresh. It is also the third course of the dinner tasting, with a red Burgundy pour.

card.front: What does Véronique mean on a menu?
card.back: With grapes, after Sole Véronique, credited to Escoffier and named for an opera. Ours is redfish, hibiscus-pickled grapes and preserved lemon beurre blanc.

components.name: Hibiscus-pickled grapes
components.explain:
Pickled grapes are grapes steeped in a sweet and sour brine of vinegar, sugar and spice, which keeps their crunch and sweetness but gives them a sharp edge. Hibiscus, the dried flower behind many red teas, adds a ruby colour and a tart, cranberry-like note.

The result is sweet, tart and floral, a bright counterpoint to rich fish and butter.

On the Redfish Véronique they stand in for the fresh muscat grapes of the French classic. If a guest is wary of fruit with fish, describe them as more like a sharp relish than a sweet fruit garnish.

card.front: What are the grapes on the Redfish Véronique?
card.back: Grapes pickled in a sweet and sour brine with hibiscus: ruby, tart and floral, a sharp relish against the fish and beurre blanc.

components.name: Preserved lemon
components.explain:
Preserved lemons are a North African staple: lemons cut, packed in salt and their own juice, and left for weeks until the rind turns soft, silky and edible. The sharp bitterness mellows into a salty, floral, almost perfumed lemon flavour.

Cooks use the rind, finely chopped, more than the flesh.

We use it twice at dinner: in the preserved lemon beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique, and with harissa on the Smoked Cauliflower. Describe it to a guest as lemon cured in salt, salty and perfumed rather than sour.

card.front: What is preserved lemon?
card.back: Lemon cured in salt and its own juice for weeks until the rind is soft: salty and perfumed. In the Véronique’s beurre blanc and on the Smoked Cauliflower.

components.name: Braised leeks and fingerling potatoes
components.explain:
Leeks are the mild, sweet member of the onion family. Braised slowly in butter and stock, they turn soft and silky, almost creamy, with none of an onion's bite.

Fingerling potatoes are small, finger-shaped waxy potatoes with thin skins; they hold their shape when cooked and taste buttery and slightly nutty.

Together on the Redfish Véronique they form the gentle base under the fish, with the hibiscus-pickled grapes and preserved lemon beurre blanc providing the brightness. They are the quiet, comforting part of the plate, which is worth saying to a guest who finds the grapes unusual.

card.front: What else is on the Redfish Véronique plate?
card.back: Braised leeks, soft and sweet, and fingerling potatoes, small waxy potatoes; the gentle base under the redfish, grapes and beurre blanc.

components.name: En papillote
components.explain:
En papillote means in paper: food sealed in a parcel and baked, so it steams in its own juices and the aromas stay trapped until the parcel is opened. New Orleans knows it from Antoine's, where Jules Alciatore created pompano en papillote for a banquet honouring the Brazilian balloonist Alberto Santos-Dumont; the puffed paper suggested a balloon.

Our Gulf Fish en Papillote wraps the fish in banana leaf instead of paper. The leaf holds moisture just as well and adds a faint grassy, tea-like aroma.

Ask at lineup whether it is opened at the table, and warn the guest to mind the steam when it is.

card.front: What does en papillote mean, and what is ours wrapped in?
card.back: In paper: sealed and baked so it steams in its own juices, made famous here by Antoine’s pompano. Ours is wrapped in banana leaf. Mind the steam.

components.name: Castelvetrano olives
components.explain:
Castelvetrano olives are the Nocellara del Belice variety from the Valle del Belice in western Sicily, named for the nearby town. They are picked young and cured briefly in lye, which removes bitterness quickly and keeps them a vivid bright green.

They are buttery, mild and almost sweet, with a crisp, meaty bite, the olive people who dislike olives often enjoy.

In the Gulf Fish en Papillote they cook with tomato, Louisiana crab, sorghum and Marcona almonds, giving the dish its bright, Mediterranean character. Warn guests that olives may come with stones unless the kitchen confirms they are pitted.

card.front: What are Castelvetrano olives?
card.back: Bright green Sicilian olives of the Nocellara del Belice variety, lye-cured so they are buttery, mild and crisp. In our Gulf Fish en Papillote.

components.name: Sorghum
components.explain:
Sorghum is a cereal grass first grown in Africa and now farmed around the world, including across the American South, where its cane is also pressed for sorghum syrup. The whole grain is round and chewy, cooked like farro or barley, with a mild, nutty taste.

It holds its bite in liquid, so it soaks up juices without turning mushy.

In the Gulf Fish en Papillote the grain cooks inside the banana leaf with the fish, drinking up the tomato and crab juices. The guide notes that sorghum itself has no wheat but asks you to confirm the whole dish with the kitchen.

card.front: What is the grain in the Gulf Fish en Papillote?
card.back: Sorghum, an African cereal grain cooked like farro: round, chewy and nutty, soaking up the tomato and crab juices inside the banana leaf.

components.name: Poussin and the Cornish hen
components.explain:
Poussin is French for a very young chicken. In Britain it means a bird under 28 days old, about a pound. The American equivalent is the Rock Cornish game hen, defined by the USDA as an immature chicken under five weeks and no more than 2 pounds: a little older and larger than a British poussin, and the nearest thing on an American menu.

Young birds are tender and mild, with a high ratio of crisp skin to meat.

Our menu says Poussin à la Moutarde and names the Cornish hen in the description, so there is no sleight of hand. It is a whole small bird and may have bones; say so to the guest.

card.front: What is a poussin, and what bird do we use?
card.back: French for a very young chicken; the menu names a Cornish hen, the American equivalent under five weeks and 2 pounds. A whole small bird, may have bones.

components.name: Sweet tea brine and frying
components.explain:
A brine is salted water that a bird soaks in before cooking; the salt seasons the meat throughout and helps it hold its juices. A sweet tea brine is a Southern fried chicken trick: strong black tea, sugar and salt. The tea's tannin and the sugar help the skin brown deeply, and the tea adds a faint, malty note.

After brining the bird is dried, coated and fried until the skin is crisp and the meat juicy.

On the Poussin à la Moutarde the sweet tea-brined Cornish hen is fried, then sauced with mustard cream, with turnips and shallots. How long it brines is a good question for the chef.

card.front: What does the sweet tea brine do for the poussin?
card.back: Salt seasons the bird and keeps it juicy; tea tannin and sugar help the skin brown deeply. A Southern fried chicken trick before frying.

components.name: Tien Dat tofu
components.explain:
Tofu is soybean milk curdled and pressed into blocks, as cheese is made from milk. Extra-firm tofu is pressed hardest, so it holds its shape in a hot pan and takes a crust.

Tien Dat is a local maker registered on the West Bank, in Marrero, across the river from the city. Its tofu is sold through the VEGGI Farmers Cooperative, the member-owned co-op of Village de L'Est, the Vietnamese American community of New Orleans East, at the Crescent City Farmers Market.

Our menu names New Orleans Tien Dat tofu on the Blackened Tofu. Say it is made fresh across the river by a local Vietnamese maker; anything more, ask the kitchen.

card.front: Where does the tofu on the Blackened Tofu come from?
card.back: Tien Dat, a local maker on the West Bank whose extra-firm tofu is sold through VEGGI, the Vietnamese American co-op of New Orleans East.

components.name: Two Brooks Farm rice grits
components.explain:
Rice grits are broken grains of rice, the pieces that crack during milling, cooked slowly into a creamy porridge like corn grits but silkier. Two Brooks Farm in Sumner, Mississippi, in the Delta, started by Mike Wagner in 1992 and run with his children, grows rice and sells rice grits and flours among its products; ducks and geese winter on its flooded fields.

The farm is in Mississippi, not Louisiana, a detail guests sometimes test.

Under the Blackened Tofu the rice grits are the soft, creamy base for the spiced crust and the preserved shiitakes. Whether they are cooked with stock is a question for the kitchen.

card.front: What are rice grits, and where do ours come from?
card.back: Broken rice grains cooked creamy like grits; ours are from Two Brooks Farm in Sumner, in the Mississippi Delta, not Louisiana.

components.name: Preserved shiitake mushrooms
components.explain:
Shiitake are mushrooms long cultivated on logs in Japan and China; the name joins shii, the tree they grew on, with take, mushroom. They are meaty and deeply savoury, rich in the natural compounds that give umami.

Preserved shiitake are most likely cured in soy or pickled, which concentrates that savoury depth; what the kitchen means by preserved is a question for the chef.

On the Blackened Tofu they bring the earthy, meaty note that makes the plate satisfying without meat, against the spiced crust and creamy rice grits. Say shee-TAH-kee.

card.front: What do the preserved shiitakes add to the Blackened Tofu?
card.back: Deep, meaty, savoury umami against the spiced crust and creamy rice grits. How the kitchen preserves them is a question for the chef.

components.name: Madeira-glazed broccolini
components.explain:
Broccolini is a cross of broccoli and Chinese kale: long, tender stems with small florets, sweeter and milder than broccoli. Madeira is the fortified wine of the Portuguese island of Madeira, deliberately heated as it ages, so it tastes of caramel, toffee and walnut with a sharp acidity.

A Madeira glaze is the wine reduced with butter or stock until syrupy, sweet and savoury at once.

On the dinner Creole Hanger Steak the glazed broccolini brings a sweet, nutty counterweight to the Creole spice and chilli crisp. Guests who avoid alcohol should know the glaze is made with wine.

card.front: What is the glaze on the Creole Hanger Steak’s broccolini?
card.back: Madeira, the heated, aged Portuguese fortified wine tasting of caramel and walnut, reduced to a sweet, savoury glaze on tender broccolini.

components.name: Pepita persillade
components.explain:
Persillade is a French finishing mix of finely chopped parsley and garlic, thrown over a dish at the last second so its fresh, sharp perfume hits the table. Pepita is Mexican Spanish for the hulled green pumpkin seed, toasted until it puffs and turns nutty.

Together they make a crunchy, garlicky, green topping.

On the Creole Hanger Steak the pepita persillade sits with a chilli crisp and Madeira-glazed broccolini: a French garnish, a Mexican seed and a Chinese condiment on a Creole-spiced steak. That mix of traditions is the modern Brennan's style and worth saying at the table.

card.front: What is a pepita persillade?
card.back: Persillade is chopped parsley and garlic; pepitas are toasted pumpkin seeds. Together a crunchy, garlicky topping on the dinner Creole Hanger Steak.

components.name: Chilli crisp
components.explain:
Chilli crisp is a Chinese condiment from Guizhou: dried chilli flakes fried slowly in oil with garlic and shallot, often with roasted beans and seeds, until crunchy. Lao Gan Ma made it famous around the world. It is a sauce you can chew, savoury, crunchy and hot.

It brings real heat, more than anything else on the dinner menu.

On the Creole Hanger Steak it gives heat and crunch with the pepita persillade. The guide asks you to warn spice-shy guests and to offer it on the side if the kitchen agrees; questions about soy or sesame in it go to the kitchen.

card.front: What is chilli crisp, and how hot is it?
card.back: A Chinese condiment of chilli fried crisp in oil with garlic: crunchy, savoury and genuinely hot. Warn spice-shy guests; ask the kitchen about serving it on the side.

components.name: Sautéing fish
components.explain:
Sautéing cooks food quickly in a little hot fat in a wide pan. For a fish fillet, the pan and fat are hot before it goes in, often skin or presentation side first; it is left alone to colour, then turned once and finished gently so it stays moist and flakes at the touch. Many kitchens dust the fillet with flour first, the meunière way, for a golden crust.

Thin, delicate fish cook in two or three minutes; thicker fillets are finished in the oven.

The children's Sautéed Gulf Fish is cooked this way, and the Pecan Gulf Fish is likely pan-roasted or sautéed to order. Know today's fish and its preparation at lineup.

card.front: How is a fish fillet sautéed?
card.back: In a little hot fat in a wide pan, presentation side first, left to colour, turned once and finished gently so it stays moist. Know tonight’s fish.

items: Sautéed Gulf Fish with Potato and Green Beans

components.name: Housemade pork sausage
components.explain:
Southern breakfast sausage is fresh, not cured or smoked: coarsely ground pork shoulder with a good share of fat, seasoned with salt, black pepper and sage, often with red pepper flakes and a little brown sugar. Formed into patties, it is pan-fried until browned and crusty outside and juicy within.

Making it in house lets the kitchen set its own seasoning and grind.

Our Housemade Pork Sausage Patty is a $9 breakfast side, a savoury partner to eggs, biscuits and grits. The spice list, and whether anything binds the meat, are questions for the kitchen if a guest asks.

card.front: What is in a Southern breakfast sausage patty?
card.back: Fresh, coarsely ground pork shoulder and fat seasoned with salt, pepper and sage, often red pepper; pan-fried crusty. Ours is made in house.

components.name: Thick-cut bacon
components.explain:
Bacon is pork belly cured with salt and usually smoked. Thick-cut slices are roughly twice the usual thickness, so they stay meaty in the middle while the edges crisp. They want a low, slow render, so the fat turns glassy and golden before the edges burn.

American bacon comes from the belly, streaky with fat, unlike the leaner back bacon of Britain.

Thick-cut bacon is a $9 breakfast side, comes with the children's eggs, and is on the Roost Burger. The breakfast menu names no brand; Nueske's appears only on the dinner succotash, so ask before saying the breakfast bacon is Nueske's.

card.front: What makes thick-cut bacon different?
card.back: Slices about twice the usual thickness, rendered slowly so they stay meaty in the middle and crisp at the edges. No brand is printed for the breakfast side.

items: Eggs Any Style with Toast and Bacon

components.name: Buttermilk biscuit
components.explain:
A Southern biscuit is a quick bread: soft wheat flour, cold butter or lard rubbed in, and buttermilk, whose acid reacts with baking soda to make it rise. The dough is folded a few times to build flaky layers, cut and baked in a very hot oven.

Cold fat makes the layers; overworking the dough makes it tough.

Our Buttermilk Biscuit is a $5 breakfast side, tender and flaky with a gentle tang. The guide suggests it for mopping up the hollandaise or marchand de vin on the egg dishes, which is the easiest way to sell it.

card.front: How do you sell the $5 Buttermilk Biscuit?
card.back: As the thing for mopping up the hollandaise or marchand de vin: a flaky Southern quick bread, cold butter and buttermilk, baked hot.

components.name: Brabant potatoes
components.explain:
Brabant potatoes are a New Orleans classic: potatoes cut into cubes, blanched or par-fried, then fried until golden and crisp and tossed in butter with garlic and parsley. They are sometimes called Louisiana fries and appear on the menus of the old Creole houses, Galatoire's and Antoine's among them.

The name is usually linked to the Brabant region of Belgium and the Netherlands, though no one has proved the connection.

We serve them as a breakfast side and with two children's breakfast plates. The French say bra-BAHN; many locals say bruh-BANT. Confirm the house finish and fryer at lineup.

card.front: What are Brabant potatoes?
card.back: A New Orleans side: cubed potatoes fried golden and tossed in butter, garlic and parsley, sometimes called Louisiana fries. Say bra-BAHN or bruh-BANT.

items: Grilled Cheese Sandwich with Brabant Potatoes

components.name: Succotash
components.explain:
Succotash is a Native American dish, older than any European kitchen in America. Its name comes from the Narragansett word msickquatash, boiled corn kernels, and the corn and beans at its heart were eaten in the north-east long before colonists arrived. The South adopted it later, with butter beans, corn and often pork.

So it is fair to call it a dish the South made its own, but not one the South invented.

Ours is a seasonal dinner side at $12: glazed summer vegetables with Nueske's applewood-smoked bacon. The vegetables change with the market, so learn tonight's mix at lineup.

card.front: Where does succotash come from?
card.back: A Native American corn and bean dish; the name is from the Narragansett msickquatash, boiled corn. Ours is glazed summer vegetables with Nueske’s bacon.

components.name: Nueske’s bacon
components.explain:
Nueske's is a family smokehouse in Wittenberg, Wisconsin. R.C. Nueske began selling the family's smoked hams, sausages and bacon in 1933, from recipes the family brought when it emigrated, driving them to the resorts of northern Wisconsin. The company is known above all for its applewood-smoked bacon, smoked over applewood for about 24 hours.

Applewood gives a sweet, rich, mellow smoke rather than the sharpness of hickory.

The menu names Nueske's on the dinner Succotash, where the bacon brings smoke and salt to the sweet glazed vegetables. The pronunciation is contested; NOO-skeez is common, so follow the house.

card.front: What is Nueske’s?
card.back: A Wisconsin family smokehouse since 1933, famous for bacon smoked over applewood for about 24 hours: sweet, mellow smoke. On our Succotash.

components.name: Harissa
components.explain:
Harissa is a North African chilli paste, most closely tied to Tunisia: dried red chillies soaked and pounded with garlic, olive oil and spices such as caraway, coriander and cumin. It is earthy and warm rather than sharp, with a slow heat.

Stirred into oil or yoghurt it becomes a sauce; brushed on vegetables it roasts into a crust.

On the Smoked Cauliflower it partners preserved lemon, salt and perfume against the paste's warmth and the smoke of the cauliflower. The guide gives it moderate heat; warn guests who are shy of spice.

card.front: What is harissa?
card.back: A North African, especially Tunisian, paste of dried chilli, garlic, oil, caraway, coriander and cumin: earthy, moderate heat. On our Smoked Cauliflower.

components.name: Smoking
components.explain:
Smoking flavours food with the smoke of smouldering wood. Hot smoking cooks and flavours together, as with bacon, tasso and andouille; cold smoking, below cooking temperature, flavours without cooking, as with smoked salmon or a smoked liquid. Different woods give different smoke: applewood sweet, hickory strong, pecan mellow.

A light touch of smoke adds savoury depth; too much tastes acrid.

On our menus smoke turns up in many forms: the Smoked Cauliflower, the smoked tomato water on the tostada, the smoked potato pavé, the smoked oyster dressing on the Caesar, and the smoked meats, andouille, tasso and Nueske's bacon.

card.front: What is the difference between hot and cold smoking?
card.back: Hot smoking cooks and flavours at once, like bacon and andouille; cold smoking flavours without cooking, like a smoked liquid or salmon.

components.name: Mimolette
components.explain:
Mimolette is a round, bright orange cheese from Lille and French Flanders. The story goes that Louis XIV's minister Colbert, at odds with the Dutch, wanted a French cheese to replace Edam; the orange colour, from annatto, set it apart. As it ages it turns hard, nutty, sweet and butterscotch-like.

Tiny cheese mites are encouraged on its rind, where they help it age and give the rind its pitted, moon-like look.

In the Shells & Cheese it is melted into a fondue with Abita Amber beer and finished with Grana Padano. Some guests love the mite story and some do not; read the table.

card.front: What is Mimolette?
card.back: A bright orange French cheese from Lille, said to be made to rival Dutch Edam; aged, it is nutty and butterscotch-sweet. Melted into our Shells & Cheese.

components.name: Abita Amber
components.explain:
Abita Brewing was founded in 1986 in Abita Springs, Louisiana, across Lake Pontchartrain from the city, by Jim Patton and Rush Cumming. Amber was its first beer and remains its flagship: a Munich-style lager of pale and caramel malts with German Perle hops, smooth, malty and lightly caramel.

A malty, low-bitterness beer is the right choice for cooking with cheese, because hops turn bitter as a sauce reduces.

In the Shells & Cheese it loosens the Mimolette fondue and adds a malty depth. The guide notes the beer's alcohol is mostly but not entirely cooked off, so tell guests who avoid alcohol.

card.front: Why is Abita Amber in the Shells & Cheese?
card.back: A malty, low-bitterness Louisiana lager, Abita’s first beer since 1986; it loosens the Mimolette fondue without turning bitter. Tell guests who avoid alcohol.

components.name: Beer cheese fondue
components.explain:
A fondue, from the French fondre, to melt, is cheese melted smoothly with a liquid, classically white wine in the Swiss pot. A beer cheese sauce uses beer instead, and a dry, aged cheese needs that liquid, and often a little starch, to melt smooth rather than turning stringy or oily.

Heat must stay gentle: boiled cheese splits.

Our Shells & Cheese folds pasta shells into a fondue of Mimolette and Abita Amber, finished with Grana Padano: rich, nutty and malty with a salty finish. It is a grown-up macaroni cheese, and an easy side to add to a steak for the table at $12.

card.front: What is the sauce in the Shells & Cheese?
card.back: A beer cheese fondue: Mimolette melted gently with Abita Amber, finished with Grana Padano, a rich, nutty, malty grown-up macaroni cheese.

components.name: Maggie’s Mushrooms
components.explain:
The menu prints Maggie's Mushrooms with no description. The likely source is Mushroom Maggie's Farm in St Francisville, Louisiana, upriver from Baton Rouge, a family farm run by Maggie Long and Cyrus Lester that grows lion's mane, oyster, pink trumpet, shiitake and chestnut mushrooms for restaurants in Baton Rouge and New Orleans.

The house has not confirmed that link, so confirm it with the chef before you tell it.

Learn three things at lineup: tonight's varieties, how they are cooked, and whether the dish uses butter or stock. It is a $12 dinner side the guide suggests beside the Chateaubriand.

card.front: What should you learn about Maggie’s Mushrooms at lineup?
card.back: Tonight’s varieties, how they are cooked, butter or stock, and whether they come from Mushroom Maggie’s Farm in St Francisville; confirm with the chef.

components.name: South Louisiana rice dressing
components.explain:
Rice dressing is a south Louisiana staple: cooked rice folded into a savoury mix of ground meat browned with the holy trinity, garlic and seasoning, often with a little roux or gravy. It is the rice equivalent of a bread stuffing, which is why it is called dressing, and it appears on Sunday and holiday tables.

Its close cousin is dirty rice, and the line between them depends on who you ask: some say dressing is ground beef and pork and dirty rice carries chicken livers and gizzards, others say the reverse.

Ours is a $12 dinner side with no description printed, so confirm the meats with the kitchen before describing it.

card.front: How does rice dressing differ from dirty rice?
card.back: Both are rice with ground meat and the trinity; which carries livers depends on who you ask. Confirm the meats in ours with the kitchen.

components.name: The breakfast and lunch sides
components.explain:
Breakfast and lunch carries seven sides, each priced on its own: the Housemade Pork Sausage Patty and Thick-Cut Bacon at $9, the Buttermilk Biscuit at $5, an Egg Any Style at $3, and Cheddar Grits, Brabant Potatoes and Creamed Spinach at $7.

They exist to round out the egg dishes. A guest who orders the Eggs Sardou or the omelette and wants a little meat can add the sausage or bacon; a biscuit catches the hollandaise or marchand de vin.

Offer one side as you confirm the entrée, matched to the plate: something crisp beside a sauced dish, something rich beside a light one. Learn every side's service note before the first table.

card.front: Which breakfast sides are $9, and which is $5?
card.back: The Housemade Pork Sausage Patty and the Thick-Cut Bacon are $9; the Buttermilk Biscuit is $5. Grits, potatoes and creamed spinach are $7, an egg $3.

components.name: The $12 dinner sides
components.explain:
Dinner carries five sides at $12 each: Succotash with Nueske's bacon, Smoked Cauliflower with preserved lemon and harissa, Shells & Cheese, Maggie's Mushrooms and South Louisiana Rice Dressing. Two of them, the mushrooms and the rice dressing, print no description, so their preparation is learned at lineup.

Sides are shared at dinner, so sell them to the table rather than to one guest.

The guide's natural pairings: Maggie's Mushrooms or Shells & Cheese with the Roasted Chateaubriand, and the Smoked Cauliflower beside the Blackened Tofu for a guest eating without meat, once the kitchen confirms the butter and stock.

card.front: Which dinner sides does the guide suggest with the Chateaubriand?
card.back: Maggie’s Mushrooms or Shells & Cheese, each $12. Dinner sides are shared plates, so offer them to the whole table, not to one guest.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p25, p31 to p33, p47)

components.name: Bananas Foster and Owen Brennan
components.explain:
Bananas Foster was created at Brennan's in 1951, while the restaurant was still Owen Brennan's Vieux Carré on Bourbon Street. Owen asked for a new dessert for a dinner honouring his friend Richard Foster, chairman of the New Orleans Crime Commission. His sister Ella and chef Paul Blangé adapted the caramelised bananas their mother made at home, and named it for Foster.

Bananas made sense: New Orleans was the main port of entry for bananas from Central and South America.

2026 is its 75th year. It is $14, minimum two per order, made at the table, and the house calls it the most-ordered item on the menu.

card.front: Who created Bananas Foster, and who is it named for?
card.back: Ella Brennan and chef Paul Blangé, in 1951, at Owen Brennan’s request; named for Richard Foster, Owen’s friend and crime commission chairman.

components.name: Bananas, butter, brown sugar and cinnamon
components.explain:
Bananas Foster starts with a caramel made in the pan at the table: butter melted with brown sugar until it bubbles, dusted with cinnamon. The bananas, ripe but still firm, are halved and quartered and laid in the caramel, turned once so they soften without collapsing.

The caramel is kept at a blond, bubbling stage, because a darker caramel would harden into toffee on the cold ice cream.

The bananas and sauce are spooned over housemade vanilla ice cream, so warm and cold meet in every spoonful. Ripe but firm fruit is the cook's secret: soft bananas turn to mush in the flame.

card.front: What goes into the pan for Bananas Foster before the rum?
card.back: Butter and brown sugar melted to a bubbling blond caramel, cinnamon, then ripe but firm bananas turned once so they soften without collapsing.

sources: research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (World Famous Bananas Foster, classical foundation)

components.name: Rum and banana liqueur
components.explain:
The printed menu names rum, and the long-standing Brennan's recipe also uses banana liqueur, which loosens the caramel and deepens the banana flavour before the rum is lit. Dark rum gives molasses and spice notes and enough strength to catch the flame.

Follow the house procedure you are trained on rather than any recipe you find elsewhere, and do not quote quantities.

Flaming burns the alcohol vapour above the pan, not all the alcohol in it: a large share stays in the sauce. For a guest who avoids alcohol, the guide steers to the Lemon Tart or the Pineapple Tarte Tatin. Which rum the kitchen pours is a question for the chef.

card.front: Does the flame burn off all the alcohol in Bananas Foster?
card.back: No. Flaming burns the vapour, and much of the rum and banana liqueur stays in the sauce; steer guests who avoid alcohol to the Lemon Tart or Tarte Tatin.

components.name: Flambé at the table
components.explain:
Flambé means flamed: spirit added to a hot pan and lit, so the alcohol vapour burns in a burst of blue and orange flame. It is theatre and flavour at once, caramelising the sauce's surface. At Brennan's it is done on a guéridon, the tableside cart.

The guide's steps are learned word for word: measure the spirit into a small vessel, never pour from the bottle near a flame, pull the pan off the flame to add it, tilt to ignite, keep a lid in reach, let the flame die before plating, and turn the burner off before leaving.

In a bright breakfast room the flame can be almost invisible, so treat the pan as lit until it clearly has died down.

card.front: What are the key safety rules for flambé at the table?
card.back: Measure the spirit first, never pour from the bottle near flame, add it off the flame, keep a lid in reach, let it burn out, turn the burner off.

components.name: Housemade vanilla ice cream
components.explain:
Classic French-style vanilla ice cream is a crème anglaise, milk, cream, sugar and egg yolks infused with vanilla, chilled and churned so it freezes smooth and dense. Real vanilla comes from the cured pod of an orchid and gives tiny black seeds and a floral, warm perfume.

Very cold, rich and plain, it is the stage for a hot sauce.

The kitchen makes its own for both flamed desserts: Bananas Foster and Cherries Jubilee are spooned over it at the table, so the hot, boozy fruit meets cold vanilla. The guide notes the ice cream likely contains egg; confirm with the kitchen when a guest asks.

card.front: What do both flamed desserts sit on?
card.back: Housemade vanilla ice cream, a churned vanilla custard: the cold, plain stage for the hot Bananas Foster and Cherries Jubilee sauces.

components.name: Cherries Jubilee
components.explain:
Cherries Jubilee is older than Bananas Foster. It is generally credited to Auguste Escoffier, who made it for one of Queen Victoria's jubilees, most often said to be the Diamond Jubilee of 1897. His recipe was stoned cherries in a thickened syrup, served in small dishes with a spoonful of warmed kirsch lit at the table, and no ice cream; the ice cream is a later, largely American habit.

It belongs to the same flamed family as Bananas Foster and crêpes Suzette.

Ours is fresh tart black cherries in a Luxardo sauce, flamed at the table over housemade vanilla ice cream, $14. Brighter and fruitier than the Foster: for a table of two, have both.

card.front: Who is credited with Cherries Jubilee, and for what?
card.back: Auguste Escoffier, for one of Queen Victoria’s jubilees, usually said to be 1897. Ours is black cherries in Luxardo sauce, flamed over vanilla ice cream.

components.name: Fresh tart black cherries
components.explain:
Cherries come in two broad families. Sweet cherries, dark red to near black, are the ones eaten fresh; sour or tart cherries are brighter red, sharper and usually cooked. The menu says fresh tart black cherries, which crosses the two, so which variety the kitchen uses is a fair question for the chef.

Cooked briefly in the pan, cherries soften and release a deep red juice that becomes the sauce.

On the Cherries Jubilee they are flamed at the table in a Luxardo sauce and spooned over vanilla ice cream. The guide notes cherries may contain pits; confirm with the kitchen before the guest takes a bite.

card.front: What should you confirm about the cherries in Cherries Jubilee?
card.back: Which variety, since tart cherries are usually red and black ones sweet, and whether any pits remain; ask the kitchen before serving.

components.name: Luxardo
components.explain:
Luxardo is the Italian family house famous for maraschino. Girolamo Luxardo founded the distillery in 1821 in Zara, on the Dalmatian coast, distilling a clear liqueur from the small, sour marasca cherry; after the Second World War destroyed the distillery, Giorgio Luxardo re-founded the firm at Torreglia, near Padua, in 1947, and the company grows its own marasca cherries there.

It also makes the dark candied cherries in syrup that bartenders prize.

The Cherries Jubilee's Luxardo sauce is cherry on cherry. The menu does not say whether it uses the liqueur or the cherries in syrup, so ask the chef which, and which spirit is lit.

card.front: What is Luxardo, and what does it bring to Cherries Jubilee?
card.back: The Italian house founded in 1821 in Zara, re-founded at Torreglia in 1947, famous for marasca cherry maraschino and candied cherries; its sauce is cherry on cherry.

components.name: New Orleans bread pudding
components.explain:
Bread pudding is an old European way to use stale bread: soaked in sweet custard and baked until soft inside and golden on top. In New Orleans it became a staple, recorded in local cookbooks from at least 1885, because the city's light French bread stales fast and drinks custard without turning to paste.

The boozy sauce came later; restaurants revived the dessert from the 1970s with whiskey and bourbon sauces, and a warm whiskey sauce is now its signature.

Ours is $14: bread pudding with a whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream for tang and pralines for crunch. Tell guests who avoid alcohol that the caramel carries whiskey.

card.front: Why is bread pudding a New Orleans classic?
card.back: The city’s light French bread stales fast and soaks up custard; local cookbooks carry it from 1885. Ours has whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines.

components.name: Whiskey caramel
components.explain:
A caramel sauce is sugar cooked until amber, then loosened with cream and butter into a pourable sauce. A whiskey caramel adds whiskey, which brings vanilla, oak and a warm, boozy edge that cuts the sweetness.

It holds better in service than the classic New Orleans whiskey sauce of butter, sugar and egg, which can split.

On the New Orleans Bread Pudding it is the warm, boozy sauce against the soft pudding and the tangy buttermilk ice cream. Which whiskey the kitchen uses is a question for the chef, and the alcohol in it is worth mentioning to guests who avoid it.

card.front: What is the sauce on the New Orleans Bread Pudding?
card.back: A whiskey caramel: amber caramel loosened with cream and butter, with whiskey for vanilla, oak and warmth. Mention the alcohol to guests who avoid it.

components.name: Buttermilk ice cream
components.explain:
Buttermilk is the tangy, slightly thick cultured milk of Southern baking. Churned into ice cream with cream and sugar, it gives a gently sour, refreshing ice cream, something like frozen yoghurt but richer.

That tang is the point: it balances sweet, rich desserts the way crème fraîche does.

On the New Orleans Bread Pudding it cools the warm pudding and cuts the sweetness of the whiskey caramel and pralines, so the dessert never feels heavy. Describe it to a guest as a tangy, Southern-style ice cream.

card.front: Why buttermilk ice cream with the bread pudding?
card.back: Its gentle tang, like a rich frozen yoghurt, cools the warm pudding and cuts the sweetness of the whiskey caramel and pralines.

components.name: Pralines
components.explain:
The praline takes its name from the seventeenth-century Maréchal du Plessis-Praslin, whose cook sugared almonds. The Ursuline nuns, who came to New Orleans in 1727, are credited by tradition with bringing the recipe; Louisiana cooks swapped in pecans and made a soft, creamy patty of brown sugar, butter and cream.

In the nineteenth century pralinières, women street vendors, many of them free women of colour, sold them in the French Quarter.

On the New Orleans Bread Pudding pralines add crunch and caramel sweetness. Say PRAH-leen; PRAY-leen marks a visitor.

card.front: Where do New Orleans pralines come from?
card.back: Named for the Maréchal du Plessis-Praslin’s sugared almonds; brought by tradition with the Ursulines in 1727 and remade with pecans. Say PRAH-leen.

components.name: The Snickers, a candy bar rebuilt
components.explain:
The Snickers is the pastry kitchen's take on the famous candy bar, taken apart and rebuilt as a plated dessert: a milk chocolate Bavarian cream for the chocolate, caramel custard for the caramel, nougat ice cream for the nougat, and roasted peanuts.

The name is a trademark, so say our Snickers lightly, as a wink rather than a claim.

It is $15 at both meals and closes the dinner tasting. The guide flags peanuts in capitals: confirm before ordering for every table. It is the dessert for the guest who wants chocolate, and the grown-up candy bar line sells it.

card.front: What is The Snickers on our dessert menu?
card.back: The candy bar rebuilt: milk chocolate Bavarian cream, caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts. Confirm peanuts before ordering.

components.name: Bavarian cream
components.explain:
A Bavarian cream, bavarois in French, is a crème anglaise set with gelatin and lightened with whipped cream, then chilled in a mould. It sits between a mousse and a custard: light, silky and holding its shape. The great nineteenth-century chef Carême codified it.

Chocolate melted into the custard turns it into a chocolate Bavarian.

The Snickers's Bavarian milk chocolate almost certainly means a milk chocolate bavarois, not chocolate from Bavaria. The guide notes Bavarian creams are usually set with gelatin, so check with the kitchen for guests who avoid it.

card.front: What is a Bavarian cream?
card.back: Crème anglaise set with gelatin and lightened with whipped cream: between a mousse and a custard. Ours is milk chocolate, in The Snickers.

components.name: Caramel custard
components.explain:
A caramel custard is eggs, milk or cream and sugar cooked gently until set, flavoured with caramel, sugar cooked to amber, which brings a toasty, slightly bitter depth. It is the family of crème caramel and flan.

Gentle heat is everything: too hot and the eggs curdle into a grainy, weeping custard.

In The Snickers it plays the caramel layer of the candy bar, silky and toasty against the milk chocolate Bavarian cream, the nougat ice cream and the salty roasted peanuts. If a guest asks, it is the soft caramel part of the bar.

card.front: What plays the caramel in The Snickers?
card.back: A caramel custard: eggs and cream cooked gently with sugar taken to amber, silky and toasty, from the same family as crème caramel and flan.

components.name: Nougat ice cream
components.explain:
Nougat is a confection of honey and sugar whipped into egg whites, usually studded with nuts, almonds, pistachios or hazelnuts; soft nougat is the chewy centre of many candy bars. As an ice cream it tastes of honey, toasted nuts and vanilla.

It is the frozen version of the candy bar's nougat layer.

In The Snickers it sits with roasted peanuts, caramel custard and milk chocolate Bavarian cream. Classic nougat often carries tree nuts besides the dish's peanuts, so ask the kitchen what is in it for any guest with a nut question.

card.front: What is nougat?
card.back: Honey and sugar whipped into egg whites, usually with nuts; as an ice cream it tastes of honey and toasted nuts. Ask the kitchen about nuts in ours.

components.name: Roasted peanuts
components.explain:
The peanut is not a true nut but a legume, a pod that ripens underground, grown across the American South. Roasting browns its natural sugars and oils, bringing out the toasty flavour, and salting makes it the classic partner to chocolate and caramel.

Salty peanuts against sweet chocolate is the whole appeal of the candy bar.

On The Snickers roasted peanuts give crunch and salt. The guide prints PEANUTS in capitals on this dessert: confirm with every table before it is ordered, and send any dietary question to the kitchen.

card.front: What must you confirm before The Snickers is ordered?
card.back: Peanuts, printed in capitals in the guide: roasted peanuts give the crunch and salt. Confirm with every table and send dietary questions to the kitchen.

components.name: The lemon tart, taken apart
components.explain:
The French tarte au citron is sweet pastry filled with a sharp lemon curd, often crowned with meringue. Our Lemon Tart takes it apart: the pastry becomes a sweet pastry crumb, the curd becomes a light yuzu mousse, the sharpness is concentrated in a lemon jelly, and the meringue is piped and toasted.

The deconstruction keeps the flavours and makes the whole dessert lighter.

It is $14 and the lightest dessert on the list. The guide names it, with the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, as the dessert to steer to for guests who avoid alcohol, since the flamed desserts and the bread pudding all carry spirits.

card.front: Which desserts do we steer guests who avoid alcohol towards?
card.back: The Lemon Tart, a lighter, deconstructed tarte au citron with yuzu mousse, and the Pineapple Tarte Tatin; the flamed desserts and bread pudding carry spirits.

components.name: Yuzu
components.explain:
Yuzu is an East Asian citrus grown in Japan and Korea, about the size of a tangerine, with a bumpy yellow skin and little juice. Its aroma is intense: it tastes like lemon, lime and mandarin at once, with a floral edge. It is the citrus in ponzu.

Its zest and juice perfume a dish far beyond their quantity.

In the Lemon Tart it flavours a light yuzu mousse, the dessert's answer to lemon curd. The guide notes the mousse is likely set with gelatin, so check with the kitchen for guests who avoid it.

card.front: What does yuzu taste like?
card.back: Like lemon, lime and mandarin at once, with a floral edge: an East Asian citrus, the citrus in ponzu. It flavours the mousse in our Lemon Tart.

components.name: Toasted meringue
components.explain:
Meringue is egg white whipped with sugar until glossy and stiff. Italian meringue whips in a hot sugar syrup, and Swiss meringue warms the whites and sugar together first; both are cooked and stable, so they hold their shape on a plate and can be browned with a torch.

Toasting caramelises the peaks into a marshmallow-like flavour with a crisp shell.

On the Lemon Tart the toasted meringue sits with the yuzu mousse, lemon jelly and sweet pastry crumb, sweet and soft against sharp citrus. Which style the pastry kitchen uses is a question for the chef.

card.front: How is the meringue on the Lemon Tart finished?
card.back: Piped and toasted with a torch, so the peaks caramelise like marshmallow; a cooked Italian or Swiss meringue holds its shape on the plate.

components.name: Lemon jelly and sweet pastry crumb
components.explain:
A lemon jelly is lemon juice, sugar and water set into a soft, clear gel, concentrated and sharp, a burst of acid in each bite. A sweet pastry crumb is sweet shortcrust, butter, sugar, flour and egg, baked and broken into crumbs, so the tart's crust becomes a crunchy scatter.

Splitting the tart this way lets each texture be at its best.

In the Lemon Tart the jelly carries the sharpness and the crumb gives the buttery crunch, around the yuzu mousse and toasted meringue. The guide lists what the pastry contains on the service note.

card.front: Where did the tart’s crust go in our Lemon Tart?
card.back: It became a sweet pastry crumb, crunchy and buttery, beside a sharp lemon jelly, the yuzu mousse and toasted meringue.

components.name: Tarte Tatin
components.explain:
Tarte Tatin is the French upside-down tart: fruit caramelised in butter and sugar in a pan, covered with pastry, baked and turned out so the pastry is underneath. It is named for Stéphanie and Caroline Tatin, who ran the Hôtel Tatin at Lamotte-Beuvron in the Sologne. The story of an accident with overcooked apples is a legend; the region already made such tarts, and Maxim's in Paris made the name famous.

Apples are classic. Pineapple is wetter and needs more browning, hence charred.

Our Pineapple Tarte Tatin is $14 with puff pastry, sweetened condensed anglaise and whipped vanilla mousse, and a dessert without spirits.

card.front: What is a tarte Tatin?
card.back: A French upside-down tart of fruit caramelised in butter and sugar, baked under pastry and turned out, named for the Tatin sisters. Ours is charred pineapple.

components.name: Charred pineapple
components.explain:
Pineapple is a tropical fruit, sweet and sharp, and much juicier than apple. Charring it, in a very hot pan, under a grill or in caramel, drives off water and caramelises its sugars until the edges blacken slightly, giving a deep, almost smoky sweetness while keeping the acidity.

That browning is what makes it work in a tart built for apples.

On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin the charred pineapple sits on puff pastry with a sweetened condensed anglaise and whipped vanilla mousse: caramelised, tangy and flaky against cool cream.

card.front: Why is the pineapple charred on the Tarte Tatin?
card.back: Pineapple is much wetter than apple; charring drives off water and caramelises its sugars for a deep, slightly smoky sweetness that keeps its tang.

components.name: Puff pastry
components.explain:
Puff pastry is a laminated dough: a block of butter wrapped in dough, then rolled and folded again and again until there are hundreds of layers. In the oven the water in the butter turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, so the pastry rises tall, crisp and flaky with no yeast at all.

It is one of the foundations of French pastry, behind the palmier and the mille-feuille.

On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin it is the flaky base under the charred pineapple. A classic Tatin is baked with the pastry on top and turned out; whether ours is baked inverted or assembled on the plate is a question for the chef.

card.front: How does puff pastry rise without yeast?
card.back: It is laminated: butter folded into dough into hundreds of layers, and steam from the butter pushes them apart in the oven.

components.name: Whipped vanilla mousse
components.explain:
A vanilla mousse is cream, or a light custard folded with whipped cream, flavoured with vanilla and whipped until airy, sometimes set lightly so it holds a shape. It is cooler and lighter than ice cream, and softer than a Bavarian cream.

Vanilla's floral warmth suits caramelised fruit.

On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin the whipped vanilla mousse cools the hot, charred pineapple alongside the sweetened condensed anglaise, so the plate has warm and cold, crisp and soft. Whether it is set with gelatin is a question for the kitchen if a guest asks.

card.front: What cools the hot pineapple on the Tarte Tatin?
card.back: A whipped vanilla mousse, airy and lighter than ice cream, served with the sweetened condensed anglaise so the plate has warm and cold, crisp and soft.

components.name: Cheddar
components.explain:
Cheddar takes its name from the English village of Cheddar, and is now made all over the world. Its curds are cut, stacked and turned, a process called cheddaring, which presses out whey and gives the cheese its dense, smooth texture. Young cheddar is mild and creamy; aged cheddar is sharp, nutty and crumbly, with crunchy crystals.

Sharp cheddar melts well and holds its flavour in a sauce.

On our menus it is stirred into the Cheddar Grits, a $7 breakfast side, creamy, rich and a little sharp, and it is the classic cheese of the pimento cheese folded into the Shrimp & Grits cake.

card.front: What cheese is in the Cheddar Grits, and what does it add?
card.back: Cheddar, the English cheese made by stacking and turning curds; sharp cheddar melts smoothly and gives the grits a rich, slightly sharp edge.

components.name: The grilled cheese sandwich
components.explain:
A grilled cheese is buttered bread around sliced cheese, cooked in a pan or on a griddle over moderate heat until the bread is golden and crisp and the cheese has melted through. Too hot, and the bread burns before the cheese melts; patience and a lid help.

It is a children's favourite because it is warm, mild and familiar.

The children's menus offer it twice: at breakfast with Brabant potatoes and at dinner with French fries, each within the $25.00 set price. The menu does not name the cheese or bread, so confirm with the kitchen if a parent asks.

card.front: How is a grilled cheese made so the cheese melts?
card.back: Buttered bread and cheese cooked over moderate heat, often with a lid, so the bread turns golden while the cheese melts through. With potatoes or fries.

items: Grilled Cheese Sandwich with Brabant Potatoes
Grilled Cheese Sandwich with French Fries

components.name: French fries
components.explain:
Good fries are usually cooked twice. A first, lower-temperature fry cooks the potato through until soft; after resting, a second, hotter fry crisps and browns the outside. Starchy potatoes give a fluffy inside, and salt goes on the moment they leave the oil, while it still sticks.

Belgium and France both claim them; the name stuck in America.

Fries come with the children's fried Gulf shrimp and grilled cheese at dinner, and the Roost serves Fries with Pink Sauce at $8, the easy add for a table with drinks and no food. Fryer questions go to the kitchen.

card.front: Why are good fries fried twice?
card.back: A lower first fry cooks the potato soft; a hotter second fry crisps and browns it. Salt them the moment they leave the oil.

items: Fried Gulf Shrimp with French Fries
Grilled Cheese Sandwich with French Fries

components.name: Buttered noodles with cheese
components.explain:
Buttered noodles are pasta boiled in well-salted water until just tender, drained and tossed straight away with butter and grated cheese, so the cheese melts into a light, glossy coating with a splash of the pasta water.

It is the plainest comfort food, which is why children love it.

On the children's dinner menu Buttered Noodles with Cheese comes within the $25.00 set price, with salami and cheese to start, ice cream and a drink. The menu names neither the pasta shape nor the cheese, so if a parent asks, the kitchen has the answer.

card.front: What comes with the children’s Buttered Noodles with Cheese?
card.back: Within the $25.00 dinner price: salami and cheese to start, the noodles tossed in butter and cheese, ice cream and a drink.

components.name: Fresh berries and whipped cream
components.explain:
Whipped cream is cold cream beaten with a little sugar, and often vanilla, until it holds soft peaks; beaten too far it turns grainy and then to butter. Fresh berries, strawberries, blueberries, raspberries or blackberries, bring colour and a sharp sweetness.

Together they are the classic topping for French toast and pancakes.

On the children's Vanilla French Toast they finish the plate within the $25.00 breakfast price. Which berries are in season changes, so check at lineup if a parent asks or a child has a favourite.

card.front: What tops the children’s Vanilla French Toast?
card.back: Fresh berries, which change with the season, and whipped cream, cold cream beaten with a little sugar to soft peaks.

items: Vanilla French Toast with Fresh Berries and Whipped Cream

components.name: Popcorn shrimp
components.explain:
Popcorn shrimp are small shrimp, or larger ones cut into bite-size pieces, dredged in seasoned flour or a light batter and fried quickly until golden, so they pop into the mouth like popcorn. The coating crisps in seconds while the shrimp stays sweet and tender.

They are eaten by the handful, which makes them a natural bar snack.

At the Roost, Popcorn Shrimp uses Louisiana shrimp with a Crystal hot sauce gastrique at $15, the step up from fries for a table staying a while. The children's breakfast offers popcorn shrimp with Brabant potatoes. Coating questions go to the kitchen.

card.front: What are popcorn shrimp?
card.back: Small, bite-size shrimp dredged and fried golden in seconds, eaten by the handful; at the Roost with a Crystal gastrique, and on the children’s breakfast.

components.name: Creole spiced nuts
components.explain:
Spiced nuts are nuts tossed with a little fat, salt and spice and roasted until fragrant and crisp, the classic bowl on a bar. A Creole seasoning brings paprika, cayenne, garlic and herbs: warm, savoury and gently hot.

Salt and spice make people thirsty, which is the point of a bar snack.

At the Roost, Creole Spiced Nuts are $6, the cheapest snack on the Bubbles list and the one to suggest the moment a drink lands. The mix of nuts is not printed, so ask the kitchen for any guest with a nut question.

card.front: When do you suggest the Creole Spiced Nuts?
card.back: The moment a drink lands: at $6 they are the cheapest Bubbles snack, warm and salty with Creole spice. Ask the kitchen which nuts are in the mix.

components.name: Crawfish
components.explain:
Crawfish are freshwater crustaceans, like small lobsters, and Louisiana produces most of the country's supply, both farmed in rice fields and caught wild in the swamps and bayous. The tail meat is sweet and rich, and the fat from the head, golden and full of flavour, is prized by Cajun cooks.

Spring is boil season, when crawfish are eaten by the pound at backyard parties.

At the Roost they fill the Crawfish Meat Pies with a chive rémoulade, the most Louisiana snack on the Bubbles list at $16. How the kitchen makes the filling is not printed, so ask before describing it.

card.front: What are crawfish?
card.back: Freshwater crustaceans like small lobsters; Louisiana raises and catches most of the country’s supply. Their sweet tails fill our Crawfish Meat Pies.

components.name: Louisiana meat pies
components.explain:
Louisiana's hand pies have a long history. The best known is the Natchitoches meat pie from the state's oldest permanent European settlement: a half-moon of pastry filled with seasoned pork and beef in gravy, traditionally fried. It was documented by 1826 and is an official state food; it may descend from Spanish empanadas or French Canadian tourtière.

Crawfish pies fill the same kind of pastry, or a full pie, with crawfish in a seasoned sauce.

The Roost's Crawfish Meat Pies follow that tradition, with chive rémoulade for dipping. Offer them to visitors who want a local taste in the courtyard.

card.front: What is a Natchitoches meat pie?
card.back: A fried half-moon hand pie of seasoned pork and beef from Natchitoches, Louisiana’s oldest settlement; our Crawfish Meat Pies follow that tradition.

components.name: Pink sauce
components.explain:
Pink sauce is the menu's name for the dip with the Roost fries, and the menu does not say what is in it. Across the South, pink dipping sauces are usually mayonnaise-based with ketchup or tomato, often with hot sauce, garlic and pickle, the family of fry sauce and of New Orleans's own pinkish rémoulades.

Because it is not printed, the guide's instruction is to ask the kitchen what is in it.
