Sell Fries with Pink Sauce at $8 as the easy add for a table with drinks and no food: salt sells the next glass. Learn the sauce's ingredients at lineup before a guest asks.

card.front: What is in the pink sauce with the Roost fries?
card.back: The menu does not say; learn it from the kitchen at lineup. Southern pink sauces are usually mayonnaise with tomato, hot sauce and pickle.

components.name: Fried pickles and chive cream
components.explain:
Fried pickles are a Southern bar classic: slices or spears of sour pickle dipped in a seasoned batter or cornmeal and fried until crisp, so the outside crunches and the inside bursts sour and juicy. A cool, creamy dip tames the heat and salt.

Ours use a medley of housemade pickles, so the vegetables and flavours vary, with a chive cream for dipping.

At $14 they are a fun share for a group at the bar; the guide suggests selling them with a crisp, acidic drink. Which pickles are in tonight's medley, and the coating, are questions for the kitchen.

card.front: What are the Roost’s Fried Pickles?
card.back: A medley of housemade pickles battered and fried, crisp outside and sour inside, with a cool chive cream; a $14 share best with a crisp drink.

components.name: The cheese board
components.explain:
A cheese board sets out a few contrasting cheeses, typically one soft, one firm and one blue or washed rind, with something sweet, something sharp and good bread. Cheeses taste best at room temperature, so they come out of the fridge before service.

The Roost's board offers three cheeses chosen by the kitchen, a seasonal chutney, Brennan's honey, fruit and nut bread.

At $24 it is the largest Bubbles snack and the natural partner for a bottle of rosé. Tonight's three cheeses are learned at lineup: know their names, milk and style before you sell it.

card.front: What must you learn about the Cheese Board at lineup?
card.back: Tonight’s three cheeses: names, milk and style. The $24 board also carries a seasonal chutney, Brennan’s honey and fruit and nut bread.

components.name: Brennan’s honey, chutney and fruit and nut bread
components.explain:
The cheese board's accompaniments each have a job. Honey brings floral sweetness that flatters salty and blue cheeses; the menu calls it Brennan's honey, and its source is a good lineup question. A chutney is fruit cooked slowly with vinegar, sugar and spice into a sweet and sour preserve, here seasonal. Fruit and nut bread is a dense loaf studded with dried fruit and nuts, made to be sliced thin under cheese.

Sweet, sharp and crunchy around three cheeses: that is the balance.

On the Roost's Cheese Board they turn a plate of cheese into a shared snack for a bottle of rosé.

card.front: What goes with the cheeses on the Roost’s Cheese Board?
card.back: Brennan’s honey for floral sweetness, a seasonal chutney for sweet and sour, and fruit and nut bread to slice under the cheese.

components.name: Short rib patties
components.explain:
A short rib burger uses beef from the rib, a richly marbled cut, ground into patties. The high fat content keeps the meat juicy and gives a deep, beefy flavour; many kitchens blend it with chuck or brisket.

Two thinner patties cook fast and give more crust than one thick one.

The Roost Burger is two beef short rib patties with bacon, cheese, pickles, onions, tomato jam and special sauce, $17, the one full plate on the Bubbles list. The guide asks you to check with the kitchen how the patties are cooked before taking a temperature.

card.front: What makes the Roost Burger rich?
card.back: Two patties of ground short rib, a richly marbled rib cut, with bacon and cheese; ask the kitchen how the patties are cooked before taking a temperature.

components.name: Tomato jam and special sauce
components.explain:
Tomato jam is tomatoes cooked slowly with sugar, vinegar and spice until thick and glossy, sweeter and deeper than ketchup, with a gentle tang. A special sauce on a burger is a house dressing, usually mayonnaise-based with pickle, mustard or ketchup, and every kitchen guards its own.

Sweet jam and creamy sauce balance the salty bacon, cheese and sharp pickles.

On the Roost Burger both go on with the pickles and onions. The menu does not print the special sauce's recipe, so for any guest who asks what is in it, the kitchen has the answer.

card.front: What sauces are on the Roost Burger?
card.back: Tomato jam, tomatoes cooked down with sugar and vinegar, sweet and tangy, and a house special sauce; ask the kitchen what is in the special sauce.

components.name: Beef tenderloin, served raw
components.explain:
The tenderloin is the long, lean muscle that runs along the inside of the backbone and does almost no work, which is why it is the most tender cut on the animal. Its grain is fine and its fat is low, so it cooks quickly and, served raw, stays cool and silky rather than chewy. Our Roasted Chateaubriand is the thick centre of the same muscle, roasted whole for two.

On the Steak Tartare with Rye the sheet names it plainly as raw beef tenderloin: chopped and dressed, never cooked. That rawness is the first thing a server says, with the consumer advisory, before the order is taken.

The sheet does not say how the kitchen cuts it, the portion, where the beef comes from or how it is held, so none of that is promised: ask the chef at lineup before you describe it.

card.front: What cut is in the Steak Tartare with Rye?
card.back: Beef tenderloin, the lean muscle along the backbone that does almost no work, so it is the most tender cut; served raw, chopped and dressed, never cooked. Give the consumer advisory first.

components.name: Montreal seasoning
components.explain:
Montreal seasoning is the steak spice of Montreal's smoked meat delis. Ours is the five the sheet prints: black pepper, caraway, coriander, chili flake and mustard seed, so it is peppery and aromatic, with its heat from the chili flake. A shop-bought blend may list other things; say only our five.

Caraway matters here. Its anise-like seed is what gives many rye breads their familiar flavour, so the seasoning and the rye tuile echo each other across the plate.

The deli story is real as far as it goes: Schwartz's, the Montreal smoked meat house, dates from 1928 and had a Romanian-Jewish founder. The tale that the spice began with a lunch at a deli in the 1940s is not verified, so tell it as a tale and give it no date. How much heat tonight's blend carries is the chef's answer.

card.front: What is in our Montreal seasoning?
card.back: The five the sheet prints: black pepper, caraway, coriander, chili flake and mustard seed, a peppery, aromatic steak spice from Montreal's smoked meat delis. Caraway echoes the rye tuile.

components.name: Vital Farms egg yolk, on the tartare
components.explain:
Vital Farms is the egg brand the sheet names for the yolk on the Steak Tartare with Rye, the same name our breakfast menu prints on the sunny-side-up egg of the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak. It began in 2007 near Austin, Texas, with twenty hens, and now works with hundreds of small family farms. Pasture-raised, on its standard, means each hen has at least 108 square feet of rotated outdoor pasture to forage on.

On the tartare the sheet lists the yolk on its own, for richness. Whether that yolk is served raw or comes from a pasteurised egg is not on the sheet, and nor is where it sits on the plate, so a guest's question about it goes to the kitchen, never to a promise.

Egg is also inside the dressing, so taking the separate yolk off does not take egg out of the plate; say so and send the question to the kitchen.

card.front: What does the sheet say about the yolk on the tartare?
card.back: A Vital Farms egg yolk, for richness: pasture-raised eggs, every hen with at least 108 square feet of outdoor pasture. Raw or pasteurised is the kitchen's answer, and egg is in the dressing too.

components.name: Rye tuile
components.explain:
A tuile, TWEEL, is French for a roof tile: a thin, crisp wafer, baked flat and often curved over a form while warm so it sets in a tile's shape. Most are sweet, but savoury ones are made too, and ours is made with rye, which gives it an earthy, malty grain flavour.

On the Steak Tartare with Rye it stands in for the toast a brasserie serves with tartare, giving crunch against the soft, cool beef and the rich yolk. Rye on its own is earthy and malty; the anise-like note people expect from rye bread comes from caraway seed, which here sits in the Montreal seasoning, so the two echo each other.

Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen. The tuile's full recipe, flour, fat and egg, is not printed: ask the chef.

card.front: What is the rye tuile on the tartare?
card.back: TWEEL: a thin, crisp wafer, named for the French roof tile, made here with rye for an earthy, malty crunch against the soft beef and the yolk. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

components.name: Capers
components.explain:
Capers are the unopened flower buds of Capparis spinosa, a scrambling shrub of hot, dry hillsides, picked small and preserved in salt or in vinegar brine. They are not tiny olives, and they are not caperberries, which are the plant's fruit, picked later and bigger. Curing is what makes them: a fresh bud is bitter, a cured one is briny, tangy and faintly floral.

In a steak tartare they are one of the oldest companions of the beef. Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire of 1903 already sends capers, onion and parsley to the table beside chopped fillet and a yolk, and the Paris brasserie tartare keeps them in the mix with shallot and mustard.

On the Steak Tartare with Rye they sit inside the tartare dressing with the Dijon, giving the salty, sharp bite that cuts the richness of the yolk. If a guest tastes something briny and bright, that is the caper.

card.front: What is a caper?
card.back: The unopened flower bud of a shrub, cured in salt or brine until briny and tangy; not an olive and not a caperberry. In our tartare dressing it is the sharp, salty bite beside the Dijon.

components.name: The tartare dressing
components.explain:
The tartare dressing is what turns chopped raw beef into a dish. The sheet lists seven things: egg yolk, Dijon, caper, shallot, hot sauce, parsley and black pepper. The yolk and the mustard are the richness and the bite, and in a classic tartare dressing they are also what binds the rest. Capers bring salt and a sharp, briny bite, shallot a gentle onion note, parsley freshness, and black pepper and hot sauce the warmth.

What the sheet does not say is the build: the proportions, whether the kitchen folds the dressing through the beef or plates it beside, and which hot sauce it uses. Those are the chef's answers, not a server's guesses.

One thing to learn by heart: egg is in this dressing as well as the separate yolk, so leaving the yolk off does not take egg out of the plate. Send that question to the kitchen.

card.front: What is in the tartare dressing?
card.back: Egg yolk, Dijon, caper, shallot, hot sauce, parsley and black pepper: yolk and mustard make the glossy binder, capers and shallot sharpen it, hot sauce warms it. Egg is in here as well as in the separate yolk.

components.name: Two tartares: Escoffier's page and the Montreal spice
components.explain:
Nobody can name the inventor of steak tartare. What can be said is that Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire of 1903 records beefsteak à l'Américaine: finely chopped fillet served with an egg yolk, with capers, onion and parsley passed alongside. That is a documented ancestor, not a single inventor.

Brennan's menus name two tartares. The dinner card's Steak Tartare Cannoli pipes the beef into a crisp potato shell with crème fraîche and a cured, grated yolk. The Fall 2026 sheet's Steak Tartare with Rye goes the other way: a classic dressing of yolk, Dijon, capers and shallot, a separate egg yolk, and Montreal seasoning with a rye tuile.

That Montreal spice carries a story of its own, the smoked meat delis of the city, where Schwartz's has stood since 1928. The tale that it was invented over a lunch in the 1940s is not verified, so tell it as a tale and give it no date.

card.front: What early written ancestor can you cite for our tartare?
card.back: Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire of 1903 records beefsteak à l'Américaine: chopped fillet with an egg yolk, capers, onion and parsley alongside. An ancestor, not an inventor: nobody can name one.

components.name: Swordfish
components.explain:
Swordfish is a large, fast ocean fish with a long flat bill, caught in warm and temperate seas around the world, the North Atlantic among them. Its flesh is firm and dense with a mildly sweet flavour, and it is cut into thick steaks or fillets rather than thin ones, which is why it is cooked more like a piece of meat than a delicate fish: a hard sear or a grill, then a gentle finish, and it dries out if it is taken too far.

On our fall menu it carries the Grenobloise garnish, where the firm flesh holds its own against brown butter, lemon and fried capers in a way a flaky fish could not.

The training sheet names no catch area, fishing method, portion or cooking method, so claim none; learn the kitchen's cut and method at lineup and describe the fish with confidence.

card.front: What kind of fish is swordfish, and how do we sell it?
card.back: A firm, dense, mildly sweet ocean fish, cut thick and cooked like a steak. The sheet prints no catch area, cut or method: learn them at lineup.

components.name: Leek fondue
components.explain:
Fondue, fon-DOO, is French for melted, and a leek fondue is leeks sliced fine and cooked slowly in butter, covered and over low heat, until they collapse into a soft, sweet, almost spreadable bed. Nothing browns; the point is sweetness without colour. Some kitchens finish it with a little cream or crème fraîche, others leave it at butter and seasoning.

It is not a cheese fondue, and a guest who hears the word may picture a pot of melted cheese, so say what it is at once: soft, slow-cooked leeks with the fish.

On the Swordfish Grenobloise it is the soft partner to the fillet and the quiet, sweet note against the brown butter, lemon and salty capers. The sheet marks dairy for the plate and does not print the fondue's own ingredients, so any question about what is in tonight's batch goes to the kitchen.

card.front: What is a leek fondue?
card.back: Leeks sliced fine and cooked slowly in butter until they melt soft and sweet, with no colour: the soft leeks with our swordfish, and never a cheese fondue.

components.name: Fried capers
components.explain:
A caper is the unopened flower bud of a Mediterranean shrub, picked by hand and preserved in salt or brine, which is where its sharp, briny, slightly floral taste comes from. The smallest are the most prized. A caperberry is the fruit that forms if the bud is left to open, bigger and milder, and not what we use.

Frying changes the caper. Drained and dried, then dropped into hot fat for a minute, the buds open like tiny flowers and turn crisp, so they add crunch and a burst of salt rather than a soft, sour pop.

On the Swordfish Grenobloise the fried capers are the salty, crisp counterpoint to the brown butter and the soft leeks, and part of what makes the garnish Grenobloise rather than a plain meunière. How the kitchen fries them, and in what, is not printed; ask at lineup.

card.front: What are capers, and why are ours fried?
card.back: The unopened flower buds of a Mediterranean shrub, preserved in salt or brine. Fried, they open and crisp, adding crunch and a burst of salt to the brown butter.

components.name: The Grenobloise garnish
components.explain:
Grenobloise, gruh-no-BLWAZ, is the classic French garnish of brown butter, lemon and capers, finished with parsley and usually croutons, most often on a sautéed fish such as sole. The cook sears the fish, then browns butter in the pan until its milk solids toast and smell of hazelnut, stops it with lemon, and spoons it over with the capers, parsley and croutons.

Think of it as meunière, the butter and lemon classic, with two additions: capers for salt and croutons for crunch. The lemon is what keeps the rich butter from sitting heavily, and the garnish is finished in the last minute so the croutons stay crisp.

Ours goes on a swordfish fillet with leek fondue, with the capers fried and the croutons cut from Leidenheimer bread. The sheet does not print how the fish itself is cooked, so learn that at lineup.

card.front: What makes a dish Grenobloise?
card.back: Brown butter, lemon and capers, with parsley and croutons, spooned over fish: meunière plus salt and crunch. Ours comes with leek fondue, fried capers and Leidenheimer croutons.

components.name: Grenobloise, of Grenoble
components.explain:
Grenobloise simply means of Grenoble, the city in the French Alps, and the name says no more than that. The name went onto a plate the way many French garnish names did, a city or a region attached to a fixed set of ingredients, and here the set is brown butter, lemon, capers and parsley, usually with croutons.

What matters at the table is that it names a treatment, not a fish. Sole is the classic, but any firm fillet can be served Grenobloise, and ours is swordfish.

The training sheet carries a story that the sauce was invented to hide spoiled fish. That story is unverified, and no kitchen masks bad fish with sauce, so do not repeat it. Tell the butter, lemon and caper story instead, and that the croutons come from Leidenheimer, the New Orleans bakery baking French bread since 1896.

card.front: Where does the name Grenobloise come from?
card.back: From Grenoble, in the French Alps: a city name attached to a fixed garnish of brown butter, lemon, capers and parsley. It names a treatment, not a fish.

components.name: Chateaubriand, the centre cut
components.explain:
Chateaubriand, shah-toh-bree-AHN, is the name butchers now use for the thick centre cut of the beef tenderloin, the muscle along the spine that does almost no work. That is why it is the most tender cut on the animal, and also why it is comparatively lean: tenderness and heavy marbling are different qualities, and a tenderloin has the first without much of the second. Lean beef has a mild flavour, so it leans on its sauce for savour, which is exactly what the Espagnole is for.

On the Chateau Espagnole the sheet prints a twelve-ounce cut. It prints no cooking method, no temperatures and no serving count, so learn those at lineup, and do not promise a plate for two because Chateaubriand is often roasted for two elsewhere; our Roasted Chateaubriand with sauce Foyot is that plate, and this one is different. The producer is not printed either, so name none until the kitchen says.

card.front: What cut is the Chateaubriand on the Chateau Espagnole?
card.back: The thick centre cut of the beef tenderloin: the most tender cut, lean and mild, printed at twelve ounces. Method, temperatures and serving count are learned at lineup.

components.name: Frascarelli
components.explain:
Frascarelli, frah-skah-REL-lee, are small, rustic pasta pieces with roots in the Marche, the region in central Italy. The traditional version there is a flour-and-water preparation, made by wetting flour so it gathers into irregular little lumps that are boiled like pasta, and the local account from Urbisaglia says the versions vary across the Marche.

The sheet describes ours as flour and egg loosely combined into irregular pieces, boiled and finished in butter, so say 'small, rustic pasta pieces finished in butter' and keep the long explanation for a guest who asks. The egg and the butter are this house's treatment, not a rule of every Marche kitchen, so do not teach them as the tradition.

On the Chateau Espagnole they are the soft, buttery comfort beside a lean cut of beef and a deep brown sauce. For what goes into tonight's batch, and whether they are made in house, ask the kitchen.

card.front: What are frascarelli?
card.back: Small, rustic pasta pieces with roots in the Marche in central Italy. Ours, the sheet says, are flour and egg loosely combined into irregular pieces, boiled and finished in butter.

components.name: Sauce Espagnole
components.explain:
Sauce Espagnole, ess-pan-YOL, is the classical French brown sauce and one of the mother sauces every kitchen teaches: brown stock, thickened with a brown roux, with tomato and aromatic vegetables, simmered for hours and skimmed until it is glossy and deep. Its job is savoury depth, not a fresh tomato character; the tomato is a small part, there for colour and a little acidity. Reduced by half with more stock it becomes demi-glace, and from it come the classical brown daughter sauces.

On the Chateau Espagnole it is the sauce under a lean centre cut of tenderloin, and lean beef needs it: the sauce supplies the richness the cut does not have. The sheet names the sauce family only, not our stock, the fat in the roux, the vegetables or how it is finished, so a question about any of those goes to the kitchen.

card.front: What is sauce Espagnole?

components.name: Finishing pasta in butter
components.explain:
To finish pasta in butter, the cook drains it a moment early, drops it into a pan with butter and a splash of its own starchy cooking water, and tosses it over the heat until the starch and the fat come together into a glossy coat on every piece. Italian cooks call this mantecare, and it is the difference between pasta in butter and pasta sitting beside a knob of it: the sauce clings, the pieces stay separate and the butter tastes sweet and round.

On the Chateau Espagnole the frascarelli are finished this way, the sheet says, and that butter gloss is why they read as comfort against the lean beef and the deep brown sauce. The sheet prints only 'finished in butter', so whether anything else goes into the pan, cheese, herbs or pasta water, is the kitchen's answer.

card.back: In general: the boiled pasta is tossed in a pan with butter, often with a splash of its cooking water, until starch and fat make a glossy coat on every piece. Whether anything else goes in is the kitchen's answer.

components.name: Espagnole, the Spanish name on a French sauce
components.explain:
Espagnole means Spanish in French, and the name has puzzled cooks for generations, since the sauce is as French as any in the repertoire. The stories told to explain it are tales, none of them proven, so tell none as fact.

What is documented is the sauce's place in the canon. Carême, earlier in the nineteenth century, grouped the French sauces under four, espagnole among them. Escoffier built Le Guide Culinaire of 1903 on four base sauces, espagnole among them, and the kitchens that came after added hollandaise and teach five mother sauces today. Five of our courtyard turtles carry those names, Espagnole among them.

At the table the point is simple: Espagnole is the French brown mother sauce, and the name alone does not make this plate Spanish. Frascarelli bring the Marche in Italy to the plate; the sauce brings France.

card.back: No: Espagnole means Spanish, but it is the French brown mother sauce, one of Carême's four and one of Escoffier's four base sauces of 1903. Five courtyard turtles carry the mother sauces' names.

components.name: Agnolotti del plin
components.explain:
Agnolotti del plin, ah-nyoh-LOT-tee del PLEEN, are the small filled pasta of Piedmont, in northern Italy, tied to the high Langhe hills around Alba. A thin sheet of pasta is dotted with small portions of filling, folded over, and pinched shut between each portion; plin is the local word for that pinch. The parcels are cut apart along the pinches, so each is small, thin-skinned and marked by a thumb and a finger.

In Piedmont the fillings vary, meat and vegetable both, and the parcels are usually dressed simply so the filling leads. Ours are plated with pork, braised collards, ricotta and Parmesan and finished with lemon pangrattato. The sheet does not say which parts are inside the pasta and which around it, nor whether the dough is made in house or carries egg, so learn the build at lineup before you describe the filling.

card.front: What are agnolotti del plin?
card.back: Small pinched pasta parcels from Piedmont: a thin sheet folded over a filling and pinched shut, plin being the pinch. Ours come with pork, braised collards, ricotta, Parmesan and lemon pangrattato.

components.name: Ricotta
components.explain:
Ricotta means recooked. It is the soft, fresh Italian cheese made by heating the whey left over from making other cheeses a second time, so the proteins still in it rise as fine white curds that are drained but never pressed or aged. The result is mild, milky and a little sweet, creamy rather than sharp, and it is the classic soft cheese of Italian filled pasta, where it loosens and lightens a filling and takes well to nutmeg and lemon.

On the Agnolotti del Plin it is one of the two cheeses with the pork and the collards, the creamy half to the Parmesan's salty half. The sheet does not say whether it is in the filling or spooned over, whether it is made in house, or whose milk it comes from. The sheet marks Nutmeg for the plate without saying where, so any question about the ricotta's seasoning goes to the kitchen.

components.name: Lemon pangrattato
components.explain:
Pangrattato, pahn-graht-TAH-toh, is Italian for grated bread: coarse breadcrumbs toasted in olive oil until golden and crisp, then scattered over pasta or vegetables for crunch. A lemon pangrattato carries lemon through the crumb, so every spoonful lands with a bright citrus edge as well as the crunch.

On the Agnolotti del Plin it is the finish, the bright crunch against soft pasta, pork, greens, a soft cheese and a salty one. The sheet prints it as Lemon Pangratto and says pangrattato in its pronunciation line, and it does not print the crumb's own recipe: which bread, what fat, zest or juice, or whether garlic, herbs or chilli go in. Call it crisp lemon breadcrumbs and let the kitchen fill in the rest at lineup.

components.name: Braising greens
components.explain:
Braising is slow, covered cooking in a little liquid, and greens take to it the way a tough cut of meat does. Collards are a sturdy leaf of the cabbage family with a stem and a rib that stay chewy if they are only wilted, so Southern kitchens cook them long and low in a flavoured liquid, often with smoked pork, until the leaves turn silky and sweet and the bitterness softens. The liquid they cook in, the pot liquor, becomes a seasoning in its own right.

On the Agnolotti del Plin the braised collards are the Southern voice beside a Piedmontese pasta, soft and earthy against the pork, the ricotta and the Parmesan. The sheet does not print what ours braise in, and it marks Alcohol for the plate without saying where, so do not describe a ham hock or a splash of wine: say slow-cooked greens and learn the braise at lineup.

card.back: Slowly, covered, in a little liquid until the sturdy leaves turn silky and sweet, the Southern way. What ours braise in is not printed, so learn it at lineup.

components.name: Plin, the pinch from the Langhe

They belong to the high Langa, the hills around Alba, and the fillings vary from kitchen to kitchen, meat and vegetable both, so the shape and the pinch are the tradition rather than any one filling.

Our Fall 2026 plate keeps the shape and sets it in the South: pork, braised collards, ricotta and Parmesan, finished with lemon pangrattato. components.name: Lamb shank
components.explain:
The shank is the lower leg of the lamb, a hard-working muscle wrapped in connective tissue and set around a bone. It is the opposite of a loin chop: cooked fast it stays tough, cooked slowly in liquid it turns tender and deeply flavoured, because hours of gentle, moist heat melt that sinew into gelatin and the meat gives up its grip on the bone.

That is why our kitchen cooks it as a daube, DOHB, the slow braise of Provence, before it goes into the pastry. The braise does the tenderising; the oven only has to crisp the crust.

The sheet does not say whether the bone comes to the table inside the pastry, whether the meat is boned and formed, or what the portion is. Learn the build at lineup and describe the lamb as tender and slow-cooked, which is the one thing the cut promises.

card.front: What is a lamb shank, and why is ours braised?
card.back: The lower leg, a working cut full of connective tissue. Fast cooking leaves it tough; a slow braise melts the sinew into gelatin and makes it tender. Ours is cooked as a daube.

components.name: Spiced lamb jus
components.explain:
Jus, ZHOO, is French for juice, and in a kitchen it means the natural cooking juices of a roast or a braise, strained and reduced into a thin, glossy sauce that tastes of the meat itself rather than of flour or cream. A lamb jus is built on lamb bones and trimmings, and it is the lightest, purest sauce a lamb can have.

Ours is spiced: the sheet names star anise, orange and a touch of cinnamon. Those are warm, aromatic flavours, the scent of a winter kitchen, and there is no chilli in the list, so a guest who asks whether it is spicy should hear warm, not hot.

What else goes into it, which stock, any wine, how far it is reduced and whether it is finished with butter, is not printed. Describe the three aromatics with confidence and send the rest to the kitchen.

card.back: The strained, reduced cooking juices of the lamb, a thin, glossy sauce made from the meat's own juices. Ours is scented with star anise, orange and a touch of cinnamon: warm, not hot.

components.name: Star anise
components.explain:
Star anise is the dried, star-shaped fruit of an evergreen tree native to south China and Vietnam, each point of the star holding one shiny seed. It tastes of liquorice, sweet, warm and a little peppery, the same note you know from the Herbsaint in a Sazerac, though the two come from different plants, and it is the flavour that anchors Chinese five-spice.

In a braise or a sauce it is used whole and sparingly, one or two stars steeped in the liquid and lifted out, because it is strong enough to take over a pot. With orange and cinnamon, as in our spiced lamb jus, it makes a warm, aromatic sauce that smells of fall rather than of heat.

The sheet names it, with orange and a touch of cinnamon, as the scent of the jus; how much goes in and what else joins it is the kitchen's business.

components.name: Daube, the slow braise
components.explain:
Daube, DOHB, is the slow-cooked meat dish of Provence: pieces of meat cooked for hours in wine with aromatic vegetables and herbs, covered and at a bare simmer, until they are tender enough to cut with a spoon. It is a dish for a tough cut and a cold evening. Beef is the best known, but Marseille's own account of the dish names lamb among the meats it can be made with, and the recipe changes from one kitchen to the next.

The method is braising: sear for colour, add the liquid and aromatics, then low heat and patience, so the tough cut's connective tissue melts into gelatin and the liquid becomes the sauce.

Our lamb shank daube goes into puff pastry afterwards. What it is braised in, which aromatics go in and whether wine stays in the finished dish are not printed; send that to the kitchen rather than guess.

card.front: What is a daube?
card.back: The slow braise of Provence: meat cooked for hours in wine and aromatics until spoon-tender. Beef is the best known; lamb is traditional too. Ours is lamb shank, wrapped in pastry afterwards.

components.name: En croûte, baked in a crust
components.explain:
En croûte, ahn KROOT, means in a crust: a filling wrapped in pastry and baked. French kitchens use it for pâté, for fish, for beef, and here for a lamb shank daube. The sheet names puff pastry, a laminated dough of many thin layers of dough and fat that steam apart in the oven and bake tall, flaky and crisp.

The challenge is moisture. A braise is wet, so a cook has to bring the meat together, chill it and seal it so the pastry bakes crisp instead of soaking through; the cooking is done before the wrapping, and the oven's job is the crust. An egg wash is the usual gloss; the sheet marks egg, and which component carries it is a question for the kitchen.

Whether the bone travels inside the pastry, how it is portioned and whether it is opened at the table are not printed; learn them at lineup.

components.name: A Provençal stew in a French crust
components.explain:
The Lamb Shank en Croûte puts two French traditions on one plate. The first is the daube, the slow wine braise of Provence, made with beef most famously and with lamb in Marseille's own telling of it. The second is en croûte, the pastry wrapping that French cooks use to turn a filling into something grand enough for a table.

Neither one needs the other. A daube is served from its pot, and pastry usually wraps something that cooks inside it. On our fall menu the two meet: a finished braise goes into puff pastry, and the spiced jus, star anise, orange and a touch of cinnamon, is what makes it a fall plate rather than a winter stew.

Tell it that way: a Provençal braise dressed up in a French crust, with a sauce that smells of the season. The sheet gives no older story for the dish, so do not invent one.

components.name: Stuffed fish terrine
components.explain:

Stuffed means there is a filling at the centre, so a slice shows one thing wrapped in another: a layer of fish around a softer or differently coloured centre.

components.name: Shrimp mousse

components.name: Chickpea panisse
components.explain:
Panisse, pah-NEESS, is the chickpea cake of Marseille. components.name: Confit fennel and fennel fronds

Fennel is the pale, crisp bulb with the taste of anise, the same note as the Herbsaint in a Sazerac, and it is one of the vegetables that belongs to a Provençal fish soup. components.name: Preserved lemon aioli
components.explain:
Aioli, eye-OH-lee, is the garlic sauce of Provence, and the word says so: ai is garlic and oli is oil in Provençal. Garlic is pounded to a paste with salt and olive oil is worked in drop by drop until the sauce is thick and glossy; most kitchens add egg yolk to hold it, which makes it a garlic mayonnaise. It is the sauce of the grand aïoli, the Provençal platter of fish and vegetables.

Ours is flavoured with preserved lemon, lemon cured in salt and its own juice for weeks until the rind turns soft, salty and perfumed rather than sour; we use it in the beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique and on the Smoked Cauliflower.

On the Marseille table the sauce beside a bouillabaisse is rouille, a rust-coloured garlic sauce with red pepper. The sheet names an aioli, not rouille, so say aioli. What is in tonight's batch is the kitchen's answer.

components.name: Bouillabaisse sauce
components.explain:
Bouillabaisse, boo-yuh-BESS, is the fish soup of Marseille, and in the city it comes in two parts: a broth, and the fish that cooked in it, served apart. The broth gives the dish its name and its character, and the usual make is fish simmered with olive oil, onion, garlic, fennel and tomato, boiled hard so the oil and the broth come together, then strained; saffron and pastis are usual, and rouille, a rust-coloured garlic sauce, is spread on croutons beside it.

A bouillabaisse sauce is that broth taken further, usually reduced so it coats a spoon and dresses the terrine and the mousse rather than filling a bowl. The flavours of the soup arrive as a sauce.

The sheet prints the name and no recipe. Whether ours carries saffron, tomato, fennel or pastis, and what the Alcohol and Nightshades marks point to, are the chef's answers; say the Marseille broth made into a sauce, and no more.

card.front: What is a bouillabaisse sauce?
card.back: The broth of the Marseille fish soup made into a sauce, reduced so it coats a spoon and sauces the terrine. What ours carries, saffron, tomato or pastis, is a lineup question.

components.name: Bouillabaisse, the fishers' soup of Marseille
components.explain:
Marseille is the old port city of Provence on the Mediterranean, and bouillabaisse is its dish. The city's own account tells it as a fishers' soup, served with the broth and the fish apart. The usual make is the catch that would not sell, boiled hard in a pot with olive oil, garlic, fennel and tomato, the broth served over croutons first and the fish after. The name is usually explained from the Provençal for boil and lower, the fire brought up hard and then down.

Panisse, the fried chickpea cake, is Marseille's too, from L'Estaque, the city's fishing quarter.

Our Fall 2026 tasting menu takes that vocabulary and builds a composed plate from it: the fish as a stuffed terrine and a shrimp mousse, the broth as a sauce, panisse for crunch, with confit fennel and a preserved lemon aioli, so a Marseille dish arrives at a Royal Street table without a bowl. Say plate, never soup.

card.front: Where does the Fish Bouillabaisse come from?
card.back: From Marseille, the port of Provence, where bouillabaisse is a fishers' soup served as broth and fish apart, and panisse a fried chickpea cake. Our tasting course rebuilds both as one composed plate.

components.name: Tuna, served raw
components.explain:
Tuna is a large, fast ocean fish with firm, meaty flesh, deep in colour, closer to a steak than to a flaky white fish. That is why it is one of the fish most often served raw in a restaurant: cut cleanly and dressed at the last moment, it stays cool, silky and clean-tasting. Crudo, KROO-doh, is the Italian word for raw, and that is the first thing a server says about this plate, with the consumer advisory, before the order goes in.

The sheet prints tuna and no more: not the species, the cut, where it comes from or whether the kitchen cures it briefly before it is dressed. Promise none of that. The aguachile dresses the fish; it does not cook it, so never say the citrus cooks the tuna.

The sheet's dietary marks leave fish off this plate, so raise that with the kitchen at lineup and keep fish in any guest discussion.

card.front: What do we say first about the Tuna Crudo?
card.back: That it is raw: crudo is the Italian word for raw, and the tuna is raw, dressed, never cooked. Give the consumer advisory first; the species and cut are lineup questions.

components.name: Salsa seca
components.explain:
Salsa seca, SAL-sah SEH-kah, means dry salsa. Where most salsas are wet, a chopped or blended sauce, a dry one is a crumbly, crunchy condiment: dried chillies toasted until they are brittle, with toasted seeds and nuts and sometimes crushed tortilla chips, with a little oil to bind them. It is spooned over a plate for crunch, smoke and a slow, toasty heat rather than for sauce, and it is a cousin of the Mexican salsa macha, the chilli and nut condiment in oil.

On the Tuna Crudo it is the crunch against the cool fish and the wet aguachile.

The sheet prints the name and no formula, and it marks Sesame and Gluten for the plate, so which seeds, nuts and grains are in tonight's batch, and what is toasted beside them, is the kitchen's answer: send every question about it to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: What is salsa seca?
card.back: SAL-sah SEH-kah, dry salsa: dried chillies toasted brittle with seeds and nuts, a crunchy condiment rather than a wet sauce, the crunch on the Tuna Crudo. What is in tonight's batch goes to the kitchen.

components.name: Burnt orange segments
components.explain:
An orange segment is usually the fruit cut free of its membrane, so the guest gets a clean, juicy piece with no pith. Burnt means the cut face is charred, under a torch, a salamander or in a very hot pan, until the sugars on the surface caramelise and darken. The char adds a bitter, smoky edge to the orange's sweetness and softens its acidity, so the fruit tastes of marmalade as much as of fresh juice.

On the Tuna Crudo the burnt orange is the citrus the sheet's tableside line calls citrus-led: it meets the sweet carrot in the aguachile, the ginger's warmth and the bitter note of the toasted chillies in the salsa seca.

How the kitchen chars the segments, how dark it takes them and how many sit on the plate are not printed: ask at lineup, and describe the char as bitter-sweet, never as burnt in the plain sense.

card.front: What does burnt orange mean on the crudo?
card.back: Orange segments cut free of their membrane, then charred on the cut face until the sugars darken: bitter-sweet, smoky and softer in acid, like marmalade. How the kitchen chars them is a lineup question.

components.name: Pickled pearl onions
components.explain:
Pearl onions are small onions, about the size of a marble, peeled whole; they are still onions, with all the bite of a larger one, only sweeter and milder once cooked or pickled. Pickling means steeping them in a brine of vinegar, usually with salt, a little sugar and spice, which keeps their crunch and gives them a sharp, sweet-sour edge, so each one is a clean, bright bite.

On the Tuna Crudo the sheet calls them a bright counterpoint: against the cool, rich fish and the warm aguachile they reset the palate the way a cornichon does beside a pâté. They also answer the burnt orange, sharp against sweet.

The sheet prints the pickle and not its liquid, its sweetener or its spice, so promise none of that. The sheet's mark Alumn is unresolved; if it means allium, these are onions, so take any onion or allium question to the kitchen.

card.front: What are the pickled pearl onions on the crudo?
card.back: Small onions, marble-sized, peeled whole and steeped in a vinegar brine, so they stay crunchy and taste sharp and sweet-sour: the bright counterpoint to the rich fish. The pickle liquid is a lineup question.

components.name: Coriander
components.explain:
Coriander and cilantro are two names for one plant, Coriandrum sativum. In most American kitchens cilantro means the fresh leaves, soft, green and citrusy, and coriander means the dried seed, warm, sweet and faintly orange-scented when toasted and ground. In Britain the leaves are coriander too, so the one word can mean either part.

The sheet prints Coriander among the listed ingredients and again among its dietary marks, and does not say which part the kitchen uses. On a plate with raw tuna, a chilli sauce and a toasted seed condiment either makes sense: the leaf as a fresh garnish, the seed in the salsa seca. Ask at lineup and say what the kitchen tells you.

Some guests dislike the leaf, which to them tastes soapy; that is a taste, not a reaction. A guest who reports a reaction to coriander is sent to the service note and the kitchen, never dismissed as a dislike.

card.front: Is coriander the same as cilantro?
card.back: Yes, one plant: cilantro is the fresh leaf and coriander usually the seed in American kitchens. The sheet does not say which part the kitchen uses, so ask at lineup; a question about a reaction goes to the kitchen.

components.name: Carrot and ginger aguachile
components.explain:
Aguachile, ah-gwah-CHEE-leh, means chilli water. It is the raw seafood preparation of Sinaloa on Mexico's Pacific coast: in its classic form, raw shrimp are covered in lime juice blended with fresh chilli, with onion and cucumber, and eaten at once, before the acid has done more than brighten them. It is a cousin of ceviche, but faster and hotter, a sauce poured over rather than a cure.

Ours is the kitchen's own version for tuna: carrot for sweetness and colour, ginger for a clean warmth, with chilli for heat. The sheet names the sauce and nothing of its build: not the acid, the chilli, the proportions or how hot the finished batch is, and the classic recipe's lime, shrimp and cucumber are not promised on our plate.

Describe it as a sweet, warm, chilli-bright sauce over raw tuna, and confirm the heat with the kitchen before you call it mild.

card.front: What is the carrot and ginger aguachile?
card.back: Ah-gwah-CHEE-leh, chilli water: the raw seafood sauce of Sinaloa, classically lime and chilli over shrimp, served at once. Ours is the kitchen's own, with carrot and ginger over tuna; its heat is a lineup question.

components.name: Crudo meets aguachile
components.explain:
Two words from two coasts meet on this plate. Crudo is the Italian word for raw, and on a menu it names raw fish or seafood dressed simply, with oil, citrus or salt, at the last moment; it is the Italian cousin of sashimi and of ceviche. Aguachile is chilli water, the raw shrimp dish of Sinaloa on Mexico's Pacific coast, lime and fresh chilli poured over the seafood and eaten at once.

Our kitchen borrows the vocabulary of both and makes something of its own: raw tuna under a carrot and ginger aguachile, with a dry salsa of toasted chillies and seeds, burnt orange, pickled pearl onions, coriander and Maldon salt. The Sinaloa story is the inspiration, not a recipe: the carrot and ginger version is this house's.

It is a course on the Fall 2026 tasting menu, a fresh, citrus-led plate with spice at a Creole house on Royal Street.

card.front: Where does the Tuna Crudo come from?
card.back: From two words: crudo, Italian for raw fish dressed simply, and aguachile, the chilli water of Sinaloa on Mexico's Pacific coast. Our carrot and ginger version with tuna is the kitchen's own, on the Fall 2026 tasting menu.

components.name: Chocolate, in the crémeux
components.explain:
Chocolate is cocoa mass, the ground roasted bean, with cocoa butter and sugar; a milk chocolate adds milk solids, and the percentage on a bar is the share that comes from the cocoa bean. In a crémeux the chocolate is more than flavour: its cocoa butter firms as the cream cools, which is what gives the crémeux its dense, glossy set, so the bar chosen decides taste and texture.

The sheet names the chocolate only as chocolate, with no maker, origin or percentage, so promise neither dark nor milk and tell no plantation story; the kitchen says which bar it is. What you can say is what the plate does with it: a smooth, deep cream, bitter nibs for crunch, lemon oil for brightness and salt to make the chocolate taste more of itself. The sheet marks Chocolate among the plate's notes, so send any question about it to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: What does the chocolate do in the crémeux?
card.back: Its cocoa butter firms as the cream cools, giving the dense, glossy set, and its flavour leads. The sheet names no maker, origin or percentage, so the kitchen says which bar it is.

components.name: Cocoa nib crumble
components.explain:
Cocoa nibs are the roasted cocoa bean broken into small pieces, with the shell winnowed away: the raw material of chocolate before anything is added to it. They are crunchy and intensely cocoa, bitter and a little fruity, and they are not sweet; a guest who hears nibs and pictures chocolate chips should be told the difference at once.

On the Chocolate Crémeux the nibs come in a crumble, a baked, crumbly mixture that gives the smooth cream its crunch and its bitter edge, the way a crisp base does under a soft tart. The crumble is a compound preparation, and the sheet prints it as one line: its flour, its fat, any nuts or other ingredients are not listed, so a question about what is in it goes to the kitchen, never to a guess from the word cocoa.

card.front: What are cocoa nibs, and why a crumble?
card.back: Roasted cocoa bean broken into crunchy, bitter pieces, chocolate before sugar: not chocolate chips. The crumble gives the smooth cream its crunch; what else is in it is the kitchen's answer.

components.name: Lemon olive oil
components.explain:
A lemon olive oil is an olive oil that carries lemon, made in one of two ways: lemons crushed together with the olives at the press, so the oil takes the fruit as it is made, or a finished oil infused with lemon zest afterwards. Either way it tastes of good olive oil first, fruity and a little peppery, with a clean lemon lift behind it.

Olive oil on chocolate is a pairing pastry kitchens reach for because the oil's fruit and pepper cut the richness of a chocolate cream without adding sugar, and the lemon makes the whole plate taste brighter. On the Chocolate Crémeux it is the citrus accent the sheet names, against the dense cream and the bitter nibs. The producer, the method and whether the kitchen makes it in house are not printed, so describe the taste and leave the rest to lineup.

card.front: What is lemon olive oil doing on chocolate?
card.back: An olive oil carrying lemon, pressed with the fruit or infused with zest. Its fruit and pepper cut the richness of the cream and the lemon brightens the plate; the maker and the method are not printed.

components.name: Maldon salt
components.explain:
Maldon salt is a flake sea salt made on the Essex coast of England, where seawater is drawn in and evaporated gently until the salt crystallises at the surface in hollow pyramids. Those pyramid-shaped flakes are the whole point: they are crisp and light, they dissolve quickly on the tongue, and a pinch gives a clean burst of salt with none of the harshness of a fine-ground salt.

It is a finishing salt, pinched over at the end rather than cooked in, and on the Chocolate Crémeux it does what salt always does to chocolate: it makes the chocolate taste more of itself and seems to make it sweeter, without adding sugar, while the crisp flakes add a second crunch beside the nibs. The sheet names it on the Tuna Crudo of the same tasting as well. Say the name as the sheet prints it, Maldon, and let the guest taste the flake.

card.front: What is Maldon salt, and why on chocolate?
card.back: A flake sea salt from the Essex coast of England, crisp hollow pyramids that dissolve fast. Pinched over at the end, it makes the chocolate taste more of itself and adds a second crunch.

producer.where: Maldon, on the Essex coast of England
producer.history:
Maldon Salt is the sea salt maker of the Essex coast of England whose name has become the word for a flake finishing salt. Seawater is drawn from the coast, filtered and evaporated slowly in open pans until the salt crystallises at the surface into hollow, pyramid-shaped flakes, which are raked out and dried; the pyramid is the shape the maker is known by. The flakes are crisp and light, dissolve quickly and give a clean salt taste, which is why kitchens keep a box at the pass to finish a plate rather than to season a pot.

At Brennan's the name is printed twice on the Fall 2026 sheets: as the finishing salt on the Chocolate Crémeux and on the Tuna Crudo, both courses of the Fall tasting menu.

components.name: Crémeux, the anglaise set with chocolate
components.explain:
Crémeux, kray-MUH, is French for creamy, and in pastry it names a family of set creams. The chocolate version starts as a crème anglaise, ahn-GLEZ: egg yolks and sugar whisked together, hot milk and cream poured in, then the custard stirred over gentle heat until it thickens enough to coat a spoon. That hot custard is poured over chopped chocolate and blended until it is a glossy emulsion, like a ganache made with custard instead of cream, and the cream is then chilled to set.

The texture is the point. Nothing is whipped in, so a crémeux is denser and silkier than a mousse and softer than a ganache: it holds a shape on the spoon and melts at once. Some kitchens add a little gelatine for a firmer set, and the sheet marks gelatine on ours; others let the chocolate's cocoa butter do the setting alone. Serving temperature matters to the texture, so learn it at lineup.

card.front: How is a chocolate crémeux made?
card.back: A crème anglaise custard poured hot over chocolate and blended to a glossy emulsion, then chilled to set: denser than a mousse, softer than ganache, with nothing whipped in. Ours is marked with gelatine.

components.name: Setting a cream with gelatine
components.explain:
Gelatine is a protein taken from animal collagen, the connective tissue of pork or beef skins and bones, or from fish; it comes as clear sheets or a powder. Softened in cold water, then melted into a warm base, it sets as the base cools into a gel that melts again at body temperature, which is why a gelatine-set cream feels cool and clean on the tongue and holds a shape on the plate.

In a chocolate crémeux gelatine is optional: a cream with enough chocolate sets on its cocoa butter alone, and a pastry kitchen adds a little gelatine when it wants a firmer, cleaner set that survives plating. The training sheet marks Gelatin on the Chocolate Crémeux, so treat it as present: a vegetarian guest's question goes to the kitchen, which also knows whether the gelatine is pork, beef or fish, and whether the course can be made without it.

card.front: Why does the sheet mark gelatine on the crémeux?
card.back: Gelatine, from animal collagen, gives a set cream a firmer, cleaner set that melts at body temperature. A crémeux can set on chocolate alone, but ours is marked with it, so its source is the kitchen's answer.

components.name: Crémeux, the pastry word for creamy
components.explain:
Crémeux is simply the French adjective creamy, and French pastry turned it into a noun for a particular kind of set cream: a crème anglaise emulsified with chocolate, or with a fruit purée, set cold and served smooth. It is a word from the professional pastry kitchen rather than a dish with a birthplace, so there is no inventor and no city to name, and the honest story is the texture: denser than a mousse, softer than a ganache, nothing whipped in.

On the Fall 2026 tasting menu the crémeux is the chocolate course, built as a study in contrast: smooth cream, crunchy bitter nibs, bright lemon oil and crisp salt. Our dinner tasting closes with The Snickers and a glass of Banyuls, chocolate's classic partner; the Fall tasting's crémeux is chocolate in the French pastry idiom instead, and the Banyuls fits it as well. The salt gives the plate its one named origin, the Essex coast of England.

card.front: Where does the word crémeux come from?
card.back: From the French for creamy: a pastry kitchen's word for a set cream of custard and chocolate, not a dish with a birthplace. Tell the texture story, not an inventor, and name the salt's Essex coast.

components.name: Black pepper
components.explain:
Black pepper is the dried berry of a vine native to the Malabar Coast of Kerala in south-western India; green, black and white peppercorns all come from the same vine at different stages. Tellicherry is a grade of large, late-picked Malabar peppercorn named for an old pepper port. Its heat is slow and warming, from a compound called piperine, and sits at the back of the mouth, unlike the sharp front heat of chilli.

Two of our sauces are built on it. New Orleans barbecue sauce, on the Louisiana Oysters and the Louisiana BBQ Lobster, is butter with plenty of black pepper, which is why the guide says peppery, not hot. A mignonette is shallot, vinegar and coarsely cracked pepper, and the French word mignonnette means that crack; ours, on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters, adds preserved Fresno chilli. Which grade the kitchen buys is a question for the chef.

card.front: What makes New Orleans barbecue sauce peppery?
card.back: Black pepper, the dried berry of an Indian vine, cooked into the butter: slow, warming heat, not chilli heat. Cracked coarse, it names the mignonette on the Grand Isle oysters.

producer.who: Black pepper, Piper nigrum, of the Malabar Coast (no grade or supplier is printed)
producer.where: The Malabar Coast of Kerala, south-western India; Vietnam is today's largest grower
producer.history:
Pepper is the dried fruit of Piper nigrum, a climbing vine of the Malabar Coast of Kerala in south-western India, where it has been grown and traded for thousands of years. Green peppercorns are the unripe berries, black ones the unripe berries dried until the skin wrinkles and darkens, and white ones the ripe berries with the skin soaked off, so the three are one plant at different stages.

Tellicherry is a grade of large peppercorn left longer on the vine, named for the port the British shipped pepper from in the 1600s, now called Thalassery. The trade has moved: by the International Pepper Community's count Vietnam grew 43 per cent of the world's 561,500 tonnes in 2020, the most of any country, with Brazil, Indonesia, India and Sri Lanka behind it.

Cooks buy pepper whole and crack or grind it to order, because its aroma fades within hours of grinding. The menus print no grade or supplier; the pepper behind the barbecue sauce and the mignonette is a question for the chef.
facts: Piper nigrum is native to the Malabar Coast of Kerala, south-western India.
Green, black and white peppercorns are one vine's berry at different stages of ripeness and preparation.
Tellicherry is a grade of large, late-picked peppercorn named for the port now called Thalassery.
In 2020 Vietnam grew 43 per cent of the world's pepper by the trade body's count, the most of any country.
Its slow, warming heat comes from piperine; chilli heat comes from a different compound.
notes: Say peppery, not hot, for the barbecue sauce on the Louisiana Oysters and the BBQ Lobster: black pepper warms, it does not burn.
The mignonette is named for its cracked pepper; mignonnette is the French word for that coarse crack.
No grade or supplier is printed: never name Tellicherry or any brand as the house pepper.
producer.sayIt: Black pepper is the dried berry of an Indian vine from the Malabar Coast, and it is what makes our New Orleans barbecue sauce peppery rather than hot.
askKitchen: Which pepper do we buy, and is it cracked to order for the mignonette?

components.name: Bittersweet and milk chocolate
components.explain:
Chocolate is made from the fermented, roasted seeds of the cacao tree, which is native to the upper Amazon; the oldest trace of its use, about 5,300 years old, was found in Ecuador. Ground, the seeds become chocolate liquor, and its share sets the style. In the United States a bittersweet or semisweet bar holds at least 35 per cent chocolate liquor, and pastry cooks usually mean 60 to 72 per cent cacao: dark, with enough sugar to bake. Milk chocolate holds at least 10 per cent liquor and 12 per cent milk solids, sweeter and softer.

The Café Brûlot Coffee Cake bakes bittersweet chocolate with chicory coffee, which deepens it, since coffee and chocolate share roasted, bitter notes. The Snickers' Bavarian milk chocolate is read as milk chocolate in a Bavarian cream, not chocolate from Bavaria. No maker is printed: a question for the chef. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: What is the difference between bittersweet and milk chocolate?
card.back: Bittersweet holds at least 35 per cent chocolate liquor, usually 60 to 72 per cent cacao, dark and only lightly sweet; milk chocolate holds less liquor and adds milk solids, sweeter and softer. The coffee cake takes the first, the Snickers the second.

sources: research/producers-food-european-protected-2026-10-06.md (section 11, the Snickers' chocolate maker not named)

components.name: Spiced citrus glaze
components.explain:
A glaze on a cake is sugar dissolved in a little liquid and set thin over the top: icing sugar beaten with citrus juice, or a syrup of sugar, juice and zest boiled briefly and brushed over the warm cake so it soaks in and dries to a sheen. It adds sweetness and shine, and here it carries the flavours the cake is named for.

Café brûlot, the New Orleans coffee flamed at the table, is made with orange and lemon peel, cinnamon and clove, and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake borrows those: the glaze is where the citrus and the warm spice live, over the chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake, with pecans for crunch and whipped crème fraîche to cut the sweetness. The menu prints only spiced citrus glaze. Which citrus, which spices, and whether any brandy goes into it, as it does into the drink, are questions for the chef.

card.front: What is the spiced citrus glaze on the coffee cake?
card.back: A thin sugar glaze carrying the café brûlot flavours, citrus peel and warm spice such as cinnamon and clove, over the chicory coffee and chocolate cake. Exactly what is in it is the chef's to say.

sources: guide.txt (the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake card)

components.name: Local raspberries
components.explain:
A raspberry is a cluster of tiny drupelets around a hollow core, which makes it the most fragile of the soft fruits: picked ripe, it keeps a day or two and bruises at a touch. It is sharper than a strawberry and more perfumed than a blackberry. Raspberries are hard to grow in Louisiana's heat; the LSU AgCenter said in 2015 that the one variety that does reasonably well here is Dorman Red, bred at Mississippi State for the southern states and grown like a blackberry.

The Framboise French Toast prints local raspberries, fresh on top, beside the raspberry coulis, so the fruit comes twice: cooked and sieved in the sauce, raw and bright on the plate. Framboise is French for raspberry. Which farm the berries come from, and whether local means Louisiana or the wider Gulf South, are questions for the chef, and the fruit may change when the season does.

card.front: Why does the French toast print local raspberries as well as a coulis?
card.back: The fruit comes twice: cooked and sieved in the coulis, fresh on top. Raspberries are fragile and hard to grow in Louisiana's heat, so the farm is a question for the chef.

components.name: Heirloom tomatoes
components.explain:
An heirloom tomato is an open-pollinated variety whose saved seed grows true, year after year, unlike a hybrid, whose seed is made by crossing two parents each season. How old a variety must be is not agreed, fifty years by one rule, a hundred by another. Heirlooms are grown for flavour and colour, not for shipping: thin skins, odd shapes, red, pink, yellow, green and near-black, like the dusky Cherokee Purple or the big pink Brandywine. They crack and bruise, so they are sold close to home.

On the Creole Tomato Tostada they are mixed with Creole tomatoes, Louisiana's summer tomato, and served raw with burrata, the okra tostada and smoked tomato water. The menu prints Louisiana heirloom, so the fruit is local; which farm grows it is a question for the chef, and the dish goes when the tomatoes do.

card.front: What makes a tomato an heirloom?
card.back: An open-pollinated variety whose saved seed grows true, kept for decades for flavour and colour rather than shipping. Mixed raw with Creole tomatoes on our seasonal tostada.

components.name: Worcestershire sauce
components.explain:
Worcestershire sauce is a thin, dark, fermented seasoning first sold in 1837 by two chemists in Worcester, England, Lea & Perrins, and the firm still makes it there. The bottle lists vinegar, molasses, sugar, salt, anchovies, tamarind, onion, garlic and spices, so it is salty, sour, sweet and deeply savoury at once, and because of the anchovies it is a fish product for a guest who asks. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

It is the savoury backbone of New Orleans barbecue shrimp, the pan sauce of butter, black pepper, Worcestershire, garlic and lemon born at Pascal's Manale in 1954, the style the guide gives for the barbecue sauce on the Louisiana Oysters and the Louisiana BBQ Lobster. A classic Caesar dressing carries it too, though ours is a smoked oyster dressing. Whether our barbecue sauce and that dressing use it, and which brand, are questions for the chef.

card.front: What is Worcestershire sauce, and why does it matter on the oysters?
card.back: A fermented English seasoning of vinegar, molasses, anchovies and tamarind, first sold in 1837. It is the savoury depth of New Orleans barbecue sauce, and a fish product; send that question to the kitchen.

sources: guide.txt (the Louisiana Oysters card: savory Worcestershire)

producer.who: Worcestershire sauce, the Worcester original of Lea & Perrins (the menu names no brand)
producer.where: Worcester, England; made on Midland Road since 1897
producer.history:
Worcestershire sauce began with two chemists of Broad Street, Worcester, John Wheeley Lea and William Henry Perrins, partners from 1823. The company's story says a governor of Bengal, Lord Sandys, brought a recipe home from India and asked them to make it up, and that the first batch was so harsh it was left in casks and forgotten until it had mellowed; the firm itself allows that the recipe's origin is unclear, and the story is tradition rather than record. The sauce went on sale in 1837, by some accounts reaching the public in 1838 once the casks had matured.

It has been made in a factory on Midland Road in Worcester since 1897. The company passed to HP Foods in 1930 and, with HP, to Heinz in 2005. The British bottle lists malt vinegar, spirit vinegar, molasses, sugar, salt, anchovies, tamarind extract, onion, garlic, spices and flavourings; the American bottle is built on distilled white vinegar and molasses and lists anchovies too.

In New Orleans it is the savoury depth of barbecue shrimp, the Pascal's Manale pan sauce of 1954, and so of the barbecue sauce on our Louisiana Oysters and BBQ Lobster. The menus print no brand, and whether the house sauce uses it at all is the chef's to confirm.
facts: First sold in 1837 by the Worcester chemists John Wheeley Lea and William Henry Perrins, partners since 1823.
The Lord Sandys story, a recipe brought home from Bengal, is company tradition; the recipe's origin is unclear.
Made on Midland Road, Worcester, since 1897.
Owned by HP Foods from 1930 and by Heinz since 2005.
The British bottle lists vinegar, molasses, sugar, salt, anchovies, tamarind, onion, garlic and spices.
The American bottle is built on distilled white vinegar and molasses, with anchovies.
notes: Anchovies make it a fish product: if the house sauce or the Caesar dressing carries it, a guest avoiding fish should hear so, and that question goes to the kitchen before the order.
The menus print no brand; never say Lea & Perrins as the house sauce until the chef confirms it.
Guests enjoy hearing the name said plainly; use the respelling beside the name.
producer.sayIt: Worcestershire is the English fermented sauce of vinegar, molasses, anchovies and tamarind, first sold in 1837, and it is the savoury depth in New Orleans barbecue sauce.
askKitchen: Does our New Orleans barbecue sauce use Worcestershire, and which brand?
Does the smoked oyster dressing on the Creole Caesar carry Worcestershire or anchovy?

components.name: Vinaigrette
components.explain:
A vinaigrette is an acid and a fat whisked together with seasoning: the French rule of thumb is about three parts oil to one part vinegar, with salt, pepper and often mustard or shallot to help the two hold for a few minutes. It is a temporary emulsion, so it is whisked again before each use. The word is the diminutive of vinaigre, vinegar.

A warm vinaigrette swaps some or all of the oil for warm fat and is spooned over at once. On the Louisiana Crab Claws the fat is brown butter, cooked until nutty and toasty, then balanced with acidity so it is rich but bright, finished with fines herbes. The guide says the claws come warm; warming cooked claws through rather than cooking them again is what keeps the meat sliding off the cartilage. Which acid the kitchen uses, lemon or vinegar, and whether shallot is in it, are questions for the chef.

card.front: What is a vinaigrette, and what is unusual about the crab claws' one?
card.back: Acid and fat whisked together, about three to one, a temporary emulsion. Ours is warm, made on brown butter instead of oil, balanced with acid and finished with fines herbes on the crab claws.

sources: research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (brown butter vinaigrette; cook's notes on warming the claws)

components.name: Pickling
components.explain:
There are two kinds of pickle. A quick pickle, a restaurant kitchen's usual, steeps vegetables or fruit in a brine of vinegar, water, salt, sugar and spice, often poured hot, and is ready in hours; nothing ferments. A fermented pickle sits in a salt brine alone and bacteria turn its sugars to lactic acid over three or four weeks, the way sauerkraut is made. A hot brine softens and seasons fast; a cold one keeps the crunch.

Our menus pickle more than cucumbers. The Louisiana Oysters print pickled collard greens, a sharp bite against the buttery barbecue sauce; the Redfish Véronique has grapes pickled with hibiscus, sweet, tart and floral; the Fried Pickles are a medley of housemade pickles and the Roost Burger prints pickles. Whether the preserved Fresno chilli on the Grand Isle oysters is salted or pickled, which brine, how long, and what is in tonight's medley are questions for the chef.

card.front: What is the difference between a quick pickle and a fermented one?
card.back: A quick pickle steeps in a vinegar brine and is ready in hours; a fermented pickle sours in salt brine over weeks. Our collards, hibiscus grapes and housemade pickles: ask the chef which.

components.name: Whipping cream
components.explain:
Whipping beats air into fat. As cold cream is whisked, its fat globules partly join and trap the bubbles, so the cream thickens to soft peaks, then firm; a minute more and it turns grainy and then to butter. Cream needs about 30 per cent fat to hold air, and United States heavy cream is at least 36 per cent, which is what a kitchen whips. Everything must be cold, the cream and the bowl.

The same technique lightens richer creams. The Framboise French Toast prints a mascarpone mousse, the rich Italian fresh cheese whipped light with cream; the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake prints whipped crème fraîche, whose tang keeps the cake from being too sweet; the Pineapple Tarte Tatin prints a whipped vanilla mousse, the Snickers' Bavarian cream is lightened with whipped cream, and the children's Vanilla French Toast prints whipped cream plainly. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: Why must cream be cold and rich to whip?
card.back: Cold fat globules join and trap the air; cream under about 30 per cent fat will not hold it, and over-beating turns it to butter. We whip cream, mascarpone and crème fraîche the same way.

components.name: Eggs
components.explain:
The egg is the breakfast kitchen's first ingredient: a white of water and protein around a yolk of fat, protein and lecithin, the emulsifier that lets a yolk hold butter in a hollandaise. The fresher the egg, the tighter the white holds when poached, and a hen that forages lays a deeper orange yolk.

Our menus cook eggs many ways: soft poached on the Hussarde and the Sardou, soft-boiled on the Owen, sunny-side up on the waffle and the breakfast hanger, folded into the Crab & Corn Omelette, any style as a side, grated hard-boiled over the Turtle Soup, and cured and grated over the tartare cannoli. The yolk also makes the hollandaise, béarnaise, Choron and Foyot.

The menus name Vital Farms on the breakfast hanger and, on the fall sheet, the fall tartare's yolk; whose eggs go into the other plates is a question for the chef. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: How many ways do we cook eggs, and whose eggs are they?
card.back: Poached, soft-boiled, sunny-side up, folded, any style, grated and cured, and the yolk makes four sauces. Vital Farms is printed on the breakfast hanger and the fall tartare's yolk; ask the chef about the rest.

components.name: Butter
components.explain:
Butter is cream churned until its fat gathers and the buttermilk runs off: about eighty per cent milk fat, with water and milk solids. The solids are what brown in a beurre noisette and what burn, so a kitchen clarifies butter, melting it and lifting off the clear fat, for hollandaise and for sautéing fish at a high heat. Cold butter whisked into a reduction makes a beurre blanc; soft butter beaten with foie gras or miso makes a compound butter.

Butter is in nearly every savoury plate we serve. It is the body of the hollandaise, béarnaise, Choron and Foyot, the beurre blanc on the redfish, the brown butter on the crab claws and in the turtle soup, the New Orleans BBQ sauce, the garlic butter finish on the Brabant potatoes, and the pan the Bananas Foster begins in.

Whose butter the kitchen buys is not printed. Questions about dairy go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: Where does butter do its work on our menus?
card.back: In every warm emulsion, hollandaise to beurre blanc, in brown butter, the BBQ sauce, the compound butters and the pan the Foster starts in. Dairy questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

components.name: Shallots
components.explain:
The shallot is a small, copper-skinned member of the onion family, growing in clusters like garlic, with a finer, sweeter flavour than an onion and none of its harshness once cooked. Minced, it dissolves into a sauce; sliced raw, it keeps a gentle bite.

French sauce cooking begins with it. Béarnaise, and so the Choron on the Sardou and the Foyot on the Chateaubriand, starts with shallot reduced in vinegar with tarragon; a beurre blanc starts the same way with white wine; a mignonette is raw shallot in vinegar; a mustard cream sauce sweats it in butter. Brennan's own published marchand de vin sweats onion, shallot and garlic together, though tonight's build is the chef's to confirm.

The menu prints shallots twice, on the Louisiana Oysters and beside the turnips of the Poussin à la Moutarde. Everywhere else they are inside the sauce, and a guest who asks about onions should hear so.

card.front: Which of our sauces begin with shallot?
card.back: Béarnaise and its daughters Choron and Foyot, beurre blanc, the mignonette and the mustard cream; our published marchand de vin sweats shallot with onion and garlic. Printed on the oysters and the poussin.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p10, p12, p18, p23, p27; the Eggs Sardou and Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak cards)
research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (section 6, Eggs Hussarde, marchand de vin properly)

components.name: Garlic
components.explain:
Garlic is a bulb of the onion family, its cloves sharp and sulphurous raw, sweet and mellow once cooked. Sliced and warmed in butter or oil it perfumes the fat; minced raw it bites; a whole clove simmered in a stock almost disappears. It burns easily, and burnt garlic turns a sauce bitter.

In the Creole kitchen it is so often added to the holy trinity that cooks joke it is the pope, and it belongs in the Creole sauce under our shrimp. It is printed on the garlic spinach of the Petite Filet Mignon, and it is the finish of the Brabant potatoes, tossed in garlic butter and parsley. A New Orleans bordelaise is a garlic butter, the reading the guide asks you to confirm for the pecan sauce on the Gulf fish, and a persillade is parsley and garlic.

Brennan's own published marchand de vin carries garlic; whether tonight's does is for the chef.

card.front: Where is garlic at work on our plates?
card.back: The garlic spinach, the Brabant potatoes, the Creole sauce, the persillade on the dinner hanger, and the New Orleans garlic butter the pecan bordelaise most likely is. Confirm the marchand de vin with the chef.

items: Grilled Cheese Sandwich with Brabant Potatoes
sources: guide.txt (pdf p5, p22; the Brabant Potatoes and Creole Hanger Steak cards)

components.name: Parsley
components.explain:
Parsley is the kitchen's green workhorse, the flat-leaf kind in most restaurant kitchens because its flavour is cleaner and stronger than the curly sort. Chopped fine at the last moment it tastes fresh, grassy and faintly peppery; cooked long it fades to almost nothing, which is why it goes on at the end.

It is one of the four fines herbes on the crab claws, half of the persillade on the dinner hanger with garlic and pepitas, the classic green in a gremolata with lemon zest, and the finish of the Brabant potatoes with garlic butter. A New Orleans bordelaise, the family the pecan sauce most likely belongs to, is butter, garlic and parsley. The Grand Isle Jewel oysters print it plainly beside the mignonette.

Which herbs go into tonight's gremolata on the omelette is the chef's answer; say herbs, citrus and almonds until you know.

card.front: Where is parsley on our menus?
card.back: Printed on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters; in the fines herbes, the persillade, the gremolata and the Brabant finish; and in a New Orleans garlic butter, which the pecan bordelaise most likely is.
