components.name: Tarragon
components.explain:
Tarragon is the herb of French sauce cooking, a slender green leaf with a sweet anise scent, close to liquorice but lighter. It is tender, bruises easily and loses its perfume in long cooking, so it goes into a reduction at the start and fresh again at the end.

It is what makes a béarnaise taste different from a hollandaise: the vinegar reduction is made with shallot and tarragon, and chopped leaves finish the sauce. That is the tarragon in the béarnaise on the breakfast hanger, in the Choron on the Eggs Sardou, where tomato joins it, and in the Foyot on the Chateaubriand, where a meat glaze does. On the Louisiana Crab Claws it is one of the fines herbes with parsley, chives and chervil.

A guest who asks what the herbal note in the Sardou sauce is can be told tarragon with confidence; the guide's own words are tangy and herbal.

card.front: What gives béarnaise, Choron and Foyot their herbal note?
card.back: Tarragon, with its sweet anise scent, reduced with shallot and vinegar at the start and chopped in at the end. It is also one of the fines herbes on the crab claws.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p12, p18, p23, p24, p50; the Eggs Sardou, Louisiana Crab Claws and Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak cards)

components.name: Red wine in the kitchen
components.explain:
Red wine in a pan does three things: its acid brightens, its tannin and colour deepen a sauce, and as it reduces its fruit concentrates into something savoury and winey. Boiling drives off most of the alcohol but never all of it, and a sauce reduced by half carries the wine's character strongly, so a thin, sharp wine makes a thin, sharp sauce.

Two of our plates are built on it. The marchand de vin, the wine merchant's sauce under the eggs on the Hussarde and the Owen, is red wine cooked with aromatics and beef stock into a glossy brown sauce. The short rib on the Eggs Owen is braised in red wine for hours, and the braising liquid, skimmed and reduced, becomes the gravy the débris falls into.

Which wine the kitchen cooks with is not printed. A guest who avoids alcohol should know both plates carry it, as the service note says.

card.front: Which plates carry red wine, and where is it?
card.back: Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen: the marchand de vin is a red wine and mushroom sauce, and the Owen's short rib is braised in red wine. Tell a guest who avoids alcohol.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p2, p17 to p19; the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen service notes)
research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (section 6, Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen, cook's notes)

components.name: Mushrooms
components.explain:
Mushrooms give a kitchen savour without meat: their glutamates are the same source of depth that aged cheese and cured ham carry, and cooking concentrates it. Sweated in butter they give up their water and brown; sliced into a brown sauce they deepen its flavour.

The marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen is, in the guide's best words, a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce, and Brennan's own published recipe sweats mushrooms with onion, shallot and garlic before the stock and wine go in. Whether tonight's sauce carries them, and which kind, is a question for the chef before you promise it.

Named mushrooms stand on two other plates with cards of their own: the preserved shiitake on the Blackened Tofu and the dinner side Maggie's Mushrooms, whose varieties are learnt at lineup.

card.front: Where are mushrooms on our menus?
card.back: Inside the marchand de vin on the Hussarde and the Owen, a red wine and mushroom sauce to confirm with the chef; preserved shiitake on the Blackened Tofu; and the Maggie's Mushrooms side.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p2, p17; the Maggie's Mushrooms and Blackened Tofu cards)
research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (section 6, Eggs Hussarde, marchand de vin properly)

components.name: Spinach
components.explain:
Spinach is a tender leaf that is mostly water: a pan heaped with it wilts to a few spoonfuls in a minute, and it must be squeezed hard or it waters down whatever it joins. Its flavour is mineral and faintly bitter, which is why butter, cream and garlic suit it so well.

We serve it three ways. Creamed, under the eggs on the Sardou with Parmesan and as a breakfast side, it is cooked down in cream until silky, as the guide says. Wilted with garlic beside the Petite Filet Mignon, it stays light and green. Wilted in brown butter and folded through the Turtle Soup, it turns nutty.

Whether the side and the Sardou's spinach are one preparation, and whether either carries stock, is confirmed with the kitchen for a guest who asks about meat. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: How do we serve spinach, and what should you confirm?
card.back: Creamed under the Eggs Sardou and as a side, wilted with garlic beside the filet, and in brown butter through the turtle soup. Confirm stock and Parmesan with the kitchen.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p5, p14, p18; the Creamed Spinach card and service note)

components.name: Tomatoes
components.explain:
The tomato is a mark of Creole cooking: a bright tomato base is what most often separates a Creole sauce from a Cajun gravy. Cooked down it gives sweetness, acid and body; raw and ripe it is juice and perfume.

On our menus it is cooked into two sauces: the Creole sauce on the Shrimp & Grits, where it simmers with the holy trinity and tasso, and the Choron on the Eggs Sardou, where tomato cooked to a thick paste is folded into béarnaise. It is printed on the Gulf Fish en Papillote, steamed in the parcel with the fish, cooked slowly into the tomato jam on the Roost Burger, and served at its ripest as the Creole tomatoes of the summer tostada, which have a card of their own.

A guest who asks why the Sardou sauce is coral-coloured should hear the answer: tomato in the béarnaise.

card.front: Where does tomato go on our menus?
card.back: Into the Creole sauce under the shrimp and the Choron on the Sardou; steamed in the en papillote, as jam on the Roost Burger, and ripe as the Creole tomatoes of the summer tostada.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p11, p18, p21, p26, p50; the Roost Burger line)
research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (section 6, Eggs Sardou and Shrimp & Grits)

components.name: Potatoes
components.explain:
Potatoes divide into two families. Starchy ones, the russets, bake fluffy and fry crisp; waxy ones, the fingerlings and new potatoes, hold their shape and stay creamy when boiled. A kitchen chooses by the job.

Ours do many jobs. The Brabant potatoes are cubes fried golden and tossed in garlic butter and parsley, the breakfast side and the children's partner for shrimp and grilled cheese. The Eggs Owen carries a Creole-spiced potato with the short rib. The breakfast hanger has a smoked potato pavé of thin layers pressed and seared; the Petite Filet Mignon a rösti of grated potato fried into a cake; the Redfish Véronique braised leeks and fingerlings; the Steak Tartare Cannoli a shell made from potato and fried. Fries come with the Roost's pink sauce and the children's dinners.

How the Creole-spiced potato on the Owen is cut and cooked is not printed; ask the chef before you describe it.

card.front: How many ways do potatoes appear on our menus?
card.back: Brabant cubes, the Owen's Creole-spiced potato, the smoked pavé, the rösti, fingerlings with the redfish, the tartare's fried potato shell and fries. Ask the chef how the Owen's potato is cooked.

components.name: Chives
components.explain:
Chives are the smallest and mildest of the onion family, hollow green stems snipped rather than chopped, with a fresh, gently oniony taste that disappears in heat. They go on at the end or into something cold, and they colour a plate green.

On our menus they are baked into the cornbread and chive waffle under the duck confit, where they turn a sweet Southern batter savoury; they are one of the four fines herbes tossed through the brown butter vinaigrette on the Louisiana Crab Claws; and at the Roost they flavour the chive rémoulade with the Crawfish Meat Pies and the chive cream that cools the Fried Pickles.

If a guest asks whether the green flecks are onion, say chives, the mild cousin of the onion.

card.front: Where do chives appear on our menus?
card.back: In the cornbread and chive waffle under the duck confit, among the fines herbes on the crab claws, and at the Roost in the chive rémoulade and the chive cream.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p12, p20; the Roost menu lines)

components.name: Wheat flour
components.explain:
Wheat flour is milled wheat, its gluten the stretchy protein that lets a dough rise and a batter cling, and the reason flour questions go to the kitchen. Soft flour makes tender biscuits and pastry; strong flour makes bread; a roux is flour cooked in fat to thicken a gumbo or a brown sauce.

Rarely printed, nearly always present: the Hussarde's English muffins, the biscuit, the French toast's brioche, the tarte Tatin's puff pastry, the roux the guide expects in the gumbo and turtle soup and the house's roux card allows in the marchand de vin and rice dressing, the likely coatings on the crispy artichokes, the grit cake, the fried hen and the fried shrimp, and the bread crisps on the Caesar.

Because so much is hidden, a question about flour, gluten or a shared fryer goes to the kitchen every time, never to memory. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: Where is wheat flour hiding on our menus?
card.back: In the breads, biscuit, brioche and pastry, in the roux of the gumbo and turtle soup, and in fried coatings. Questions about flour or gluten go to the service note and the kitchen.

components.name: Mustard
components.explain:
Mustard is the ground seed of a plant in the cabbage family, mixed with liquid. Crushed and wetted, the seed releases its sharp heat, and the seed and liquid set the style. Dijon is brown seed with white wine and vinegar, smooth and sharp; whole-grain leaves the seeds whole; yellow is the mild one.

Heat dulls it, so it goes in at the end. On the Duck Confit Waffle it sharpens maple syrup into a mustard maple syrup, sweet and tangy against the duck fat and foie gras butter. On the Poussin à la Moutarde it finishes a mustard cream sauce, the Burgundian bistro pairing with chicken; the classic stirs it in off the heat. The chive rémoulade on the Crawfish Meat Pies carries it too, French or Creole.

Which mustard the kitchen uses, Dijon or whole-grain, is not printed on any plate, so say mustard, as the menu does, until the chef tells you more.

card.front: Which plates carry mustard, and which mustard is it?
card.back: The mustard maple syrup on the Duck Confit Waffle, the mustard cream sauce on the Poussin à la Moutarde and the chive rémoulade at the Roost. Dijon or whole-grain is not printed; say mustard and ask the chef.

producer.who: Dijon mustard, the kind and maker not printed
producer.where: Dijon and Burgundy, France; the seed today largely from Canada
producer.history:
Dijon has been France's mustard town for centuries, and the modern style dates from 1856, when Jean Naigeon of Dijon replaced the vinegar in his mustard with verjuice, the sour juice of unripe grapes. Today's Dijon is brown mustard seed ground with white wine, vinegar, water and salt in place of that verjuice: smooth, pale and sharp.

The name is not protected. A 1937 decree defined Dijon mustard by its method, not its town, so the name is generic: it can be made anywhere. France needs about 35,000 tonnes of seed a year and buys about 80 per cent of it from Canada, from the prairies of Alberta and Saskatchewan; when drought there halved the crop in 2021, French shelves ran short of Dijon in 2022. The protected name is Moutarde de Bourgogne, an IGP registered in 2009, which must be made with seed grown in Burgundy and Bourgogne white wine; Edmond Fallot of Beaune makes one with Bourgogne Aligoté. The best-known old name is Maille, founded in Paris in 1747 by Antoine-Claude Maille, a supplier to the court of Louis XV, which Maurice Grey of Grey Poupon bought in 1885.

Brennan's prints mustard twice, in the mustard maple syrup on the Duck Confit Waffle and the mustard cream sauce on the Poussin à la Moutarde, and names no kind or maker. The guide calls Burgundy Dijon mustard's home when it pairs the poussin with a Mâcon, a fair line for the table, but not a claim that the kitchen's mustard is Dijon.

components.name: Basil
components.explain:
Basil is the sweet, clove-scented herb of the Mediterranean summer, at its best raw or barely warmed: heat and time turn it dark and dull, so a kitchen tears or slices it at the last moment. Sweet Italian basil is the kind most kitchens keep, and it loves tomato, corn, lemon and butter.

The menu prints it once, on the Crab & Corn Omelette, with lemon and the house-made miso butter, where it keeps a rich plate fresh and gives the guide its words, a bright herbal crunch, beside the Marcona almond gremolata. Whether it is torn into the filling, scattered over the top or blended into the gremolata is the chef's detail.

On the food menus the omelette is its only home, so do not promise it elsewhere; a guest who dislikes it can ask the kitchen whether it can be left off.

card.front: Where is basil on our menus, and what does it do?
card.back: Only on the Crab & Corn Omelette, with lemon and miso butter, where its fresh, clove-scented leaf keeps the rich eggs and crab bright. How it is added is the chef's detail.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p22 to p23, the Crab & Corn Omelette card)

components.name: Beef short rib
components.explain:
Short ribs are cut from the lower rib cage, the plate and chuck end of the animal, where layers of meat, fat and connective tissue sit on short lengths of bone. Grilled quickly they are chewy; cooked slowly the collagen melts to gelatin, the meat turns soft and gives a rich gravy, which is why kitchens braise them.

On the Eggs Owen the short rib is braised in red wine until it falls apart and pulled into its own reduced liquid, the débris under the egg and the two sauces. At the Roost the same cut is ground: two beef short rib patties, marbled enough to stay juicy, make the Roost Burger.

The menu names Creekstone Farms on the hanger steaks and the Chateaubriand but not on the short rib; whose beef it is, and how the patties are cooked, are questions for the chef.

card.front: What is short rib, and where do we serve it?
card.back: A marbled, sinewy cut from the lower ribs that braising turns soft: the red wine-braised débris on the Eggs Owen and, ground, the two patties of the Roost Burger. Whose beef is the chef's answer.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p19; the Roost Burger line)

components.name: Vinegar
components.explain:
Vinegar is wine, cider or grain alcohol fermented a second time into acetic acid, sharp and clean, and each kind carries a little of what it was made from. In the kitchen a spoonful does what lemon does: it brightens, cuts fat and balances sweetness.

It is the start of the hollandaise family's sharper daughters: béarnaise, and so the Choron on the Sardou and the Foyot on the Chateaubriand, begins with vinegar reduced with shallot and tarragon, and the guide notes the vinegar in the Sardou's sauce when it chooses the wine. A beurre blanc reduces vinegar and white wine; a mignonette is raw shallot in vinegar; a vinaigrette, like the brown butter one on the crab claws, is fat sharpened with acid.

It is also the pickle: the pickled collards on the Louisiana Oysters, the hibiscus-pickled grapes on the redfish, and the housemade pickles fried at the Roost and the pickles on the burger.

card.front: Where does vinegar work on our plates?
card.back: In the reductions under béarnaise, Choron, Foyot and beurre blanc, in the mignonette and the brown butter vinaigrette, and in every pickle: the collards, the grapes and the Roost's pickles.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p10 to p12, p18, p23 to p25; the Eggs Sardou pairing palate line)

components.name: Mayonnaise
components.explain:
Mayonnaise is a cold emulsion: egg yolk whisked with a little acid, then oil added slowly until the yolk's lecithin holds it in a thick, pale cream. It is the hollandaise idea without the heat, and the base of most of the South's cold sauces.

On our menus it is the binder in the pimento cheese folded into the grit cake under the Shrimp & Grits, cheddar and sweet pimientos held together with it. Across the South a pink sauce for fries and a burger's special sauce are usually mayonnaise with ketchup or tomato, pickle and spice, the family the Roost's Pink Sauce and the Roost Burger's special sauce most likely belong to, and a French rémoulade is mayonnaise with mustard, capers and herbs, where a Creole one may skip it.

None of those recipes is printed, nor whether the kitchen makes its mayonnaise or buys it; egg questions and recipe questions go to the kitchen.

card.front: Where is mayonnaise at work on our menus?
card.back: Binding the pimento cheese in the grit cake, and most likely in the Roost's pink sauce, the burger's special sauce and, if it is the French style, the chive rémoulade; none is printed, so the kitchen confirms.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p20 to p21; the Roost menu lines)

components.name: Curing with salt and sugar
components.explain:
Curing is the oldest way of keeping meat: salt pulls water out, seasons it through and firms it, and sugar softens the salt and feeds the browning. A dry cure is rubbed on; a brine is a salted bath. The cured thing is then smoked, roasted, confited or fried.

Our menus carry several. The Hussarde's Canadian bacon is pork loin cured with salt, sugar and ground coffee, then smoked or roasted. The waffle's duck leg is cured in salt before it is cooked slowly in fat; the classic cure adds garlic and herbs. Tasso in the Shrimp & Grits sauce is cured, spiced, hot-smoked pork shoulder. The Cornish hen is brined in sweet tea before frying. The tartare's egg yolk is buried in salt and sugar until it grates. The other bacons, from the breakfast side to the Succotash, are cured pork belly.

How long any of these cures, and which are made in house, are the chef's answers.

card.front: What does a cure do, and which of our plates carry one?
card.back: Salt and sugar season meat through and firm it before smoking, roasting or confit. The coffee-cured bacon, the duck confit, tasso, the sweet tea brine, the cured yolk and every bacon.

components.name: Compound butter
components.explain:
A compound butter is soft butter beaten with something that flavours it, then chilled so a slice or a spoonful can be dropped onto hot food and melt into a sauce on the plate. The French classic is maître d'hôtel butter, with parsley and lemon, for a grilled steak; a kitchen can beat in herbs, garlic, anchovy, miso, foie gras or toasted nuts.

The plate's own heat finishes it.

Two of our plates print one. The foie gras butter on the Duck Confit Waffle is fattened liver puréed into butter, melting into the waffle's pockets with the mustard maple syrup. The house-made miso butter on the Crab & Corn Omelette is the fermented paste beaten into butter, salty and savoury against the sweet crab and corn. The pecan bordelaise on the Gulf fish, if it is the New Orleans garlic butter the guide says to confirm, is a close cousin with toasted pecans worked in.

card.front: What is a compound butter, and which plates carry one?
card.back: Soft butter beaten with a flavouring and melted by the plate's heat: the foie gras butter on the waffle, the miso butter on the omelette and, most likely, the pecan bordelaise.

sources: research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (section 6, Duck Confit Waffle, Pecan Gulf Fish and Crab & Corn Omelette)

components.name: Stock and glace
components.explain:
Stock is water in which bones and aromatics have simmered for hours, strained and skimmed: the savoury liquid most sauces, soups and braises are built on. Brown stock, from roasted bones, is deep and gelatinous; chicken and fish stocks are lighter. Reduced hard, brown stock becomes glace de viande, GLAHS duh vee-AHND, a syrup that sets firm when cold and deepens any sauce.

Escoffier built his sauce families on stock, and our brown sauces do: the marchand de vin under the Hussarde and the Owen is red wine and beef stock, the short rib braise is wine and stock, and sauce Foyot on the Chateaubriand is béarnaise with meat glaze whisked in. Stock also underlies the gumbo, the turtle soup, the Creole sauce, the braised leeks and, likely, the lobster's white bean stew.

Which stocks the kitchen keeps, and whether a vegetable plate touches one, is the chef's answer. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: What is stock, and what is a glace?
card.back: Stock is bones and aromatics simmered for hours and strained, the base of our brown sauces, soups and braises; glace is brown stock reduced to a syrup, the richness in sauce Foyot.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p2, p14 to p19, p24, p25)

components.name: White wine in the kitchen
components.explain:
Dry white wine is a seasoning in a French kitchen. Boiled down with shallot and vinegar it loses its alcohol and keeps its acid and fruit, and that reduction is the floor under our sauces: Escoffier's béarnaise starts with white wine and vinegar reduced with shallot, tarragon, chervil and crushed pepper, and the Foyot and the Choron are built on it. A beurre blanc is cold butter whisked into the same kind of reduction, and the mustard cream sauce opens with shallot in butter and a splash of white wine cooked away.

So wine stands behind the béarnaise on the breakfast hanger, the sauce Foyot on the Chateaubriand, the Choron on the Eggs Sardou, the preserved lemon beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique and the mustard cream on the poussin. Which wine the kitchen reduces is not printed, and a trace of alcohol can remain, so a guest who avoids it altogether is sent to the kitchen.

card.front: Which of our sauces begin with white wine reduced?
card.back: Béarnaise, Foyot and Choron, the beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique and the poussin's mustard cream all start on a white wine and shallot reduction. Which wine is the chef's to say.

sources: guide.txt (the Redfish Véronique 45 second line: a butter sauce with white wine)

components.name: Hibiscus
components.explain:
The hibiscus in a kitchen is not the garden flower but Hibiscus sabdariffa, called roselle: the fleshy red calyx that wraps the seed pod, dried until it looks like a dark petal. Its origin is argued between Sudan and West Africa, and the big growers today are China, Sudan and Thailand, with Mexico rising. Steeped in hot water it gives a ruby liquid, sharp with fruit acids and tasting of cranberry: the agua de Jamaica of Mexico, the bissap of West Africa and the karkadé of Egypt.

On the Redfish Véronique the kitchen pickles grapes with it, so the grapes come out red, tart and faintly floral against the butter sauce. Say hih-BIS-kus. Whether the pickle is made with dried calyces or a brewed tea, and where they come from, is a question for the chef.

card.front: What is the hibiscus in the Véronique's pickled grapes?
card.back: The dried red calyx of roselle, Hibiscus sabdariffa, an African plant grown in Sudan, China, Thailand and Mexico; steeped, it turns the pickle ruby and tart, like cranberry.

producer.who: Hibiscus, the roselle calyx; the source not printed
producer.where: As sourced: an African plant grown in Sudan, China, Thailand and Mexico
producer.history:
Roselle, Hibiscus sabdariffa, is the hibiscus of food and drink: a tall annual whose fleshy red calyces, the cups around each seed pod, are picked and dried. Where it began is argued. Some favour Sudan, where it may have been domesticated about 6,000 years ago, others West Africa, others the stretch from India to Malaysia; there is a fibre strain and a food strain, and the food strain is the one in the kitchen.

The trade today is spread across three continents. China, Sudan and Thailand are the major growers; Sudanese roselle is held to be the finest, but an American trade embargo and large scale planting in Mexico, Thailand and China moved the market, and Mexico's own crop grew by more than half between 2009 and 2019. Every culture that grows it drinks it: agua de Jamaica in Mexico, the dried calyces boiled eight to ten minutes and sweetened; bissap in West Africa; karkadé in Egypt.

The calyx is tart with fruit acids and deep red with the same family of pigments as a red grape skin, so a pickling liquid made with it colours whatever sits in it. On the Redfish Véronique that is the grapes. The menu prints hibiscus and nothing more: whether the kitchen uses whole dried calyces or a brewed tea, and whose, is not public.
facts: The hibiscus of the kitchen is Hibiscus sabdariffa, roselle; the part used is the dried red calyx around the seed pod.
Its origin is argued between Sudan, where it may have been domesticated about 6,000 years ago, and West Africa.
China, Sudan and Thailand are the major growers; Mexico's crop grew 56.2 per cent between 2009 and 2019.
In Mexico it is flor de Jamaica; agua de Jamaica is the calyces boiled eight to ten minutes with sugar.
The same drink is bissap in West Africa and karkadé in Egypt.
Steeped, it is tart and ruby, tasting of cranberry; that is what colours and sharpens the pickled grapes.
notes: Say the grapes are pickled with hibiscus, the tart red flower of hibiscus tea; a guest who knows agua de Jamaica has the taste already.
The hibiscus is a flavour and a colour, not a sweetener: the pickle is sharp, so describe the grapes as a relish, not a fruit garnish.
Where the kitchen buys its hibiscus is not printed; never name a country or a brand as the house's.
Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Our grapes are pickled with hibiscus, the tart red flower behind hibiscus tea, so they come out ruby and sharp against the lemon butter sauce.

components.name: Table grapes
components.explain:
A table grape is a grape bred to be eaten, not pressed: thin skinned, crisp, juicy and usually seedless, sweeter to bite than a wine grape and lower in sugar. In the United States nearly all of them, about 99 per cent, grow in California, which is where a grape on an American plate most likely began unless the menu says otherwise.

The French classic behind our Redfish Véronique calls for peeled muscat grapes warmed in the sauce. Ours are a modern turn on that: grapes pickled in a hibiscus brine, so they keep their crunch and sweetness under a red, tart skin, and eat more like a relish than a fruit. The variety and the grower are not printed, so say grapes, pickled with hibiscus, and let the chef name the rest.

card.front: Where do the Véronique's grapes come from?
card.back: A table grape, bred to eat rather than press; about 99 per cent of American table grapes grow in California. The variety and the grower are not printed, so ask the chef.

sources: research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (Redfish Véronique: the classic is poached sole with peeled muscat grapes)

components.name: Leeks
components.explain:
The leek is the mildest of the onion family, a long white shaft of tightly rolled leaves grown by earthing up soil around the plant to keep it pale. It is an ancient crop of the eastern Mediterranean, bred from the wild vineyard allium, and the emblem of Wales, worn in the legend on Saint David's word so the Welsh could tell friend from foe. Because it grows in banked soil, grit lodges between its layers: a cook splits it lengthwise and washes it under running water before anything else.

The white and pale green are the tender part; the dark tops go to stock. Braised slowly in butter and a little stock, leeks turn silky and sweet with no bite at all, which is the job they do under the Redfish Véronique, beside the fingerling potatoes, as the quiet base for the fish, the pickled grapes and the beurre blanc.

card.front: Why does a cook split and wash a leek before cooking it?
card.back: Leeks grow earthed up in soil, so grit lodges between the rolled leaves; split lengthwise and rinsed, then braised in butter and stock, they turn silky under the Redfish Véronique.

sources: guide.txt (the Redfish Véronique card: braised leeks are soft and gently sweet)

components.name: Banana leaf
components.explain:
A banana leaf is the broad, waxy leaf of the banana plant, used as a wrapper and a plate wherever bananas grow: across Southeast Asia, where the habit began, through India, and in Mexico and Central America, where Oaxacan tamales are steamed in it. It is sold fresh or frozen, the central rib is cut away, and a pass over a flame or a dip in hot water turns it glossy and pliable so it folds without cracking. It is not eaten.

In a parcel it does what paper does, traps the steam, and adds what paper cannot: a faint grassy, tea-like scent and a green banana note. That is the house's turn on en papillote for the Gulf Fish en Papillote. Bananas grow all over south Louisiana as garden plants, but where the kitchen's leaves come from is not printed, so the source is a question for the chef.

card.front: What does the banana leaf do that paper would not?
card.back: It traps the steam like paper and adds a faint grassy, green banana scent; softened over a flame so it folds, it wraps the Gulf fish and is not eaten.

producer.who: Banana leaf; the source not printed
producer.where: As sourced: the banana's home is Southeast Asia, and the leaf is a wrapper from there to Oaxaca
producer.history:
The banana leaf as a cooking wrapper belongs first to Maritime Southeast Asia, where it is a standard part of traditional cooking, and the Austronesian peoples carried the habit across the islands as far as tropical Polynesia. Bananas did not reach the Americas until the Spanish brought them in the 1500s; since then the leaf has become the common wrapper of Central America and southern Mexico, where Oaxacan tamales are steamed in it and take on a green banana aroma.

The leaf is waterproof, so folded around food it holds in moisture and aroma while the parcel bakes or steams. It is sold fresh in bundles and frozen in flat packs, and frozen leaves keep for up to six months. Before use the thick central rib is cut out and the leaf is softened over a flame or in hot water until it shines and bends, or it splits along the veins when folded.

Louisiana is banana country of a sort: the plants grow throughout the state as ornamentals, a freeze kills the top growth while the rhizome often survives under mulch, and south of Interstate 10 they frequently fruit. That says nothing about the restaurant's supply. The menu prints banana leaf and no source, so where the leaves come from, fresh or frozen, is a question for the chef.

Bananas reached the Americas with the Spanish in the 1500s; the leaf is now the common wrapper of Central America and southern Mexico.
Oaxacan tamales are often steamed in banana leaves, which give a green banana aroma.

Bananas grow throughout Louisiana as ornamentals and often fruit south of Interstate 10.

Ask at lineup whether the parcel is opened at the table, and warn the guest of the steam when it is.
Where the leaves come from is not printed: never claim a local or a particular source.
Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

components.name: Turnips
components.explain:
The turnip is a root of the cabbage family, Brassica rapa, white fleshed with a mustard-sharp bite raw that cooks away into sweetness. It is one of the old crops: genetic work places its first domestication in the mountains near Afghanistan between 3,500 and 6,000 years ago, and it had reached Japan by 700 AD. Two kinds reach a restaurant: the purple top, firm and peppery, cooked through, and the small white Hakurei, bred in Japan in the middle of the last century, sweet enough to eat raw.

The French way with a turnip is to glaze it: cooked in a little water, butter and sugar until the liquid reduces to a shine. On the Poussin à la Moutarde the turnips come with shallots for a gentle sweetness against the mustard cream, as the guide says. The menu prints turnips and shallots and no method, so which turnip and how it is cooked are questions for the chef.

card.front: What do the turnips do on the Poussin à la Moutarde?
card.back: With the shallots they give a gentle sweetness against the mustard cream; raw a turnip is peppery, cooked it turns sweet. Which turnip and how it is cooked is the chef's.

sources: guide.txt (the Poussin card: turnips and shallots for a gentle sweetness)

components.name: Sweet tea
components.explain:
Sweet tea is the house drink of the American South: black tea brewed strong, sugared while it is hot so the sugar dissolves, then poured over ice. The oldest printed recipe is in a Virginia cookbook of 1879, made then with green tea; black tea took over, and the first printed black tea version is said to be a Boston cookbook of 1884. Tea itself is the leaf of Camellia sinensis, black tea the fully oxidised leaf, and nearly all of it is imported; the one large tea farm in the country is on Wadmalaw Island near Charleston.

In the kitchen it is a brine. The Poussin à la Moutarde is a Cornish hen soaked in sweet tea with salt before it is fried: the salt seasons the bird and keeps it juicy, the tea's tannin and the sugar help the skin brown deep. Which tea, how sweet and how long are the chef's details.

card.front: Why is the Cornish hen brined in sweet tea?
card.back: A Southern fried chicken trick: the salt seasons the bird and holds its juices, the tea's tannin and the sugar brown the skin. Sweet tea is black tea sugared hot, then iced.

producer.who: Sweet tea, the Southern brine; the tea not printed
producer.where: The American South; the tea leaf itself imported, bar one farm on Wadmalaw Island, South Carolina
producer.history:
Cold tea in America began as punch: the oldest printed recipes are green tea punches with spirits or wine, such as the tea punch in The Kentucky Housewife of 1839. The oldest printed sweet tea is in Housekeeping in Old Virginia, a Virginia community cookbook of 1879: green tea steeped, two teaspoons to a quart, poured over ice with sugar in each goblet and a squeeze of lemon suggested. Mrs Lincoln's Boston Cook Book of 1884 is cited as the first printed iced tea made with black tea, and black tea is what the South drinks now, brewed strong and sweetened while hot.

Tea is the leaf of Camellia sinensis; black tea is the leaf fully oxidised before it is dried. Almost all tea drunk in the United States is imported. The one large scale tea farm in the country is the Charleston Tea Garden on Wadmalaw Island, South Carolina, 127 acres with about 40 under tea, whose bushes descend from plants the French botanist André Michaux brought to the Carolinas in the late 1700s; smaller farms work in Alabama, Hawaii, Oregon and Washington.

On the dinner menu sweet tea is a brine: the Poussin à la Moutarde is a Cornish hen soaked in sweet tea with salt before frying, the Southern fried chicken way. The menu names the brine and nothing else. Which tea is brewed, how much sugar and salt go in, whether the tea is made in house and how long the bird sits are open questions for the chef.
facts: The oldest printed sweet tea recipe is in Housekeeping in Old Virginia, 1879, made with green tea, ice, sugar and lemon.
Mrs Lincoln's Boston Cook Book of 1884 is cited as the first printed iced tea made with black tea.
Earlier cold teas were punches with spirits or wine, such as the tea punch in The Kentucky Housewife of 1839.
Tea is the leaf of Camellia sinensis; black tea is the leaf fully oxidised before drying.
The Charleston Tea Garden on Wadmalaw Island, South Carolina, is called the only large scale tea farm in the United States, 127 acres.
Its bushes descend from Camellia sinensis plants André Michaux brought to the Carolinas in the late 1700s.
notes: Say sweet tea brine: strong black tea, sugar and salt, which seasons the hen and helps the skin brown; it is a brine, so the tea leaves at most a faint malty note.
Which tea the kitchen brews, how sweet the brine is and how long the hen sits are the chef's; the guide lists them as open questions.
Sugar in the brine is for browning and seasoning; the fried hen is savoury, not sweet, which a guest may ask.
Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

components.name: Pepitas, pumpkin seeds
components.explain:
Pepita is Mexican Spanish for the pumpkin seed, pepita de calabaza, the little seed of the squash, and in Mexico it means the hulled kernel: flat, olive green and oily. The green pepita of commerce comes from oilseed squashes bred to grow their seed without the thick white hull, a single gene, best known in the Styrian oil pumpkin of Austria. The squash itself, Cucurbita pepo, is one of the oldest crops of the Americas, its remains in a cave in Oaxaca as much as ten thousand years old.

Toasted dry or in a film of oil until they puff and crackle, pepitas turn nutty and crisp; raw they are soft and grassy. On the Creole Hanger Steak they are folded into the persillade of parsley and garlic for crunch. Say peh-PEE-tah. Where the kitchen's seeds come from is not printed; the chef knows.

card.front: What is a pepita, and what does it do on the dinner hanger?
card.back: The hulled green pumpkin seed, pepita de calabaza in Mexican Spanish, toasted until nutty and crisp; it gives the parsley and garlic persillade its crunch. Say peh-PEE-tah.

producer.who: Pepitas, the hulled pumpkin seed; the grower not printed
producer.where: As sourced: Mexico's seed by name, Austria's by breeding; the kitchen's supplier is not printed
producer.history:
The squash is American before it is anything else. Remains of Cucurbita pepo from Guilá Naquitz cave in Oaxaca, Mexico, are dated between 10,000 and 8,000 years ago, older than maize and beans, though one early seed in that series is argued to sit within the wild size range. Mexico kept the seed as food: pepita de calabaza, the little seed of the squash, hulled, toasted and ground into sauces, or salted as a snack.

The hull-less seed is a quirk of breeding. In most squashes the kernel sits inside a thick white coat; a single recessive gene strips that coat away, leaving a naked, deep green, oily seed. The best known hull-less cultivar is the Styrian oil pumpkin of Styria in Austria, where pumpkins have been grown for fruit and seed for about 200 years, the naked seed appeared around 1880, and the seed is pressed into a dark green oil. Commercial green pepitas come from oilseed varieties of this kind, whichever country grows them.

In the kitchen the seed is toasted dry or in a film of oil until it puffs, crackles and turns nutty, then salted. On the Creole Hanger Steak pepitas go into the persillade, the French last second finish of parsley and garlic, for crunch. The menu prints pepita persillade and no origin, so where the seeds are grown is a question for the chef.
facts: Pepita is Mexican Spanish, pepita de calabaza, the little seed of the squash; in Mexico it means the hulled seed.
Cucurbita pepo remains from Guilá Naquitz cave in Oaxaca are dated between 10,000 and 8,000 years ago.
A single recessive gene makes the seed grow without its thick white hull, leaving the green pepita.
The Styrian oil pumpkin of Austria is the best known hull-less cultivar; Styria has grown pumpkins for seed for about 200 years, and the naked seed appeared around 1880.
Toasted, pepitas puff and turn nutty and crisp; raw they are soft and grassy.
notes: Say pumpkin seeds first, then pepitas, so every guest follows; peh-PEE-tah.
They are a seed, not a nut; a guest who asks about nuts is sent to the service note and the kitchen.
Where the kitchen's seeds are grown is not printed: never claim Mexican or Austrian seed as the house's.
Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Pepitas are toasted pumpkin seeds, peh-PEE-tah; we fold them into a persillade of parsley and garlic for crunch on the Creole Hanger Steak.
askKitchen: Where do the pepitas come from, and are they toasted in house?

sources: guide.txt (the Creole Hanger Steak card: pepitas, pumpkin seeds, for crunch)

components.name: Paprika and cayenne
components.explain:
Paprika and cayenne are the same plant at two ends of a scale: Capsicum annuum, the pepper Columbus carried home from the Americas around 1493. Paprika is the sweet or mildly hot pod dried and ground fine: it reached Hungary under Ottoman rule in the 16th century and by the 19th was the national spice, grown around Szeged and Kalocsa; Spain's pimentón de la Vera is dried over oak smoke. It gives colour, sweetness and a gentle warmth, and it scorches easily, so it goes into a rub or in late. Cayenne is a thin hot pod ground whole, named by a folk association with the town in French Guiana, and used by the pinch.

Together they are the red in every Louisiana blend: the classic blackening mix is paprika led with cayenne, and Creole seasoning is built on both. What the house blend holds, and how hot the tofu's crust is, is the kitchen's to say.

card.front: What is the difference between paprika and cayenne?
card.back: One plant, Capsicum annuum: paprika is the sweet or mild pod ground fine for colour and warmth, from Hungary and Spain; cayenne is a hot pod ground whole, used by the pinch.

sources: components/dishes.json (the Housemade Creole spice and Blackening cards)
research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (Blackened Tofu: Prudhomme's paprika and cayenne blend)

components.name: Steak temperatures, rare to well done
components.explain:
A steak's temperature is the first thing a server writes on the ticket. Rare is a cool red centre; medium-rare a warm red centre, about 130 to 135°F inside; medium pink and warm; medium-well a trace of pink; well done cooked through and grey. The federal guidance for a whole cut of beef is 145°F with a three minute rest, and cooking below that, as most steak houses do, is a stated preference. A cook pulls the meat early because it keeps cooking as it rests, rising 5 to 15°F.

Our hangers are at their best medium-rare to medium: past medium the loose grain tightens and tastes of liver. The Chateaubriand serves two, so ask the temperature once for the table, and the Petite Filet's temperature is taken with the tasting order, not when the course fires. Take it as you take the order, repeat it back, and write it down.

card.front: What is medium-rare, and where is a hanger steak at its best?
card.back: A warm red centre, about 130 to 135°F. The hangers are best medium-rare to medium; past medium they tighten and taste of liver. Write the temperature on the ticket.

sources: guide.txt (both hanger service notes: ask temperature, best medium-rare to medium; the Chateaubriand and Petite Filet service notes)

components.name: Resting and slicing across the grain
components.explain:
Two habits make a steak eat well after it leaves the heat. The first is the rest: a few minutes on a board before it is cut, during which the centre keeps cooking by 5 to 15°F, so the cook pulls it early and lets the rest finish it. The old story that the juices soak back into the fibres is contested; what is sure is that meat cut while it is hottest bleeds the most, so a short rest keeps the plate dry and the slice juicy.

The second is the knife. Muscle fibres run in one direction, and a slice cut across them leaves short fibres that part easily, where a slice along them chews like rope. The hanger's loose grain is sliced across after its rest, a Chateaubriand is rested about ten minutes and carved thick across the grain, and the duck breast on the tasting is sliced the same way.

card.front: Why is a hanger steak rested, then sliced across the grain?
card.back: The rest finishes the cooking and keeps the juices in the slice; cutting across the fibres leaves short fibres that part easily, where a slice along them chews like rope.

sources: research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (the hanger: rested, sliced across the grain; the Chateaubriand cook's notes: rest ten minutes, carve thick across the grain; the duck: slice across the grain)

components.name: Roasting whole and carving for two
components.explain:
Roasting a joint whole, rather than cutting it into steaks first, keeps the centre moist and evenly rosy while the outside browns. A Chateaubriand is roasted at a moderate heat until its centre reads about medium-rare, then rested about ten minutes and carved in thick slices across the grain, so every slice has a crust and a pink heart. Ours is roasted whole for two, and one temperature serves the whole roast, which is why the guide says to ask once for the table.

It takes longer than a single steak: confirm the timing with the kitchen and set it before the order, so the table is not waiting in silence. Carving at the table belongs to the guéridon tradition the house keeps for its flamed desserts; whether tonight's roast is carved at the table or in the kitchen is confirmed at lineup, so ask before you promise it.

card.front: Why is the Chateaubriand roasted whole, and what do you ask first?
card.back: Whole, it stays moist and evenly pink inside a browned crust, carved thick for two. Ask one temperature for the table, confirm the timing, and ask at lineup who carves it.

sources: guide.txt (the Chateaubriand card and service note: roasted whole, ask temperature once, confirm timing, ask at lineup whether it is carved tableside)

components.name: Glazing
components.explain:
A glaze is a shine that tastes of something. For a vegetable it is a French classic: the pieces are cooked in a shallow pan with a little water, butter, salt and often a pinch of sugar, under a paper lid, until the liquid cooks away and what is left coats each piece in a sweet, savoury gloss; Escoffier's Vichy carrots of 1903 are the model, and glazed turnips are made the same way. For a roast or a fruit the glaze is a syrup, a reduced stock or a reduced wine brushed on and set under heat until it clings.

The menu prints glazed four times: the summer squash beside the Chateaubriand, the Madeira-glazed broccolini on the Creole Hanger Steak, the cane syrup-glazed peaches with the Rohan duck and the Succotash's summer vegetables. Beyond the Madeira and the cane syrup it names, what each glaze is made of is a question for the chef.

card.front: How is a vegetable glazed?
card.back: Cooked in a little water, butter and a pinch of sugar until the liquid reduces to a gloss that coats it; Escoffier's Vichy carrots are the model. Our squash, broccolini and peaches are glazed.

sources: pages/brennansneworleans-menus-pasted-2026-10-03.txt (glazed summer squash, Madeira-glazed broccolini, glazed summer vegetables)
guide.txt (the Rohan duck card: cane syrup-glazed peaches)

components.name: Braising vegetables
components.explain:
Braising is slow cooking in a little liquid under a lid. With a tough cut of meat it is hours of work that melts sinew into gelatine; with a vegetable it is gentler and quicker, and the aim is texture. Leeks, fennel, endive or celery are laid in one layer in a shallow pan with butter and a little stock or wine, covered, and cooked low until the liquid has nearly gone and the vegetable is soft right through, glossy and sweet, tasting of itself and of the butter.

The braised leeks on the Redfish Véronique are the house's vegetable case: silky, mild and a little sweet, the calm base under the fish and the sharp hibiscus grapes. The short rib on the Eggs Owen is the meat case, braised in red wine, which has its own card. What the kitchen braises the leeks in, stock, wine or butter alone, is a question for the chef.

card.front: What does braising do to a leek?
card.back: Cooked low in a covered pan with butter and a little stock until the liquid is nearly gone, the leek turns soft through, glossy and sweet: the base under the Redfish Véronique.

sources: guide.txt (the Redfish Véronique card: braised leeks are soft and gently sweet)

components.name: Reduction
components.explain:
To reduce is to boil a liquid down until less of it says more. Wine and vinegar lose their alcohol and most of their water and keep their acid and fruit; stock thickens on its own gelatine into a glaze; cream thickens on its fat. The cook judges it by eye and by the spoon, by half, by two thirds, to a syrup, and the whole character of a sauce is set in that pan before any butter goes in.

It is the first step of most of our sauces. Béarnaise, Foyot and Choron begin with white wine and vinegar reduced with shallot and tarragon; the beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique the same; the mustard cream on the poussin reduces a splash of wine and then the cream; the marchand de vin on the Hussarde and the Owen is a red wine reduction with stock; and the Madeira on the Creole Hanger Steak's broccolini is reduced to a glaze.

card.front: What is a reduction, and which of our sauces start with one?
card.back: A liquid boiled down to concentrate it: wine, vinegar, stock or cream. Béarnaise, Foyot, Choron, beurre blanc, the mustard cream, the marchand de vin and the Madeira glaze all begin there.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p17: marchand de vin, a savory red wine reduction)
components/dishes.json (the béarnaise, beurre blanc, mustard cream sauce and Madeira-glazed broccolini cards)

components.name: Searing and the Maillard reaction
components.explain:
Searing is the hard, hot start that gives meat its crust. The surface is patted dry, because water holds a pan at the boil and nothing browns until it has gone, then laid in a smoking pan and left alone until it releases. The brown is the Maillard reaction, my-YAR, named for the French chemist who described it in 1912: at roughly 140 to 165 C the meat's amino acids and sugars react into hundreds of new flavour compounds and the dark pigments of a crust. It does not seal in juices, an old story, but it is where most of a steak's savour comes from.

Our hangers are cooked hot and fast, the Petite Filet is seared hard and finished gently, the Owen's short rib is seared before it braises, a roast like the Chateaubriand is usually seared first, and blackening is searing taken to its edge, a spice crust set in seconds on the Blackened Tofu.

card.front: What is the Maillard reaction, and why pat meat dry first?
card.back: The browning of amino acids and sugars on a hot, dry surface into a crust's flavour, described by Maillard in 1912; water holds the pan at the boil, so nothing browns until it has gone.

components.name: USDA beef grades: Prime, Choice and Select
components.explain:
USDA grades are a quality stamp, not a cut. A federal grader scores a carcass on marbling, the flecks of fat within the muscle, and on maturity, the animal's age, and the packer pays for the service by choice. Prime is the most marbled beef from young cattle, Choice the broad middle with small to moderate marbling, Select the leanest. Prime was scarce for decades, a few per cent of graded beef; the USDA's own grading reports put it near 10 per cent in 2024 and 2025, and weekly counts since have run higher as marbling has climbed.

Marbling melts as the steak cooks, basting the muscle from inside, so a Prime steak eats richer and more tender. Brennan's prints Prime once, on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak; Creekstone grades Prime and Choice, so say Prime only where the menu does, and never promote the dinner hanger or the Chateaubriand unless the kitchen confirms it.

card.front: What does USDA Prime mean, and which plate prints it?
card.back: The top federal grade for marbling and youth, about a tenth of graded beef in recent USDA reports. Printed only on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak; do not call the other beef Prime unless confirmed.

sources: research/producers-food-beef-eggs-duck-2026-10-06.md (Creekstone: USDA Prime and Choice; Prime printed on the breakfast hanger only)

components.name: Pork and its cuts
components.explain:
Pork is the meat of the pig, cured, smoked, ground and spiced into much of the Louisiana larder. The belly, streaky with fat, becomes bacon once it is cured and smoked. The shoulder, the Boston butt above and the picnic below, is the sausage cut, ground with its own fat; the loin gives the lean Canadian bacon. Most American pork is raised in the Midwest, Iowa above all, and the menu names no farm.

On our menus pork is the housemade sausage patty and the thick-cut bacon at breakfast, the coffee-cured Canadian bacon on the Hussarde, the tasso in the Shrimp & Grits sauce, the andouille in the gumbo, the 'nduja in the lobster's beans, the Nueske's bacon in the Succotash, and the bacon on the children's eggs and the Roost Burger.

Whether the rice dressing carries pork, whether the salami on the children's dinner is pork, and what any cure or spice blend holds are lineup questions.

card.front: Which of our plates carry pork?
card.back: The sausage patty and the thick-cut bacon, the Hussarde's Canadian bacon, tasso in the Shrimp & Grits, andouille in the gumbo, 'nduja with the lobster, Nueske's bacon in the Succotash, and the bacon on the children's eggs and the burger.

items: Eggs Any Style with Toast and Bacon
sources: guide.txt (pdf p5, p15, p17, p20, p29, p31, p32; the children's and Roost menus)

components.name: Buttermilk
components.explain:
Buttermilk was once the thin, tart liquid left in the churn after cream became butter, soured by the bacteria already living in the cream. What a dairy sells today is cultured buttermilk: milk soured on purpose with lactic bacteria, thicker and more acid, and the one nearly every kitchen bakes with. Its acid is what the baker wants: it reacts with baking soda to make a biscuit rise, and it tenderises the crumb and leaves a gentle tang.

On our menus it is printed twice. The Buttermilk Biscuit, the $5 breakfast side, is the Southern quick bread built on that reaction; the New Orleans Bread Pudding is finished with buttermilk ice cream, whose tang cuts the whiskey caramel and the pralines.

Buttermilk and the ice cream are both made from milk. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen. Which buttermilk the kitchen buys is not printed; ask the chef before you say more.

card.front: What does buttermilk do in the biscuit?
card.back: Its acid reacts with baking soda to lift the dough, tenderises the crumb and leaves a gentle tang. Cultured buttermilk is milk soured with lactic bacteria. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

sources: research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (sections 7 and 8, Buttermilk Biscuit and New Orleans Bread Pudding)

components.name: Corn
components.explain:
Corn, maize to most of the world, was domesticated in the Balsas valley of southern Mexico about nine thousand years ago and is the grain of the Americas. It reaches a kitchen in several forms. Sweet corn is picked young, while the kernels are full of sugar and milky juice, and eaten as a vegetable. Field corn, the dent kinds, is left to dry hard and ground: coarse for grits, finer for cornmeal and cornbread. Hominy is dried corn soaked in an alkali, which loosens the hull and changes the flavour.

On our menus corn is the Cheddar Grits and the fried pimento cheese grit cake under the Shrimp & Grits, the cornmeal in the cornbread and chive waffle, and the roasted sweet corn in the Crab & Corn Omelette.

Whether tonight's Succotash carries corn, as the traditional dish does, is learned at lineup; so is whose corn the grits are ground from.

card.front: Which forms of corn are on our menus?
card.back: Grits and the grit cake, both ground dried field corn; the cornmeal in the cornbread waffle; and roasted sweet corn, picked young, in the Crab & Corn Omelette. Ask at lineup whether tonight's Succotash carries corn.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p20, p21, p22, p30, p31)
research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (sections 6 and 7, Shrimp & Grits, Duck Confit Waffle, Cheddar Grits)

components.name: Summer vegetables
components.explain:
Summer vegetables are the ones a Louisiana garden gives in the heat: okra, summer squash and eggplant picked young, sweet corn, field peas and butter beans, tomatoes and peppers. Okra seeded in midsummer comes in from late August and keeps bearing until the weather cools in late October or November, so the late summer menu sits in the thick of the season. The mix on a plate changes with the market from week to week.

On our menus they are printed twice: the glazed summer vegetables in the dinner Succotash, cooked with Nueske's bacon, and the roasted and glazed summer squash beside the Roasted Chateaubriand.

Neither plate prints which vegetables, so tonight's mix is learned at lineup and never guessed: a guest who avoids a particular vegetable is answered from the chef, not from memory. The Succotash carries bacon, so it is never offered as a meatless side.

card.front: What are the summer vegetables in the Succotash?
card.back: The menu prints only glazed summer vegetables with Nueske's bacon; the mix changes with the market, okra, squash, corn, peas and beans among the season's. Learn tonight's at lineup before you describe it.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p24, p31; the Succotash service note)

components.name: Pasta shells
components.explain:
Pasta shells are conchiglie, kon-KEEL-yeh, Italian for seashells: a short dried pasta shaped like a scallop shell, ridged outside and hollow within, pressed through a shaped die. Dried pasta at its plainest is durum wheat semolina and water; durum is the hardest wheat, and its semolina gives a dough that holds its shape through boiling and cooks to a firm bite. The shell is a shape of southern Italy, Puglia in particular, and it was made for sauce: every curve and ridge holds some.

That is why the shape suits the Shells & Cheese, where the shells carry a fondue of Mimolette and Abita Amber finished with Grana Padano. The children's dinner has buttered noodles instead, a plainer shape.

Pasta is wheat. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen. Which brand the kitchen buys is not printed.

card.front: Why shells for the Shells & Cheese?
card.back: Conchiglie, Italian for seashells, are ridged, hollow durum wheat pasta made to hold sauce in every curve; here they carry the Mimolette and Abita Amber fondue. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p32; the Shells & Cheese card and service note)

components.name: Louisiana rice
components.explain:
Rice is Louisiana's grain. It is grown on the prairie of the southwest, where planting began in earnest in the early 1880s and the 1890 crop made Louisiana the leading rice state; Crowley, in Acadia Parish, became the centre of the industry and the home of the LSU rice station from 1909. Long grain is the Louisiana habit: grains that cook separate and firm rather than clinging, the right thing under a gumbo or folded through a dressing. The flooded fields double as crawfish ponds once the rice is cut.

On our menus rice is the popcorn rice under the Seafood Gumbo, an aromatic long grain with its own card, and the base of the South Louisiana Rice Dressing. The rice grits under the Blackened Tofu are from Two Brooks Farm in Mississippi, not Louisiana.

The dressing prints no description, so whose rice it is, and which meats go in, are learned at lineup.

card.front: Where does Louisiana rice come from?
card.back: The southwest prairie around Crowley, in Acadia Parish, rice country since the 1880s and home of the LSU rice station. Long grain, firm and separate, under our gumbo and in the rice dressing.

components.name: Rendering fat
components.explain:
Rendering is melting fat out of its tissue over low, steady heat until the clear fat runs and what is left turns crisp. Pork fat rendered is lard, beef fat tallow, poultry fat schmaltz. The rule is patience: fat pushed too hard browns and spits before it has melted, so a cook starts bacon in a cool pan and a duck breast skin down in a cold one, pouring off the fat as it comes.

On our menus it is the thick-cut bacon, best cooked slowly so the fat turns glassy before the edges burn; the sausage patty browning in its own fat; the Nueske's bacon in the Succotash; the Rohan duck breast, roasted so its fat cap renders and the meat stays rosy; and the duck leg of the Duck Confit Waffle, cooked slowly in rendered fat.

Whether the kitchen keeps its bacon fat or duck fat for other cooking is a question for the chef.

card.front: What does it mean to render bacon?
card.back: To cook it low and slow so the fat melts out and turns glassy before the edges burn, leaving the thick-cut slices meaty in the middle and crisp at the edges. The same patience cooks the duck breast.

sources: research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (sections 3, 6 and 7, Roasted Rohan Duck Breast, Duck Confit Waffle, Thick-Cut Bacon)

components.name: Baking soda and baking powder
components.explain:
Quick breads rise without yeast. Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, an alkali that gives off carbon dioxide the moment it meets an acid such as buttermilk, so a soda dough goes straight into a hot oven. Baking powder carries its own dry acid beside the soda; the double-acting kind lifts once when wetted and again in the heat. The chemistry is nineteenth century: baking powders appeared in England in the 1840s, and in 1856 Eben Horsford patented the American one sold as Rumford.

On our menus the Buttermilk Biscuit is the clear case, buttermilk and soda lifting folded layers of cold butter or lard and soft flour, and the cornbread and chive waffle under the duck confit is a cornmeal quick bread cooked in a waffle iron.

Whether the coffee cake or the financiers rise this way is not printed; ask the chef. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: How does the Buttermilk Biscuit rise without yeast?
card.back: Baking soda meets the acid in buttermilk and gives off carbon dioxide in the oven, lifting folded layers of cold butter or lard and soft flour. Baking powder carries its own acid; the cornbread waffle rises the same way.

sources: research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (sections 6 and 7, Duck Confit Waffle and Buttermilk Biscuit)

components.name: Blanching and shocking
components.explain:
Blanching is a short plunge into boiling salted water, and shocking is the plunge into iced water that follows, which stops the cooking at once. The heat kills the enzymes that would dull a green vegetable, so a blanched green keeps its colour and its bite for days, and the ice keeps it from cooking on in its own heat. Blanched food is finished later, squeezed, sautéed, fried or sauced, which is why restaurants do it: the long part of the work happens before service.

On our menus the classic method behind the creamed spinach, under the Eggs Sardou and as a side, is spinach blanched, shocked, squeezed hard and chopped before the cream, and Brabant potatoes, on the breakfast side and the children's plates, start as cubes blanched or par-fried before their final crisping.

Whether ours are made that way, and which vegetables the kitchen blanches ahead on a given night, are the chef's answers, never a guess.

card.front: What are blanching and shocking?
card.back: A short boil in salted water, then iced water to stop the cooking: the green keeps its colour and bite. Classic creamed spinach is blanched, shocked and squeezed before the cream, and Brabant potatoes start blanched or par-fried; confirm ours with the chef.

sources: research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (sections 6 and 7, Eggs Sardou and Brabant Potatoes)
