components.name: Grinding and forming patties
components.explain:
Ground meat is meat put through a grinder with its own fat, and the fat is the point: a lean grind cooks dry. A breakfast sausage is coarsely ground pork shoulder with a good share of fat, seasoned and formed by hand into a patty; a burger is ground beef pressed just enough to hold, since overworking it makes it dense. Both are cooked from cold in a hot pan or on a griddle, and both are cooked through or to the temperature the kitchen sets, since grinding carries the meat's surface all through it.

On our menus the Housemade Pork Sausage Patty is ground and formed in house; the Roost Burger is two beef short rib patties; and the South Louisiana Rice Dressing is traditionally rice folded through browned ground meat, though ours prints no description.

What goes into the sausage, whether anything binds it, and how the burger patties are cooked are kitchen questions.

card.front: What makes a good sausage patty or burger?
card.back: Meat ground with enough of its own fat, seasoned, formed by hand and not overworked, then cooked from cold in a hot pan. What goes into our sausage and how the burger patties are cooked are kitchen questions.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p29, p32; the Roost menu)
research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (section 7, Housemade Pork Sausage Patty, South Louisiana Rice Dressing)

components.name: Cooking pasta
components.explain:
Dried pasta is cooked in a large pot of well salted boiling water, stirred at the start so it does not stick, and pulled when it is al dente, firm to the bite with no chalky centre. A shape with a hollow, like a shell, is drained but not rinsed, because the starch left on its surface helps a sauce cling, and a little of the cooking water loosens a cheese sauce that has tightened. Pasta that will be finished in a sauce comes out a minute early, since it keeps cooking in the heat.

On our menus the Shells & Cheese folds pasta shells into a beer and cheese fondue, and the children's dinner tosses buttered noodles with cheese.

Whether the shells are cooked to order or held and reheated for service is the kitchen's method, not printed, so ask the chef. Pasta is wheat. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: How is pasta cooked for the Shells & Cheese?
card.back: In well salted boiling water to al dente, drained and never rinsed so the starch helps the Mimolette fondue cling. Whether the shells are cooked to order is a kitchen question. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p32; the children's dinner menu)

components.name: Lemon
components.explain:
The lemon is a citrus thought to have begun in India, growing in southern Italy by about the year 200 and now planted almost entirely in California and Arizona for the American crop, mostly as Eureka and Lisbon, two varieties of the same sharp, thin-skinned fruit. The juice's acid is almost all citric, the cook's cleanest sourness, and the zest holds the oils that carry the perfume.

A squeeze wakes a sauce, a curd or a jelly; salted and cured for weeks, the peel turns soft and savoury as preserved lemon.

Lemon is printed on five of our plates: the lemon curd in the Blackberry Trifle, the lemon in the Crab & Corn Omelette, the preserved lemon in the Redfish Véronique's beurre blanc and on the Smoked Cauliflower with harissa, and the lemon jelly in the Lemon Tart. Which lemons the kitchen buys is a question for the chef.

card.front: Where does lemon appear on our food menus?
card.back: Five plates: the curd in the Blackberry Trifle, the Crab & Corn Omelette, the preserved lemon on the Redfish Véronique and the Smoked Cauliflower, and the jelly in the Lemon Tart.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p8, p21, p24, p31 and p37, the plates that print lemon)

components.name: Apples
components.explain:
The domestic apple descends from a wild apple of the Tian Shan mountains of Kazakhstan, carried west along the trade routes until it became the orchard fruit of Europe and America; today Washington state grows around two thirds of the American crop. Varieties differ most in how they bake: a firm, tart apple holds its shape and keeps its acid, while a soft sweet one collapses into sauce.

For the Baked Apple on the Traditional Breakfast a whole apple is peeled, cored and trimmed flat so it stands, then baked under its oat, pecan and raisin crumble until soft and glazed with brown sugar; whether that glaze is the crumble's sugar caramelising in the apple's juice or brushed on is a question for the chef.

It eats warm, soft and cinnamon sweet, with sweetened crème fraîche for tang. Which apple the kitchen uses, and whether the tasting portion is a whole or a half, are questions for the chef.

card.front: Which apple is in the Baked Apple, and how is it cooked?
card.back: The menu names no variety, so ask the chef. A whole apple is peeled, cored, trimmed to stand and baked under the oat, pecan and raisin crumble until soft, then glazed with brown sugar.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p4, the Baked Apple card)

components.name: Rolled oats
components.explain:
Oats began as a weed in the wheat and barley fields of the Near East and became a crop only when farming reached the cool, wet north of Europe, where they thrive and wheat struggles; they are the grain of Scottish porridge and of many a British crumble. Rolled oats are the whole hulled grain, steamed to soften it and still the enzyme that turns its oil rancid, flattened between rollers and lightly toasted, which is why they cook fast and keep.

In a crumble they give chew and a toasty, nutty flavour, and they brown without burning.

On the Baked Apple the oatmeal of the printed crumble is rolled oats with pecans, raisins, brown sugar and cinnamon, baked on the apple until crisp. Oats are often milled beside wheat, and the guide says they may carry gluten, so that question goes to the kitchen. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: What are rolled oats, and where do we use them?
card.back: The whole oat grain, steamed, flattened and toasted so it cooks fast. They are the oatmeal in the Baked Apple's crumble; the guide sends the question of gluten in oats to the kitchen.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p4, the Baked Apple card and service note)

components.name: Raisins
components.explain:
A raisin is a grape dried until most of its water has gone and its sugar has concentrated, which is why a handful tastes like candy. Nearly every raisin sold in America comes from the San Joaquin Valley of California, within about sixty miles of Fresno, and about nine in ten are Thompson Seedless grapes, sun-dried for two to three weeks on paper trays between the vine rows; golden raisins are the same grape dried by machine and treated with sulphur to keep their colour.

In a crumble raisins plump again in the heat and turn jammy, sweet with a little tartness against the oats and pecans.

On the Baked Apple they sit in the oatmeal, pecan and raisin crumble the menu prints, with the brown sugar glaze and sweetened crème fraîche. Whether any go into the bread pudding, as a classic New Orleans recipe would, is a question for the chef.

card.front: Where do raisins come from, and where are they on our menu?
card.back: Almost all from California's San Joaquin Valley, mostly Thompson Seedless grapes dried in the sun. They are in the Baked Apple's crumble; whether the bread pudding carries any is a question for the chef.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p4, the Baked Apple card)
research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (Baked Apple; New Orleans Bread Pudding, the questions for the chef)

components.name: Sweetened condensed milk
components.explain:
Sweetened condensed milk is cow's milk cooked down under vacuum until about sixty per cent of its water has gone, with a heavy charge of sugar, roughly forty per cent of the tin, so that it keeps for years in a sealed tin without refrigeration. Gail Borden, a surveyor and newspaperman who had lived in Texas, patented the process in 1856, and the Union army's orders in the Civil War made it an American staple. It is thick, glossy and sweet, with a cooked, caramel-milk taste; heated longer it turns into dulce de leche.

In pastry it brings sweetness, body and that toffee note in one spoonful.

On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin the kitchen makes the crème anglaise, the pouring custard, with it, so the sauce tastes of caramelised milk against the charred pineapple and the puff pastry. Which brand the kitchen uses is not printed; ask the chef.

card.front: What makes the anglaise on the Pineapple Tarte Tatin taste of caramel?
card.back: Sweetened condensed milk: milk cooked down with sugar until thick and toffee-like, stirred into the pouring custard. Gail Borden patented it in 1856; no brand is printed, so ask the chef.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p37 to p38, the Pineapple Tarte Tatin card)

producer.who: Sweetened condensed milk, Gail Borden's invention (no brand is printed)
producer.where: The United States, first in Connecticut and New York, where Eagle Brand began
producer.history:
Gail Borden was born in New York in 1801, lived in Texas from 1829 as a surveyor and newspaper publisher, and laid out the city of Galveston, before he turned to preserving food. He took the idea of the vacuum pan from the Shakers, who used one to condense fruit juice and extracts, and used it to draw the water out of milk at low heat; sugar did the preserving. His first patent application was refused as nothing new, and the patent was granted in 1856.

The first factories were in Connecticut, and the business nearly failed before the Civil War turned it: the Union army became its biggest customer, and Borden licensed the patent to other makers to meet the demand. The Eagle Brand name and its bald eagle trademark were first used in 1858 by the company's own account; after Borden and the J.M. Smucker Co. it has belonged to Eagle Family Foods since the end of 2015. Borden died in 1874.

The tin on the shelf is still what he made: whole milk with about sixty per cent of its water drawn off and roughly forty per cent sugar, thick, glossy and faintly caramel, able to keep for years unopened. Cooked longer it becomes dulce de leche. At Brennan's it is printed once, in the sweetened condensed anglaise beside the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, where it gives the pouring custard its caramel-milk flavour. The menu names no brand.
facts: Gail Borden's patent for condensed milk was granted in 1856, after a first application was refused as nothing new.
The process draws the water out of milk under vacuum at low heat; the sugar, about forty per cent of the tin, is the preservative.
The Eagle Brand name and its bald eagle trademark date from 1858, by the company's own timeline; Eagle Family Foods has owned the brand since the end of 2015.
The Union army was the first big customer, in the Civil War, and the demand made the product an American staple.
Borden was born in New York in 1801, lived in Texas as a surveyor and newspaperman, and died in 1874.
Heated long enough, sweetened condensed milk turns into dulce de leche, the caramelised milk spread of Latin America.
notes: Say caramel-milk, not caramel: the anglaise tastes of cooked, sweetened milk, and the Tatin's caramel comes from the charred pineapple.
The menu prints no brand, so never name Eagle Brand or any other as the kitchen's tin.
It is the sweet cousin of evaporated milk, which is condensed without sugar; a guest who asks the difference gets that one line.
Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.
producer.sayIt: Sweetened condensed milk is milk cooked down with sugar until thick and toffee-like, an American invention of 1856, and it gives our Tatin's custard its caramel-milk note.
askKitchen: Which sweetened condensed milk does the pastry kitchen use in the Tatin's anglaise?
Is the anglaise made with egg yolks as well as the condensed milk?

components.name: Caramel, sugar cooked to amber
components.explain:
Caramel is sugar taken past melting until it browns, above about 160 C, when it breaks into hundreds of new compounds that taste toasty, bitter and nutty as well as sweet. A dry caramel is sugar alone in the pan; a wet caramel starts with water and crystallises less easily. Light amber is mild, dark amber bitter and deep, black is burnt. Cream, butter or a spirit added at the end stops the cooking and makes a sauce.

The sugar in fruit and in brown sugar browns the same way under heat, which is why charred pineapple, a brown sugar glaze and a pan of bananas all taste of caramel.

On our menus: Bananas Foster's blond butter and brown sugar caramel at the cart, the whiskey caramel on the bread pudding, the caramel custard in The Snickers, the Tarte Tatin's charred pineapple, the Baked Apple's brown sugar glaze, the duck's candied hazelnuts and the Popcorn Shrimp's gastrique.

card.front: What is caramel, and how many of our plates lean on it?
card.back: Sugar cooked past melting until it browns and turns toasty and bitter-sweet. Seven plates: Bananas Foster, the bread pudding, The Snickers, the Tarte Tatin, the Baked Apple, the duck's hazelnuts and the gastrique.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p4, p7, p33 to p38, the plates that print caramel, a glaze or charred fruit)
components/dishes.json (whiskey-caramel, caramel-custard, charred-pineapple, baked-apple-crumble, candied-hazelnuts, gastrique-crystal)

components.name: Churning ice cream
components.explain:
Ice cream is a sweetened cream or custard frozen while it is stirred. The churn's paddle scrapes ice crystals off the cold wall as they form and folds in air, so the crystals stay tiny and the texture smooth rather than icy; the air it takes on is called overrun, and a dense restaurant ice cream carries far less of it than a supermarket tub. A French style base is a crème anglaise, egg yolks cooked with milk, cream and sugar; a Philadelphia style base is cream and sugar with no egg. The base is chilled overnight before churning, then hardened in a freezer and tempered a few minutes before scooping.

Housemade means the pastry kitchen makes its own, so each flavour is built for its plate.

Four of ours: the vanilla under Bananas Foster and Cherries Jubilee, the buttermilk on the bread pudding, the nougat in The Snickers. Whether each base carries egg is a question for the kitchen.

card.front: Why is churned ice cream smooth, and which of ours are housemade?
card.back: The paddle keeps the ice crystals tiny and folds in a little air. The vanilla under both flambés, the buttermilk on the bread pudding and the nougat in The Snickers; egg in each is a kitchen question.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p33 to p36, the four desserts that print ice cream; p34, ice cream likely contains egg)

components.name: Custard, stirred and baked
components.explain:
A custard is egg cooked gently in milk or cream until the egg proteins set the liquid. Stirred on the stove it stays pourable and is crème anglaise, taken off the heat when it coats the back of a spoon, about 82 to 84 C, because a few degrees more scrambles the egg into grains. Baked in the oven, in a water bath, it sets into a sliceable cream: crème caramel, flan, the inside of a bread pudding. Set cold with gelatin and lightened with whipped cream it becomes a Bavarian.

Egg yolk alone makes a richer, silkier custard; whole egg sets firmer.

Ours: the sweet custard the bread soaks in for the New Orleans Bread Pudding, the caramel custard and the Bavarian in The Snickers, the sweetened condensed anglaise beside the Pineapple Tarte Tatin, and the anglaise base of a French style vanilla ice cream, likely ours; the kitchen confirms it.

card.front: What is the difference between a stirred custard and a baked one?
card.back: Stirred anglaise stays pourable and comes off the heat as it coats a spoon; baked custard sets sliceable in a water bath. Ours: the bread pudding, The Snickers, the Tatin's anglaise and the ice cream bases.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p33 to p38, the desserts; p34, the ice cream likely contains egg)

components.name: Mousse, folding in air
components.explain:
Mousse is the French word for foam. A dessert mousse is a flavoured base, a fruit purée, a custard, melted chocolate or a soft cheese, lightened with whipped cream or whipped egg white folded in with a spatula in slow strokes, so the bubbles survive. It is the air that makes it feel light on the tongue even when the base is rich. Many restaurant mousses take a little gelatin so they hold a shape on the plate for hours; one with none must be served soon after it is made.

Cold is its friend: warm cream will not whip, and a warm base deflates the foam.

Three of ours: the yuzu mousse at the heart of the Lemon Tart, the whipped vanilla mousse beside the Pineapple Tarte Tatin and the mascarpone mousse on the Framboise French Toast. Whether each is set with gelatin is a question for the kitchen when a guest asks.

card.front: What makes a mousse a mousse?
card.back: Air: a flavoured base lightened with whipped cream or egg white folded in gently. Ours are the yuzu mousse, the whipped vanilla mousse and the mascarpone mousse; gelatin in each is a kitchen question.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p9, p36 to p38, the three plates that print a mousse)

components.name: Charring
components.explain:
Charring is cooking the surface of a food hard and fast, on a grill, under a salamander, in a dry cast iron pan or with a torch, until the edges blacken. Two things happen at once: the sugars caramelise and the proteins brown, and the blackened edges add a bitter, smoky note that balances sweetness. It is not the same as burning the whole piece; the inside stays juicy, and the char is a thin skin of flavour.

Fruit with plenty of sugar chars well: pineapple, peaches, citrus halves, stone fruit on a grill.

On the Pineapple Tarte Tatin the pineapple is charred, as the menu prints, so its sugars caramelise and its water cooks off, the way apples caramelise in butter and sugar in the classic tart. That gives the fruit its deep, slightly smoky sweetness while its acid stays bright. How the kitchen chars it, pan, grill or torch, is a question for the chef.

card.front: What does charring do to the pineapple on the Tarte Tatin?
card.back: A hard, fast surface cook blackens the edges: the sugars caramelise, the water cooks off and a bitter, smoky note balances the sweetness while the inside stays juicy and bright.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p37 to p38, the Pineapple Tarte Tatin card)

components.name: Setting with gelatin
components.explain:
Gelatin is made from collagen, the protein of skin and bone, usually from pigs, sometimes cattle or fish, dried into sheets or powder. Soaked, melted into a warm base and chilled, it sets a liquid into a gel that melts again at body temperature, which is why a jelly feels so clean in the mouth. Pastry kitchens grade sheets by strength and use as little as will hold the shape. Agar, from seaweed, and pectin, from fruit, set without any animal.

A jelly is a juice set this way; a Bavarian is a custard set and lightened with cream.

On the Lemon Tart the lemon jelly and the yuzu mousse are likely set with gelatin, and the guide says the Bavarian in The Snickers usually is. Gelatin is usually from pork, so a vegetarian guest, or one who avoids pork, needs the kitchen's answer, never a guess. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: Which desserts are likely set with gelatin, and what is it?
card.back: Collagen from skin and bone, usually pork, that sets a liquid and melts in the mouth. The Lemon Tart's jelly and mousse, and the Bavarian in The Snickers; the kitchen confirms each.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p36, the Snickers service note; p36 to p37, the Lemon Tart card)

components.name: Candying nuts
components.explain:
Candying a nut means cooking it in sugar until the sugar sets around it. Two finishes come from one pan. If the syrup is stirred as it cools, the sugar crystallises into a sandy, opaque coat, and the New Orleans praline is that finish taken further: pecans in brown sugar, butter and cream stirred until it sets into a soft, creamy patty. If the syrup is left alone until it caramelises, the nuts come out in a glassy, clear amber shell, the praline of the French pastry kitchen, which is crushed for crunch.

Toasting the nuts first matters more than anything: a raw nut inside candy tastes flat.

Both finishes are on our menus: the glassy candied hazelnuts on the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast and the pralines on the New Orleans Bread Pudding. Both go sticky in humid air, so they are made close to service. Nut questions go to the kitchen and the service note.

card.front: How do candied hazelnuts differ from pralines?
card.back: Same pan, two finishes: sugar left to caramelise gives the hazelnuts a glassy amber shell; sugar stirred as it cools crystallises into the soft, creamy New Orleans praline of pecans, butter and brown sugar.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p7, the duck's candied hazelnuts; p35, the pralines)
research/dossier-the-kitchen.md (Roasted Rohan Duck Breast cook's notes; New Orleans Bread Pudding)

components.name: Baking a bread pudding
components.explain:
Bread pudding is a baker's answer to yesterday's loaf. Day-old bread is torn or cubed and soaked in a sweet custard of eggs, milk or cream, sugar and vanilla until it has drunk it up, often with a little spice and dried fruit, then baked, sometimes in a water bath, until the custard sets soft inside and the top turns golden and crisp. Stale bread matters: fresh bread turns to paste, while a dry crumb holds its shape and stays tender. In New Orleans the airy local French loaf is the traditional bread, because its open crumb soaks custard without collapsing.

It is served warm, with a sauce poured over at the last moment.

On the New Orleans Bread Pudding the kitchen's version comes with a whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines. Which bread the kitchen bakes with, which whiskey goes into the caramel and whether raisins go into the pudding are questions for the chef.

card.front: Why does bread pudding want stale bread?
card.back: A dry crumb drinks the sweet custard and holds its shape in the oven; fresh bread turns to paste. New Orleans uses its airy French loaf. Which bread our kitchen uses is a question for the chef.

sources: guide.txt (pdf p35, the New Orleans Bread Pudding card)

components.name: Bread and toast
components.explain:
Bread is flour, water, salt and yeast, kneaded, left to rise and baked. Toast is sliced bread browned under a grill or in a toaster until the surface dries and the Maillard reaction turns it nutty and golden; the same browning crisps the buttered bread of a grilled cheese on the griddle and the custard-soaked slices of French toast in the pan.

On our menus bread is the children's toast, the sandwich bread of both grilled cheeses, the vanilla French toast, the housemade citrus brioche of the Framboise French Toast, the housemade English muffins of the Eggs Hussarde, the Leidenheimer crisps on the Creole Caesar, the bread pudding and the fruit and nut bread on the cheese board.

The menu does not say which loaf the toast or the grilled cheese is cut from, so a parent who asks gets the kitchen's answer. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: Where does bread appear on our menus?
card.back: As the children's toast and grilled cheeses, the vanilla and Framboise French toasts, the Hussarde's English muffins, Leidenheimer crisps on the Caesar, the bread pudding and the cheese board's fruit and nut bread. Which loaf: ask the kitchen.

components.name: Cheese
components.explain:
Cheese is milk set into curd with rennet or acid, drained of its whey, salted and then pressed or ripened. Fresh cheeses such as burrata and mascarpone are eaten young and soft; cheddar is pressed and aged for months; Grana Padano and Parmesan are aged until hard enough to grate. Young, moist cheeses melt smoothly, which is why a grilled cheese or a cheese sauce wants a young cheddar or a soft slice, while hard, aged ones season a dish more than they melt.

Our menus print a cheese by name on the Cheddar Grits, the Eggs Sardou, the Creole Caesar, the Shells & Cheese, the Shrimp & Grits, the tostada and the mascarpone mousse of the Framboise French Toast, and no name on the grilled cheeses, the buttered noodles, the children's salami and cheese starter, the Roost Burger and the cheese board. Where none is named, the kitchen tells us. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: Which cheese is in the grilled cheese or on the Roost Burger?
card.back: The menu names none, so the kitchen tells us. It does name cheddar on the grits, Parmesan on the Sardou, Grana Padano on the Caesar and the shells, Mimolette in the fondue and burrata on the tostada.

components.name: Onions
components.explain:
The onion is the bulb of Allium cepa, a plant grown for at least seven thousand years and thought to come from Central Asia. Raw, it is sharp and pungent; sliced thin it gives a burger bite and crunch; cooked slowly in fat its sugars soften and brown into sweetness, and simmered it melts into the base of a soup or a sauce. The sharpness lives in the cut cells, which is why a sliced onion is hotter than a whole one.

On our menus onions are printed on the Roost Burger, where they sit with the pickles against the tomato jam, and as the first third of the holy trinity, with celery and bell pepper, in the Creole sauce of the Shrimp & Grits and the South Louisiana Rice Dressing. The trinity, which has its own card, opens the gumbo and the turtle soup.

Whether the burger's onions are raw, pickled or cooked is not printed; the kitchen knows.

card.front: Where are onions on our menus?
card.back: Printed on the Roost Burger, against the pickles and the tomato jam, and as the first third of the holy trinity in the Creole sauce and the rice dressing; the trinity card covers the gumbo and the turtle soup.

components.name: Green beans
components.explain:
Green beans are the young pods of the common bean, Phaseolus vulgaris, picked while the seeds inside are still small and the pod is tender enough to eat whole. The bean came to the world's kitchens from Mexico and the Andes, and the thin French type is sold as haricots verts. Old varieties carried a tough string down the seam; the stringless pod was bred in the nineteenth century, so today they need only topping. Cooked briefly in salted water and then dressed with butter or finished in a hot pan, they stay bright green and keep a snap; cooked long they go soft and olive-coloured.

On our menus they are printed once, beside the potato with the children's sautéed Gulf fish on the children's dinner.

How the kitchen cooks them, plain, buttered or sautéed, is not printed, so ask the chef before promising a child a plain bean.

card.front: Where are green beans on our menus, and how are they cooked?
card.back: Once, beside the potato with the children's sautéed Gulf fish. Cooked briefly they stay bright and snap; whether ours are plain, buttered or sautéed is a question for the chef.

items: Sautéed Gulf Fish with Potato and Green Beans

components.name: Housemade pickles
components.explain:
A pickle is a vegetable preserved in brine or vinegar: the cucumber by default, but anything with crunch, okra, green beans, carrots, peppers, onions or green tomatoes, can go into the jar. A quick vinegar pickle is sharp within a day; a brine pickle ferments over weeks and turns sour and complex. Salt, sugar, dill, garlic and spice set the house style.

Fried pickles are a Southern bar classic that began in Arkansas: the first were sold in the summer of 1963 at a drive-in in Atkins, across the road from a pickle plant. Ours are a medley of housemade pickles, fried crisp, with a chive cream.

On our menus pickles are printed at the Roost on the Fried Pickles and on the Roost Burger, where they cut the rich short rib. Which vegetables are in tonight's medley, and whether the burger's pickle is the same, are not printed, so ask at lineup.

card.front: What is in the medley of housemade pickles?
card.back: The menu does not say: pickles the kitchen makes, fried crisp, with chive cream, and pickles again on the Roost Burger. Ask at lineup which vegetables are in tonight's medley.

components.name: Salami
components.explain:
Salami is the Italian family of cured sausages: pork, sometimes with beef, minced with salt, pepper, garlic and often wine, stuffed into a casing, fermented for a few days and then hung to dry for weeks or months. The salt and the drying are the preservation; the fermentation gives the gentle sourness, and the long hang the firm, sliceable texture. Genoa salami, named for the city in Liguria, is the mild, garlicky style of the deli counter.

On our menus salami is printed once, as the salami and cheese starter that opens every children's dinner, in place of the sliced fruit that opens the children's breakfast. It is a plate of cured meat and cheese that a child can eat while the grown-ups order.

Which salami and which cheese the kitchen sets out is not printed; ask at lineup before describing the plate to a parent. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: What opens the children's dinner?
card.back: A salami and cheese starter, cured Italian sausage with cheese, in place of the breakfast's sliced fruit; then the plate, a scoop of vanilla ice cream and a kid's drink. Which salami: ask at lineup.

Sautéed Gulf Fish with Potato and Green Beans

components.name: Sliced fresh fruit
components.explain:
Fresh fruit on a breakfast plate is the simplest course a kitchen sends: ripe fruit, peeled where it needs it and sliced, nothing cooked and nothing added. Fruit is at its sweetest in its own season, and a kitchen that cuts to order can change the plate from week to week.

On our menus sliced fresh fruit is printed as the first course of every children's breakfast, the course to send out as soon as the ticket is in, so the child is eating while the grown-ups order. It is the breakfast counterpart of the salami and cheese starter that opens the children's dinner.

The card does not say which fruit, so ask the kitchen what is cut today before you promise a child a strawberry. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: What opens the children's breakfast?
card.back: Sliced fresh fruit as the first course, so the child eats while the grown-ups order; then the plate, a scoop of vanilla ice cream and a kid's drink. Which fruit: ask the kitchen.

Vanilla French Toast with Fresh Berries and Whipped Cream

components.name: Short pastry, for pies and tarts
components.explain:
Short pastry is flour rubbed with cold fat, butter or lard, until it looks like coarse crumbs, then bound with just enough cold water to hold, rested and rolled thin. The fat coats the flour and keeps its proteins from forming long strands, which is what makes the crust short: tender and crumbly rather than chewy. The dough can be baked, or, for a hand pie, folded over a filling, crimped and fried.

The Louisiana meat pie is a half-moon of this kind of pastry around a savoury filling, traditionally fried, and the Roost's Crawfish Meat Pies print crawfish and a chive rémoulade, and nothing of the pastry. The sweet pastry crumb on the Lemon Tart is a sweet short dough, with sugar and egg, baked and broken up.

Whether our pies are fried or baked, and how the pastry is made, is not printed; ask the chef. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: What makes a pastry short?
card.back: Cold fat rubbed into flour before the water goes in, so the crust bakes tender and crumbly. It wraps the Crawfish Meat Pies; whether ours are fried or baked is a question for the chef.

components.name: Dredging, breading and batter
components.explain:
Fried food needs a coat, and kitchens use three. A dredge is a roll in seasoned flour or cornmeal, the thinnest crust, the usual coat for popcorn shrimp and fish. A standard breading goes flour, then beaten egg, then crumb, breadcrumb, cornmeal or panko, for a thicker, crunchier shell that clings to pickles and chicken. A batter is flour whisked with liquid, water, milk, buttermilk or beer, so the food is dipped wet and fries into a puffed, light crust. Every coat does the same job: it dries and browns in the oil while the food inside steams.

On our menus a coat goes on the popcorn shrimp at the Roost and on the children's breakfast, the children's fried Gulf shrimp, the Fried Pickles and the fried Cornish hen of the poussin.

Which coat the kitchen uses on each, and whether the fryers are shared, are questions for the kitchen every time.

card.front: What are the three coats for frying?
card.back: A dredge in seasoned flour or cornmeal, a breading of flour, egg and crumb, or a wet batter. Which coat goes on our popcorn shrimp, fried shrimp, pickles and hen is a kitchen question.

items: Fried Gulf Shrimp with French Fries

components.name: Toasting bread and nuts
components.explain:
Toasting is dry heat on something already baked or already edible: bread under a grill, nuts in a low oven or a dry pan. The surface loses water, its sugars and proteins brown in the Maillard reaction, and the flavour turns nutty, sweet and a little bitter at the edge. Nuts also release their oils as they warm, so a toasted nut tastes twice as strong as a raw one. Bread toasts in minutes; nuts take ten to fifteen in a moderate oven and burn a minute after they are done.

On our menus toast comes with the children's eggs and bacon; the Creole spiced nuts are roasted with their fat and spice until crisp; Leidenheimer crisps are toasted slices on the Creole Caesar; and roasted peanuts finish the Snickers.

If a guest wants toast light or dark, pass it to the kitchen. Dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

card.front: Why does toasting change the taste of bread and nuts?
card.back: Dry heat drives off water and browns sugars and proteins, the Maillard reaction, so the flavour turns nutty and sweet; nuts also release their oils. Toast, spiced nuts, Leidenheimer crisps and roasted peanuts.

items: Eggs Any Style with Toast and Bacon

entries.label: An American apple crisp
entries.same: Apple baked soft under an oat and brown sugar crumble with warm spice, served warm with something cool and creamy.
entries.different: Ours is one whole apple, not a dish of sliced fruit, with pecans and raisins in the crumble and sweetened crème fraîche beside it.

entries.label: Searing a steak hard
entries.same: Searing hard for a crust, finishing gently and resting is the classic method for a filet; the kitchen confirms its own.
entries.different: The technique is general; our plate adds a crisp potato rösti, garlic spinach and a 4 oz Côtes du Rhône pour on the breakfast tasting.

entries.label: A bistro steak frites
entries.same: Beef cooked to the guest’s temperature with crisp potato on the side.
entries.different: Ours is the tender filet, small enough for a tasting course, with a Swiss rösti instead of fries and garlic spinach.

entries.label: New Orleans BBQ shrimp
entries.same: The same buttery, peppery New Orleans barbecue pan sauce, never smoked and never tomato.
entries.different: Ours puts lobster in place of head-on shrimp and serves it over a white bean stew with ’nduja instead of with French bread.

entries.label: French magret, started in a cold pan
entries.same: A duck breast rendered skin-down slowly, then served rosy and sliced across the grain.
entries.different: Ours is a Rohan breast with cane syrup-glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts, a Louisiana take on duck with fruit.

entries.label: The English trifle
entries.same: Layers in a glass of fruit, a creamy set layer and cake, built so the colours show.
entries.different: Ours swaps custard for blackberry and lemon curds, sponge for almond financiers, and adds a coconut chia pudding; no sherry, no whipped cream.

entries.label: French pain perdu
entries.same: Bread soaked in egg and milk and fried in butter, the original French toast.
entries.different: Ours uses housemade citrus brioche with mascarpone mousse, raspberry coulis and local raspberries, sold as a starter to share.

entries.label: Café brûlot, the flaming coffee
entries.same: Coffee, citrus peel and warm spice, the flavours of New Orleans’ flaming after-dinner coffee.
entries.different: The drink is coffee flamed with brandy at the table; our cake bakes chicory coffee into chocolate cake, with the spice in a citrus glaze and no flame.

entries.label: Chargrilled oysters
entries.same: Gulf oysters cooked in a rich, buttery sauce, the New Orleans way of eating oysters hot.
entries.different: Chargrilled oysters cook on the half shell over flame with garlic butter and cheese; ours sit in BBQ sauce with pickled collards and saltine crumble.

entries.label: An Italian caprese
entries.same: Ripe raw tomatoes with fresh, milky cheese, a summer plate that depends on the tomato.
entries.different: Ours uses Creole tomatoes and creamy burrata on a crisp okra tostada, with smoked tomato water instead of olive oil and basil.

entries.label: Dungeness crab with drawn butter
entries.same: Sweet, cooked crab eaten with the fingers and dressed in warm butter.
entries.different: Ours are Louisiana blue crab claws warmed in a brown butter vinaigrette with fines herbes, with the pincer left on as a handle.

entries.label: Brown butter
entries.same: The vinaigrette starts as butter browned to a nutty hazelnut colour, as the technique teaches.
entries.different: We stop the brown butter with acid and shallot to make a warm vinaigrette, then finish it with fines herbes.

entries.label: Shucking oysters to order
entries.same: Oysters opened to order at the hinge, the muscle cut clean and the liquor kept in the shell.
entries.different: The technique is the method; ours are farmed Grand Isle Jewels served on ice with a preserved Fresno chilli mignonette.

entries.label: Oysters with classic mignonette
entries.same: Raw oysters with a vinegar, shallot and cracked pepper sauce spooned on by the guest.
entries.different: Our mignonette adds preserved Fresno chilli and parsley for a gentle, fruity warmth.

entries.label: Sicilian cannoli
entries.same: A crisp fried tube filled and eaten by hand in a couple of bites.
entries.different: The Sicilian cannoli is sweet pastry with ricotta; ours is a savoury potato shell piped with steak tartare, crème fraîche and cured egg yolk.

entries.label: Paris brasserie steak tartare
entries.same: Raw, hand-cut, seasoned beef with a rich egg element.
entries.different: The brasserie raw yolk becomes grated cured yolk, and the toast or fries become a crisp potato cannoli.

entries.label: Making a roux
entries.same: The soup is thickened and deepened by flour cooked in fat, as the technique teaches.
entries.different: Creole turtle soup is traditionally dark; ours is turtle meat with sherry, brown butter spinach and grated egg. How dark ours goes, ask the chef.

entries.label: English mock turtle soup
entries.same: A rich, dark, meaty soup in the old turtle soup tradition, often finished with sherry.
entries.different: Mock turtle uses no turtle at all, usually calf’s head or veal; ours prints 100% turtle meat.

entries.label: Chicken and andouille gumbo
entries.same: A roux gumbo built on the trinity with smoky andouille, served over rice; a reviewer called ours thick with dark roux.
entries.different: Ours is a seafood gumbo of shrimp, crab and oysters with andouille, over Louisiana popcorn rice, instead of chicken.

entries.label: The classic Caesar salad
entries.same: Crisp lettuce, an egg and lemon emulsion dressing, hard Italian cheese and toasted bread.
entries.different: Ours uses gem lettuce, a smoked oyster dressing in place of anchovy, Grana Padano and Leidenheimer crisps instead of croutons.

entries.label: Burgundy’s oeufs en meurette
entries.same: Poached eggs in a red wine sauce on toasted bread, rich and winey.
entries.different: Ours adds coffee-cured Canadian bacon, a housemade English muffin and hollandaise on top, so it carries two sauces.

entries.label: Eggs Benedict
entries.same: Poached eggs and Canadian bacon on an English muffin under hollandaise.
entries.different: The Hussarde adds marchand de vin, a red wine and mushroom sauce, under the egg, and our bacon is coffee-cured.

entries.label: Hollandaise
entries.same: Choron is built on the hollandaise method, a warm yolk and butter emulsion.
entries.different: Choron is béarnaise with tomato, sharper and herbal, where the classic Sardou uses plain hollandaise.

entries.label: Antoine’s Eggs Sardou
entries.same: Poached eggs with artichokes, named for the playwright Victorien Sardou.
entries.different: Antoine’s original had ham, anchovy and truffle and no spinach; ours has crispy artichokes, Parmesan creamed spinach and Choron.

entries.label: Pinot Noir braised short ribs
entries.same: Short rib braised slowly in red wine until it falls apart in a glossy sauce.
entries.different: Ours pulls the meat into débris and serves it as an egg dish with hollandaise, marchand de vin and a soft-boiled egg.

entries.label: Grillades and grits
entries.same: A New Orleans brunch of beef slow-cooked in a rich gravy, eaten in the morning.
entries.different: Grillades are braised beef medallions over grits; ours is short rib débris with a Creole-spiced potato and two classic sauces.

entries.label: Fried chicken and waffles
entries.same: Crisp poultry on a waffle with a sweet syrup, savoury and sweet together.
entries.different: Ours uses a confit Rohan duck leg on a cornbread and chive waffle, with foie gras butter, mustard maple syrup and an egg.

entries.label: Confit duck leg
entries.same: Duck leg salted and cooked slowly in duck fat, then crisped skin-side down.
entries.different: Ours is a Rohan leg served on a waffle for breakfast rather than with potatoes.

entries.label: Charleston shrimp and grits
entries.same: Shrimp over grits, a coastal breakfast dish of the South.
entries.different: Charleston uses a bacon pan gravy over soft grits; ours is a tomato Creole sauce with tasso over a fried pimento cheese grit cake.

entries.label: Trout amandine
entries.same: A pan-cooked fish finished with a nutty butter sauce.
entries.different: Ours uses the day’s Gulf fish with pecans instead of almonds, topped with lump crab, over cauliflower purée and collards.

entries.label: Sole meunière
entries.same: A fillet cooked in butter and finished with a browned butter sauce.
entries.different: Ours carries a pecan bordelaise and lump crab, with cauliflower purée and wilted collards.

entries.label: The French omelette
entries.same: Beaten eggs cooked quickly in butter around a warm filling.
entries.different: Ours is filled with lump crab and roasted corn and finished with miso butter, lemon, basil and a Marcona almond gremolata.

entries.label: Resting meat, slicing across the grain
entries.same: The hanger is rested and sliced across its loose grain, as the technique teaches.
entries.different: Our plate adds Creole spice, a smoked potato pavé, a Vital Farms egg and French béarnaise.

entries.label: French onglet with béarnaise
entries.same: Hanger steak cooked rare to medium-rare with a tarragon butter sauce.
entries.different: Ours is Creole-spiced Creekstone Prime, served at breakfast with a sunny-side-up egg and a smoked potato pavé.

entries.label: British Sunday roast beef
entries.same: A whole joint of beef roasted, rested and carved for the table to share.
entries.different: Ours is the lean centre-cut tenderloin for two with sauce Foyot and glazed summer squash, not a fattier roasting joint with gravy.

entries.label: Chateaubriand with béarnaise
entries.same: The thick centre cut of tenderloin, roasted for two, with a hollandaise family sauce.
entries.different: Our sauce is Foyot, béarnaise enriched with meat glaze, so it is deeper and more savoury.

entries.label: Sole meunière
entries.same: A delicate fish in a classic French butter sauce.
entries.different: Ours is redfish with a preserved lemon beurre blanc, hibiscus-pickled grapes, braised leeks and fingerlings.

entries.label: Escoffier’s Sole Véronique
entries.same: Fish with grapes in a butter-rich French sauce.
entries.different: Ours uses redfish for sole, a beurre blanc for the cream sauce, and hibiscus-pickled grapes for fresh muscat.

entries.label: Salmon en papillote
entries.same: Fish sealed in a parcel and baked so it steams in its own juices.
entries.different: Ours wraps Gulf fish in banana leaf, not paper, with crab, sorghum, Marcona almonds, Castelvetrano olives and tomato.

entries.label: Lapin à la moutarde
entries.same: A French bistro dish in a mustard cream sauce.
entries.different: The bistro dish braises rabbit in the sauce; ours fries a sweet tea-brined Cornish hen and sauces it, with turnips and shallots.

entries.label: Buttermilk fried chicken
entries.same: Brined poultry, coated and fried until the skin is crisp and the meat juicy.
entries.different: Ours brines in sweet tea, uses a whole small Cornish hen, and adds a French mustard cream sauce.

entries.label: Blackened redfish
entries.same: The same Louisiana blackening: a spice crust seared in a very hot cast-iron pan.
entries.different: Ours blackens local Tien Dat tofu and serves it over rice grits with preserved shiitakes.

entries.label: Steak with chimichurri
entries.same: A beefy steak finished with a raw parsley and garlic sauce.
entries.different: Ours is a Creole-spiced hanger with pepita persillade, chilli crisp and Madeira-glazed broccolini.

entries.label: Biscuits with sausage
entries.same: A Southern breakfast of seasoned fresh pork sausage.
entries.different: Ours is a housemade patty served on its own as a $9 side, without the biscuit.

entries.label: Rendering fat
entries.same: Thick bacon is cooked slowly so its fat renders and turns glassy before the edges burn.
entries.different: The technique is general; ours is a $9 breakfast side of thick-cut slices.

entries.label: Buttermilk biscuits
entries.same: A Southern quick bread of cold fat and buttermilk, baked hot for flaky layers.
entries.different: Ours is a single biscuit served as a $5 side for mopping up the egg dishes’ sauces.

entries.label: Poaching eggs
entries.same: One of the styles a guest can ask for, cooked out of the shell below a simmer.
entries.different: Ours is any style the guest asks for, as a $3 side.

entries.label: Grillades and grits
entries.same: Slow-cooked, creamy Southern grits served at breakfast.
entries.different: Ours are cheddar grits served as a $7 side rather than under braised beef.

entries.label: Pommes de terre sarladaises
entries.same: Potatoes fried golden and finished with garlic and parsley.
entries.different: Sarladaises are sliced and fried in duck fat; Brabant potatoes are cubed, fried and tossed in butter.

entries.label: Béchamel, the mother sauce
entries.same: Creamed spinach is often bound with a light béchamel or reduced cream.
entries.different: Ours is a side of spinach cooked down in cream, not the sauce on its own; whether it carries Parmesan is a kitchen question.

entries.label: Steakhouse creamed spinach
entries.same: Spinach bound with cream, the classic side beside steaks and eggs.
entries.different: Ours echoes the Parmesan creamed spinach under our Eggs Sardou; confirm with the kitchen whether it is the same preparation.

entries.label: Delaware succotash
entries.same: A succotash of sweet summer vegetables, the Native American dish the East Coast kept.
entries.different: Ours is glazed summer vegetables with Nueske’s applewood-smoked bacon, changing with the season.

entries.label: Brined whole roast cauliflower
entries.same: Cauliflower cooked until browned and deeply savoury, served as a dish in its own right.
entries.different: Ours is smoked rather than roasted whole, with preserved lemon and harissa.

entries.label: Harissa
entries.same: The same North African chilli paste that seasons our cauliflower.
entries.different: Here it is a component, with preserved lemon, on a smoked vegetable side.

entries.label: Baked mac and cheese
entries.same: Pasta folded into a rich cheese sauce, a comfort side.
entries.different: Ours uses shells in a Mimolette and Abita Amber beer fondue, finished with Grana Padano, not a baked cheddar sauce.

entries.label: Sautéing
entries.same: Mushrooms are most often cooked fast in a hot pan so they brown rather than stew.
entries.different: The kitchen’s preparation of tonight’s Maggie’s Mushrooms is learned at lineup.

entries.label: Dirty rice
entries.same: Rice cooked with seasoned ground meat and the holy trinity.
entries.different: Which of the two carries livers depends on who you ask; confirm the meats in our rice dressing with the kitchen.

entries.label: Bananas Foster
entries.same: Bananas in a butter, brown sugar and cinnamon caramel, flamed with rum over vanilla ice cream.
entries.different: Ours is the original, created by Brennan’s in 1951 on Bourbon Street, made at the table for at least two.

entries.label: Flambé
entries.same: The spirit is lit in the pan at the table, as the technique teaches.
entries.different: Our flambé follows the house’s seven safety steps, learned word for word.

entries.label: Flambé
entries.same: Spirit lit in the pan at the table for a burst of flame over the fruit.
entries.different: Our Cherries Jubilee is flamed with a Luxardo sauce over housemade vanilla ice cream.

entries.label: Escoffier’s cherries jubilee
entries.same: Cherries in a thickened syrup with spirit lit at the table.
entries.different: Escoffier lit kirsch and served no ice cream; ours uses a Luxardo sauce over vanilla ice cream.

entries.label: Peach and bourbon bread pudding
entries.same: Bread baked in sweet custard with a whiskey note.
entries.different: Ours has no peaches: it is New Orleans style with a whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines.

entries.label: Crème anglaise to the nappe
entries.same: A Bavarian cream begins as a stirred custard cooked until it coats the spoon.
entries.different: Ours sets the custard with gelatin and whipped cream and flavours it with milk chocolate.

entries.label: The Snickers candy bar
entries.same: Chocolate, caramel, nougat and peanuts.
entries.different: Ours is plated: milk chocolate Bavarian cream, caramel custard, nougat ice cream and roasted peanuts.

entries.label: Tarte au citron
entries.same: Sharp lemon, sweet pastry and, often, meringue.
entries.different: Ours is taken apart: yuzu mousse, lemon jelly, sweet pastry crumb and toasted meringue, lighter than a filled tart.

entries.label: Tarte Tatin
entries.same: Fruit caramelised in butter and sugar on crisp pastry.
entries.different: Ours uses charred pineapple on puff pastry with a sweetened condensed anglaise and whipped vanilla mousse, instead of apples.

compare.item: Eggs Any Style with Toast and Bacon

entries.label: Poaching eggs
entries.same: Poached is one of the styles a child can ask for.
entries.different: The children’s plate is eggs any style with toast and bacon, within the $25.00 set price.

entries.label: Calabash fried shrimp
entries.same: Small shrimp in a light coating, fried quickly until golden.
entries.different: Ours is a children’s breakfast plate of popcorn shrimp with Brabant potatoes.

compare.item: Vanilla French Toast with Fresh Berries and Whipped Cream

entries.label: French pain perdu
entries.same: Bread soaked in egg and milk and fried in butter.
entries.different: The children’s version is vanilla French toast with fresh berries and whipped cream.

compare.item: Grilled Cheese Sandwich with Brabant Potatoes

entries.label: A diner grilled cheese
entries.same: Buttered bread and melted cheese cooked golden in a pan.
entries.different: Ours comes with Brabant potatoes, within the children’s $25.00 breakfast price.

compare.item: Fried Gulf Shrimp with French Fries

entries.label: Calabash fried shrimp
entries.same: Shrimp in a light coating, fried golden.
entries.different: Ours is fried Gulf shrimp with French fries on the children’s dinner menu.

entries.label: Pasta al burro
entries.same: Pasta tossed with butter and grated cheese.
entries.different: Ours is the children’s dinner plate, within the $25.00 set price.

compare.item: Sautéed Gulf Fish with Potato and Green Beans

entries.label: Sole meunière
entries.same: A fish fillet sautéed in butter.
entries.different: The children’s plate is the day’s Gulf fish, sautéed, with potato and green beans and no rich sauce.

compare.item: Grilled Cheese Sandwich with French Fries

entries.label: A diner grilled cheese
entries.same: Buttered bread and melted cheese cooked golden in a pan.
entries.different: Ours comes with French fries, within the children’s $25.00 dinner price.

entries.label: Dry-pan toasting nuts
entries.same: Nuts toasted until fragrant and crisp.
entries.different: Ours are seasoned with Creole spice and served as a $6 bar snack.

entries.label: The Aussie meat pie
entries.same: Savoury filling in pastry, a pie eaten in the hand.
entries.different: Ours are crawfish hand pies in the Louisiana tradition, with chive rémoulade for dipping.

entries.label: The Natchitoches meat pie
entries.same: A Louisiana half-moon hand pie with a seasoned filling.
entries.different: Natchitoches pies are pork and beef; ours are filled with crawfish.

entries.label: Boardwalk vinegar fries
entries.same: Crisp, salty fries meant to be eaten with a drink.
entries.different: Ours come with a pink dipping sauce instead of vinegar.

entries.label: Full-sour dill pickles
entries.same: Sour, crunchy pickles, the base of the snack.
entries.different: Ours are a medley of housemade pickles, battered and fried, with chive cream.

entries.label: Calabash fried shrimp
entries.same: Small shrimp, lightly coated and fried golden.
entries.different: Ours are Louisiana shrimp with a Crystal hot sauce gastrique for dipping.

entries.label: A French cheese course
entries.same: A few contrasting cheeses at room temperature with bread.
entries.different: Ours adds a seasonal chutney, Brennan’s honey and fruit and nut bread, as a bar snack to share.

entries.label: The smash burger
entries.same: Two thin beef patties with cheese, pickles and onions, crusty from the griddle.
entries.different: Ours uses short rib patties with bacon, tomato jam and a special sauce.

entries.label: The Table's knife cuts: dice
entries.same: A brasserie tartare starts as a knife cut: cold, trimmed beef taken to a fine, even dice, the dice ladder the Table teaches.
entries.different: Ours is never cooked: the beef is dressed with Dijon, capers and yolk and served raw, and how the kitchen cuts it is the chef's answer.

entries.label: The Paris brasserie steak tartare
entries.same: Hand-cut raw beef with shallot, caper, mustard and yolk, served with something crisp on the side.
entries.different: Ours swaps toast for a rye tuile and adds Montreal seasoning, caraway and coriander among it, so the rye and the caraway echo a deli rye loaf.

entries.label: Sole meunière, the butter and lemon classic
entries.same: Butter cooked in the pan to hazelnut brown, stopped with lemon, finished with parsley and spooned over a fish.
entries.different: Grenobloise adds capers and croutons to the meunière formula; ours fries the capers, cuts the croutons from Leidenheimer bread and uses firm swordfish with leek fondue.

entries.label: A veal or chicken piccata
entries.same: Lemon, butter and capers spooned over the protein, a sharp, rich finish.
entries.different: Piccata deglazes with wine or stock into a pan sauce; Grenobloise is browned butter rather than a sauce, with croutons and parsley, and ours is on fish.

entries.label: Sauce Espagnole and demi-glace, the brown mother
entries.same: Brown stock thickened with a brown roux, with tomato and aromatic vegetables, simmered long and skimmed to a glossy, deep brown sauce.
entries.different: The recipe stops at the sauce and its demi-glace; our plate puts it under a twelve-ounce centre cut of tenderloin with butter-finished frascarelli.

entries.label: Chateaubriand with béarnaise, the bistro classic
entries.same: The thick centre cut of the tenderloin, seared, finished gently and rested, sliced and served with a rich sauce.
entries.different: Béarnaise is a butter and egg emulsion with tarragon; Espagnole is a stock and roux brown sauce, and ours comes with frascarelli, not potatoes.

entries.label: Ravioli del Plin, the pinched parcels
entries.same: A thin sheet of pasta folded over small portions of filling and pinched shut between them, the plin, then cut apart, boiled and dressed simply.
entries.different: Ours plates the parcels with pork, braised collards, ricotta and Parmesan and a lemon pangrattato crunch, a Southern setting the recipe does not have.

entries.label: A ricotta and spinach ravioli
entries.same: Fresh pasta sealed around a soft filling, with ricotta and a hard grated cheese, boiled and finished lightly so the filling leads.
entries.different: Ravioli are cut squares sealed by pressing; plin are pinched between fillings, smaller and thinner, and ours carry pork and collards rather than spinach.

entries.label: Daube Provençale, the classic braise
entries.same: Meat cooked slowly in wine with aromatics until spoon-tender, the braising liquid becoming the sauce.
entries.different: The classic is served from the pot; ours is lamb shank, wrapped in puff pastry and baked, with a spiced jus of star anise, orange and cinnamon.

entries.label: A meat pot pie
entries.same: Slow-cooked meat under a baked pastry crust, comfort for a cold night.
entries.different: A pot pie bakes a gravy and filling under a lid; ours wraps the braised lamb in puff pastry and serves a spiced jus with it.

entries.label: The Marseille bouillabaisse
entries.same: The flavours of the Marseille fish soup: fish, the bouillabaisse broth, and a garlic sauce beside it, rouille there and aioli here.
entries.different: The classic is a soup in two services, broth then fish, with rouille on croutons; ours is a plate, the broth made a sauce, with panisse and preserved lemon aioli.

entries.label: Le Grand Aïoli, the Provençal platter
entries.same: Provençal fish with a garlic aioli at the heart of the plate, the sauce doing as much work as the fish.
entries.different: The grand aïoli is poached fish and boiled vegetables around a bowl of aioli; ours is a terrine and a mousse with a bouillabaisse sauce, with panisse and confit fennel.

entries.label: A classic ceviche
entries.same: Raw fish with citrus, chilli, onion and coriander, served cold and at once, the heart of the fish still raw.
entries.different: A ceviche steeps the fish in lime a few minutes, edges turning milky; ours is tuna dressed at the last moment under a carrot and ginger aguachile.

entries.label: The Sinaloa shrimp aguachile
entries.same: Aguachile, chilli water: raw seafood under a chilli and citrus sauce with onion, eaten at once.
entries.different: The classic is shrimp in lime and fresh chilli; ours is tuna under a carrot and ginger version, with salsa seca, burnt orange and pickled pearl onions.

entries.label: Crème anglaise, stirred to the nappe
entries.same: Egg yolks, sugar and milk or cream stirred over gentle heat until the custard coats a spoon: the base every chocolate crémeux starts from.
entries.different: The crémeux pours that hot custard over chocolate, blends it to a glossy emulsion and chills it to a dense, set cream; ours is marked with gelatine.

entries.label: A chocolate pot de crème
entries.same: A rich, smooth, spoonable chocolate custard served cold, dense rather than airy, often finished with a little salt.
entries.different: A pot de crème is baked in a water bath and set by its eggs; a crémeux is stirred and set by its chocolate; ours adds nibs and lemon oil.
